headline: The great shrinking
description: Changing the arithmetic of everyday shopping, shrinkflation leaves consumers to pay more for what used to be enough
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
I have been watching my favourite chocolate biscuit shrink before my very eyes. It used to be a decent-sized biscuit, the sort you could look forward to dunking in a glass of milk. Now it is so small and thin that I sometimes wonder if I have picked up the wrong one. The biscuits in the packet seem to have lost weight, too, though my bill at the checkout shows no such signs of slimming down, and is consistently putting on weight.

It is not just biscuits. Chocolate bars have become thinner, crisp packets seem to contain more air than crisps, and even burgers seems to have joined the general retreat. Everything, it appears, is shrinking except the price tag.

You settle down with a bag of crisps in front of the TV to binge your favourite show, but it lasts only for half an episode. Your breakfast toast are burning more than toasting, because they have become Ozempic thin, your cereal box that lasted a month, now finishes in less than three weeks, the ketchup bottle is thinner, chicken breast fillets need less pounding because they are not as chunky as they used to be, almost everything you buy and use in the house is shrinking, either that, or you have become a giant!

Remember, the 1989 sci-fi comedy Honey, I Shrunk the Kids, in which a scientist accidentally shrinks his children with an experimental machine? There is no such machine at work in our supermarkets, but the results can sometimes seem just as startling. Biscuits, chocolate bars, crisps, detergent bags, soap bars, bakery items, restaurant portions, and other everyday products appear to be getting smaller, thinner and lighter, while their prices stubbornly refuse to follow suit. This is no science fiction, but an economic sleight of hand with a name: shrinkflation.

Through this disappearing act where you keep thinking, is it me, or has this really shrunk, manufacturers reduce the size, weight or quantity of a product while keeping its price the same, or lowering it by so little that the consumer still ends up paying more for less. It is a neat trick, particularly when the new, smaller version looks much like the old one on the supermarket shelf. You may not notice the difference immediately, but you will notice how quickly the packet empties.

The clever thing about shrinkflation is that it does not require a price hike to make consumers pay more. We have become accustomed to checking price tags, wincing at the increase and deciding whether a product is still worth buying. But how many of us check the weight of a packet of biscuits against the one we bought last month? Or count the number of crisps in a bag? We are more likely to notice a price increase than a reduction of a few grams, a thinner slice or a slightly smaller bar of soap.

Manufacturers know this. When production costs rise, reducing the quantity in a package can seem a safer option than raising its price outright. Consumers who might switch brands after a conspicuous price hike may continue buying a familiar product without realising that its value for money has changed. Brand loyalty, habit and the sheer inconvenience of comparing every item on a shopping list all work in the manufacturer's favour.

The packaging does not necessarily help. A familiar box or wrapper can create the impression that nothing has changed, even when the contents have. A packet may look much as it always has, while holding fewer pieces or a lower net weight. Unless shoppers examine the fine print, the change can pass unnoticed.

For Hassan Khan, a motorcycle rider from Yakatoot, Peshawar, the struggle to feed his family has become a daily calculation of what he can afford and what he must do without. Living in a rented house with his wife and two children, Khan says his earnings are barely enough to put two meals on the table. Yet the rising cost of living has brought another worry even when he pays more for essential household products. He believes he is getting less in return.

The price of a one-kilogramme formula milk his child drinks had risen from Rs1,000 to Rs1,500, while the quantity of milk inside appears to have decreased. “The carton is the same, but there is a world of difference in the quantity,” says Khan.

For Khan, the problem extends beyond milk to other everyday products, where prices have increased while their perceived quality or quantity has fallen. He said there is little visible relief for consumers despite the existence of price-control committees, leaving families like his to absorb the additional costs. Khan’s experience illustrates a concern increasingly relevant to household spending when prices rise, consumers may pay more for the same product, reduce the quantity they buy, or switch to cheaper alternatives.

The scale of the financial strain in Peshawar is reflected in a recent survey by the Institute of Regional Studies (IRS), which found that 89 per cent of households rely on borrowing to meet routine expenses, while 95.1 per cent struggle to repay their loans.

Presenting the findings, IRS Chairman Dr Muhammad Iqbal Khalil said the study covered 462 households in Peshawar and was based on focus group discussions and consultations with relevant stakeholders. The findings suggest that for many families, inflation is no longer simply a matter of higher market prices; it has become a debt problem.

According to the IRS survey, households reported an increase of 35 per cent to 40 per cent in the cost of living, with low-income communities bearing a particularly heavy burden. In these neighbourhoods, 48.7 per cent of families said they had been severely affected by inflation. Although 67.3 per cent of surveyed households reported an increase in income, their expenses had risen even faster, leaving them with less money for essential needs, Dr Khalil said while explaining the results.

National inflation figures offer a broader picture of the pressure on consumers. According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), consumer prices rose by 10.26 per cent year-on-year in September 2026, while the monthly rate increased by 1.27 per cent compared with August. The annual rate had eased from 11.1 per cent in August, but the September figures still showed that prices were rising rather than returning to earlier levels.

The IRS survey found that 93 per cent of households had experienced an increase in electricity, gas and fuel expenses, while 84.6 per cent reported higher transport costs. Dr Khalil said increases in petroleum prices had placed additional pressure on household budgets and restricted people's mobility. Because fuel is used in transporting goods and operating vehicles, changes in petroleum prices can also affect the cost of moving food and other necessities to markets, adding another layer of pressure for consumers.

Food remains one of the most difficult expenses to manage. According to the IRS survey, 86.4 per cent of households reported an increase in food expenditure, while some said they had been forced to switch to cheaper food items to keep spending within their means. For families with limited incomes, such adjustments can mean replacing preferred products with less expensive alternatives, buying smaller quantities or cutting back on certain items altogether. The survey findings show the extent of the reported financial pressure, although they do not establish how much each household has reduced its food intake.

A little less, for a little more

The practice is not new, but happening in other countries too. In the US, shrinkflation became a political issue in 2024, when President Joe Biden publicly criticised manufacturers for reducing quantities while maintaining prices. His administration also backed proposed legislation aimed at addressing deceptive pricing practices.

A 2025 report by the US Government Accountability Office, which examined household products between 2019 and 2024, found that downsizing contributed to inflation in several categories. Household paper products saw a three per cent-point contribution, snacks 2.6 per cent points, and candy and chewing gum 2.3 per cent points over the period.

The report also found that downsizing affected less than five per cent of the products examined across seven categories. That is an important qualification: shrinkflation is not necessarily happening to everything on the shelf. But it can be particularly noticeable in popular, frequently purchased products, where consumers are accustomed to buying the same item repeatedly. Every grocery list has bread, soap, detergent, butter, toilet rolls, tissue paper boxes, matches, biscuits, chicken and condiments, for instance and mostly that is where the shrinkage works for the manufacturer.

Paper products such as toilet paper and paper towels were among the categories more likely to be affected. Packaged foods, including cereals, coffee and snacks, have also featured in discussions about downsizing. The underlying calculation is simple enough. If a product costs the same but contains less, the price per unit of product rises, even though the price printed on the shelf does not.

Whose job is it to notice?

Consumers can protect themselves to some extent by comparing net weights, checking the number of pieces in a pack and looking at the price per 100 grams or kilogram where unit pricing is available. If a favourite product seems to run out faster than it used to, the label may offer an explanation. Keeping an old packet or taking a photograph of its weight can also help establish whether anything has changed.

But it is worth asking how much vigilance we can reasonably expect from people who are already trying to make a household budget stretch. Few shoppers have the time to inspect every label, memorise the previous weight of every product or calculate the unit price of each item in a trolley. Nor should consumers have to become amateur investigators to establish whether they are receiving the quantity they believe they are buying.

There are ways to make such changes more transparent. France, for instance, requires retailers to display information about product downsizing in stores, while Australia has considered measures to improve the consistency of unit-price labelling.

Due to the consistently increasing petroleum product prices and the continued pressure of inflation in our country, food items are becoming further out of reach of the common man, while complaints related to reductions in the quality, weight and quantity in packaging of goods are also increasing alongside price hikes.

Kainat Shahid, a housewife in Lahore, sees on a daily basis that prices are increasing. In addition, changes have also occurred in quality and weight. According to her, inflation has badly affected household budgets, and now more money has to be spent to buy the same quantity of goods as before.

Some consumers have complaints about reductions in the quantity of packaged products, possible differences in the weight of loose goods, and the quality of food. They say that if the quantity is reduced despite an increase in price, or if a product of the required quality is not available, the consumer has to bear a double loss.

An increase in petroleum product prices can raise the costs of freight, the transportation of agricultural produce and the delivery of goods to markets, with the possibility that these costs will be passed on to retail prices. However, to understand the reasons for price increases in different goods, it is necessary to examine production costs, wholesale rates, transportation expenses and profit margins separately.

Pakistan's consumers have little reason to expect that a scrutiny similar to that in the developed countries will arrive here automatically. In a market where shoppers already contend with rising prices and household budgets under pressure, quietly reducing quantities adds another layer of uncertainty. The question is not whether manufacturers can ever justify changing a product's size when costs rise. It is whether consumers should be left to discover those changes for themselves.

A smaller biscuit may seem a trivial matter. But when the same calculation is repeated across the weekly shopping basket, the difference is no longer confined to the tea break. And if the price remains unchanged, the shopper may never know quite how much less is being bought for the same money.

According to Ayub Mehar, a former adviser to the Economic Cooperation Organisation, when inflation increases, the cost for producers also increases, as a result of which they reduce the quantity of their products. To prevent this, the better solution is to formulate economic policies through which the cost of products does not increase in the first place. For this, the federal government can offer exemptions in various taxes, reduce the interest rate, and provide subsidies to producers under various heads.

Speaking to The Express Tribune, Mehar said that because there are various regulatory bodies in the country, companies cannot increase the prices of goods according to their own wishes. Therefore, when the cost of goods increases, they reduce the quality of their products. For example, in such a situation, some pharmaceutical companies do not reduce the quantity of their products but reduce their quality. Meanwhile, when pressure from government health regulatory bodies increases, those companies stop manufacturing certain medicines altogether.

According to Mehar, the most dangerous aspect of shrinkflation is that some companies reduce their services. For example, in the education sector, some schools close their cafeterias, while others reduce their use of air conditioning. Similarly, services are also reduced in the travel and hotel industries.

Meanwhile, the Consumer Rights Commission of Pakistan, is an independent, non-profit, and non-governmental organisation established in 1998 under the Trust Act, 1882. As the country's first national consumer organisation, it is dedicated to promoting consumer protection, market governance, and citizens' rights.

The Sindh Consumer Protection Act was passed in Sindh in 2014, but it makes no direct mention of “shrinkflation”. Section 21-A of the said law deals only with preventing “false or misleading” information. Under this provision, it is illegal to provide incorrect information regarding the quality, weight or quantity of any product.

In 2023, the Sindh government amended the said law and established consumer courts in the province, but ordinary people do not approach them. According to local lawyer Advocate Muhammad Ismail Memon Rajput, most people are not well informed about consumer rights. Even those who have some awareness are reluctant to approach consumer courts because of lengthy court proceedings. He said that he had not yet seen anyone come to a consumer court with a complaint related to “shrinkflation.”

According to Abdullah Malik, head of civil society, reducing the size of packaging is not, in itself, illegal in every case. However, the weight stated on the packet, the actual quantity and the price must be correct. Similarly, providing accurate weight when selling loose goods and checking food quality are basic requirements for consumer protection.

In Punjab, a legal system exists for monitoring the prices of essential commodities and preventing unjustified profiteering, while district administrations, relevant departments and food safety authorities are responsible for taking action within their respective jurisdictions. Despite this, the real question is how effective the results have been in enforcing official price lists, inspecting shops, verifying weights and taking action against substandard food. Merely issuing official price lists is not enough. It is also necessary to monitor their implementation and action against those who violate them.

Citizens have demanded that official price lists be displayed at prominent places in markets, that loose goods be weighed in front of consumers, and that the quantities of packaged products be checked regularly. Samples should be collected to assess the quality of milk, meat, ghee, cooking oil and other food products, and action should be taken on the basis of laboratory analysis. Alongside this, an easy system should also be provided for registering complaints about price violations, underweight goods and poor quality, and for resolving those complaints.

According to economist and Dean of Punjab University’s Hailey College, Dr Hafiz Zafar Ahmed, monitoring weight and quality alongside prices also becomes important so that consumers can obtain goods of the required quantity and appropriate quality for the amount they pay.

He said that a situation of uncertainty has increased because industries are facing daily increases in the cost of raw materials. As a result, industries are now caught in a dilemma, as the prices of the raw materials they purchase keep increasing.

There is a need for federal and provincial governments to regularly publish comparative data on the prices of essential commodities and for district administrations to transparently make public the results of price-control operations, fines, weight violations and food-quality checks. Only through effective monitoring and the uniform enforcement of the law can efforts to prevent unjustified profiteering and provide relief to ordinary consumers be made effective.

Dr Ahmed believes that the government should establish an organised system to control consumer prices, particularly grocery prices, so that the common man can be protected from inflation.

When asked about complaints concerning quantity, quality and measurements, officials from the K-P Food Safety and Halal Food Authority and the district administration shared that they conduct regular raids and take action against shopkeepers and other traders found violating standards or compromising on measurements, quality and quantity.

Yet enforcement against such violations does not necessarily address the less obvious problem of products that shrink while their prices remain unchanged. When the packet gets smaller but the bill does not, consumers are left paying more for less — one shopping trip at a time.

content_blocks.text: The clever thing about shrinkflation is that it does not require a price hike to make consumers pay more. We have become accustomed to checking price tags, wincing at the increase and deciding whether a product is still worth buying. But how many of us check the weight of a packet of biscuits against the one we bought last month? Or count the number of crisps in a bag? We are more likely to notice a price increase than a reduction of a few grams, a thinner slice or a slightly smaller bar of soap.

I have been watching my favourite chocolate biscuit shrink before my very eyes. It used to be a decent-sized biscuit, the sort you could look forward to dunking in a glass of milk. Now it is so small and thin that I sometimes wonder if I have picked up the wrong one. The biscuits in the packet seem to have lost weight, too, though my bill at the checkout shows no such signs of slimming down, and is consistently putting on weight.

It is not just biscuits. Chocolate bars have become thinner, crisp packets seem to contain more air than crisps, and even burgers seems to have joined the general retreat. Everything, it appears, is shrinking except the price tag.

You settle down with a bag of crisps in front of the TV to binge your favourite show, but it lasts only for half an episode. Your breakfast toast are burning more than toasting, because they have become Ozempic thin, your cereal box that lasted a month, now finishes in less than three weeks, the ketchup bottle is thinner, chicken breast fillets need less pounding because they are not as chunky as they used to be, almost everything you buy and use in the house is shrinking, either that, or you have become a giant!

Remember, the 1989 sci-fi comedy Honey, I Shrunk the Kids, in which a scientist accidentally shrinks his children with an experimental machine? There is no such machine at work in our supermarkets, but the results can sometimes seem just as startling. Biscuits, chocolate bars, crisps, detergent bags, soap bars, bakery items, restaurant portions, and other everyday products appear to be getting smaller, thinner and lighter, while their prices stubbornly refuse to follow suit. This is no science fiction, but an economic sleight of hand with a name: shrinkflation.

Through this disappearing act where you keep thinking, is it me, or has this really shrunk, manufacturers reduce the size, weight or quantity of a product while keeping its price the same, or lowering it by so little that the consumer still ends up paying more for less. It is a neat trick, particularly when the new, smaller version looks much like the old one on the supermarket shelf. You may not notice the difference immediately, but you will notice how quickly the packet empties.

The clever thing about shrinkflation is that it does not require a price hike to make consumers pay more. We have become accustomed to checking price tags, wincing at the increase and deciding whether a product is still worth buying. But how many of us check the weight of a packet of biscuits against the one we bought last month? Or count the number of crisps in a bag? We are more likely to notice a price increase than a reduction of a few grams, a thinner slice or a slightly smaller bar of soap.

Manufacturers know this. When production costs rise, reducing the quantity in a package can seem a safer option than raising its price outright. Consumers who might switch brands after a conspicuous price hike may continue buying a familiar product without realising that its value for money has changed. Brand loyalty, habit and the sheer inconvenience of comparing every item on a shopping list all work in the manufacturer's favour.

The packaging does not necessarily help. A familiar box or wrapper can create the impression that nothing has changed, even when the contents have. A packet may look much as it always has, while holding fewer pieces or a lower net weight. Unless shoppers examine the fine print, the change can pass unnoticed.

For Hassan Khan, a motorcycle rider from Yakatoot, Peshawar, the struggle to feed his family has become a daily calculation of what he can afford and what he must do without. Living in a rented house with his wife and two children, Khan says his earnings are barely enough to put two meals on the table. Yet the rising cost of living has brought another worry even when he pays more for essential household products. He believes he is getting less in return.

The price of a one-kilogramme formula milk his child drinks had risen from Rs1,000 to Rs1,500, while the quantity of milk inside appears to have decreased. “The carton is the same, but there is a world of difference in the quantity,” says Khan.

For Khan, the problem extends beyond milk to other everyday products, where prices have increased while their perceived quality or quantity has fallen. He said there is little visible relief for consumers despite the existence of price-control committees, leaving families like his to absorb the additional costs. Khan’s experience illustrates a concern increasingly relevant to household spending when prices rise, consumers may pay more for the same product, reduce the quantity they buy, or switch to cheaper alternatives.

The scale of the financial strain in Peshawar is reflected in a recent survey by the Institute of Regional Studies (IRS), which found that 89 per cent of households rely on borrowing to meet routine expenses, while 95.1 per cent struggle to repay their loans.

Presenting the findings, IRS Chairman Dr Muhammad Iqbal Khalil said the study covered 462 households in Peshawar and was based on focus group discussions and consultations with relevant stakeholders. The findings suggest that for many families, inflation is no longer simply a matter of higher market prices; it has become a debt problem.

According to the IRS survey, households reported an increase of 35 per cent to 40 per cent in the cost of living, with low-income communities bearing a particularly heavy burden. In these neighbourhoods, 48.7 per cent of families said they had been severely affected by inflation. According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), consumer prices rose by 10.26 per cent year-on-year in September 2026, while the monthly rate increased by 1.27 per cent compared with August. The annual rate had eased from 11.1 per cent in August, but the September figures still showed that prices were rising rather than returning to earlier levels.

The IRS survey found that 93 per cent of households had experienced an increase in electricity, gas and fuel expenses, while 84.6 per cent reported higher transport costs. Dr Khalil said increases in petroleum prices had placed additional pressure on household budgets and restricted people's mobility. Because fuel is used in transporting goods and operating vehicles, changes in petroleum prices can also affect the cost of moving food and other necessities to markets, adding another layer of pressure for consumers.

Food remains one of the most difficult expenses to manage. According to the IRS survey, 86.4 per cent of households reported an increase in food expenditure, while some said they had been forced to switch to cheaper food items to keep spending within their means. For families with limited incomes, such adjustments can mean replacing preferred products with less expensive alternatives, buying smaller quantities or cutting back on certain items altogether. The survey findings show the extent of the reported financial pressure, although they do not establish how much each household has reduced its food intake.

A little less, for a little more

The practice is not new, but happening in other countries too. In the US, shrinkflation became a political issue in 2024, when President Joe Biden publicly criticised manufacturers for reducing quantities while maintaining prices. His administration also backed proposed legislation aimed at addressing deceptive pricing practices.

A 2025 report by the US Government Accountability Office, which examined household products between 2019 and 2024, found that downsizing contributed to inflation in several categories. Household paper products saw a three per cent-point contribution, snacks 2.6 per cent points, and candy and chewing gum 2.3 per cent points over the period.

The report also found that downsizing affected less than five per cent of the products examined across seven categories. That is an important qualification: shrinkflation is not necessarily happening to everything on the shelf. But it can be particularly noticeable in popular, frequently purchased products, where consumers are accustomed to buying the same item repeatedly. Every grocery list has bread, soap, detergent, butter, toilet rolls, tissue paper boxes, matches, biscuits, chicken and condiments, for instance and mostly that is where the shrinkage works for the manufacturer.

Paper products such as toilet paper and paper towels were among the categories more likely to be affected. Packaged foods, including cereals, coffee and snacks, have also featured in discussions about downsizing. The underlying calculation is simple enough. If a product costs the same but contains less, the price per unit of product rises, even though the price printed on the shelf does not.

Whose job is it to notice?

Consumers can protect themselves to some extent by comparing net weights, checking the number of pieces in a pack and looking at the price per 100 grams or kilogram where unit pricing is available. If a favourite product seems to run out faster than it used to, the label may offer an explanation. Keeping an old packet or taking a photograph of its weight can also help establish whether anything has changed.

But it is worth asking how much vigilance we can reasonably expect from people who are already trying to make a household budget stretch. Few shoppers have the time to inspect every label, memorise the previous weight of every product or calculate the unit price of each item in a trolley. Nor should consumers have to become amateur investigators to establish whether they are receiving the quantity they believe they are buying.

There are ways to make such changes more transparent. France, for instance, requires retailers to display information about product downsizing in stores, while Australia has considered measures to improve the consistency of unit-price labelling.

Due to the consistently increasing petroleum product prices and the continued pressure of inflation in our country, food items are becoming further out of reach of the common man, while complaints related to reductions in the quality, weight and quantity in packaging of goods are also increasing alongside price hikes.

Kainat Shahid, a housewife in Lahore, sees on a daily basis that prices are increasing. In addition, changes have also occurred in quality and weight. According to her, inflation has badly affected household budgets, and now more money has to be spent to buy the same quantity of goods as before.

Some consumers have complaints about reductions in the quantity of packaged products, possible differences in the weight of loose goods, and the quality of food. They say that if the quantity is reduced despite an increase in price, or if a product of the required quality is not available, the consumer has to bear a double loss.

An increase in petroleum product prices can raise the costs of freight, the transportation of agricultural produce and the delivery of goods to markets, with the possibility that these costs will be passed on to retail prices. However, to understand the reasons for price increases in different goods, it is necessary to examine production costs, wholesale rates, transportation expenses and profit margins separately.

Pakistan's consumers have little reason to expect that a scrutiny similar to that in the developed countries will arrive here automatically. In a market where shoppers already contend with rising prices and household budgets under pressure, quietly reducing quantities adds another layer of uncertainty. The question is not whether manufacturers can ever justify changing a product's size when costs rise. It is whether consumers should be left to discover those changes for themselves.

A smaller biscuit may seem a trivial matter. But when the same calculation is repeated across the weekly shopping basket, the difference is no longer confined to the tea break. And if the price remains unchanged, the shopper may never know quite how much less is being bought for the same money.

According to Ayub Mehar, a former adviser to the Economic Cooperation Organisation, when inflation increases, the cost for producers also increases, as a result of which they reduce the quantity of their products. To prevent this, the better solution is to formulate economic policies through which the cost of products does not increase in the first place. For this, the federal government can offer exemptions in various taxes, reduce the interest rate, and provide subsidies to producers under various heads.

Speaking to The Express Tribune, Mehar said that because there are various regulatory bodies in the country, companies cannot increase the prices of goods according to their own wishes. Therefore, when the cost of goods increases, they reduce the quality of their products. For example, in such a situation, some pharmaceutical companies do not reduce the quantity of their products but reduce their quality. Meanwhile, when pressure from government health regulatory bodies increases, those companies stop manufacturing certain medicines altogether.

According to Mehar, the most dangerous aspect of shrinkflation is that some companies reduce their services. For example, in the education sector, some schools close their cafeterias, while others reduce their use of air conditioning. Similarly, services are also reduced in the travel and hotel industries.

Meanwhile, the Consumer Rights Commission of Pakistan, is an independent, non-profit, and non-governmental organisation established in 1998 under the Trust Act, 1882. As the country's first national consumer organisation, it is dedicated to promoting consumer protection, market governance, and citizens' rights.

The Sindh Consumer Protection Act was passed in Sindh in 2014, but it makes no direct mention of “shrinkflation”. Section 21-A of the said law deals only with preventing “false or misleading” information. Under this provision, it is illegal to provide incorrect information regarding the quality, weight or quantity of any product.

In 2023, the Sindh government amended the said law and established consumer courts in the province, but ordinary people do not approach them. According to local lawyer Advocate Muhammad Ismail Memon Rajput, most people are not well informed about consumer rights. Even those who have some awareness are reluctant to approach consumer courts because of lengthy court proceedings. He said that he had not yet seen anyone come to a consumer court with a complaint related to “shrinkflation.”

According to Abdullah Malik, head of civil society, reducing the size of packaging is not, in itself, illegal in every case. However, the weight stated on the packet, the actual quantity and the price must be correct. Similarly, providing accurate weight when selling loose goods and checking food quality are basic requirements for consumer protection.

In Punjab, a legal system exists for monitoring the prices of essential commodities and preventing unjustified profiteering, while district administrations, relevant departments and food safety authorities are responsible for taking action within their respective jurisdictions. Despite this, the real question is how effective the results have been in enforcing official price lists, inspecting shops, verifying weights and taking action against substandard food. Merely issuing official price lists is not enough. It is also necessary to monitor their implementation and action against those who violate them.

Citizens have demanded that official price lists be displayed at prominent places in markets, that loose goods be weighed in front of consumers, and that the quantities of packaged products be checked regularly. Samples should be collected to assess the quality of milk, meat, ghee, cooking oil and other food products, and action should be taken on the basis of laboratory analysis. Alongside this, an easy system should also be provided for registering complaints about price violations, underweight goods and poor quality, and for resolving those complaints.

According to economist and Dean of Punjab University’s Hailey College, Dr Hafiz Zafar Ahmed, monitoring weight and quality alongside prices also becomes important so that consumers can obtain goods of the required quantity and appropriate quality for the amount they pay.

He said that a situation of uncertainty has increased because industries are facing daily increases in the cost of raw materials. As a result, industries are now caught in a dilemma, as the prices of the raw materials they purchase keep increasing.

There is a need for federal and provincial governments to regularly publish comparative data on the prices of essential commodities and for district administrations to transparently make public the results of price-control operations, fines, weight violations and food-quality checks. Only through effective monitoring and the uniform enforcement of the law can efforts to prevent unjustified profiteering and provide relief to ordinary consumers be made effective.

Dr Ahmed believes that the government should establish an organised system to control consumer prices, particularly grocery prices, so that the common man can be protected from inflation.

When asked about complaints concerning quantity, quality and measurements, officials from the K-P Food Safety and Halal Food Authority and the district administration shared that they conduct regular raids and take action against shopkeepers and other traders found violating standards or compromising on measurements, quality and quantity.

Yet enforcement against such violations does not necessarily address the less obvious problem of products that shrink while their prices remain unchanged. When the packet gets smaller but the bill does not, consumers are left paying more for less — one shopping trip at a time.

Keeping an old packet or taking a photograph of its weight can also help establish whether anything has changed.

But it is worth asking how much vigilance we can reasonably expect from people who are already trying to make a household budget stretch. Few shoppers have the time to inspect every label, memorise the previous weight of every product or calculate the unit price of each item in a trolley. Nor should consumers have to become amateur investigators to establish whether they are receiving the quantity they believe they are buying.

There are ways to make such changes more transparent. France, for instance, requires retailers to display information about product downsizing in stores, while Australia has considered measures to improve the consistency of unit-price labelling.

Due to the consistently increasing petroleum product prices and the continued pressure of inflation in our country, food items are becoming further out of reach of the common man, while complaints related to reductions in the quality, weight and quantity in packaging of goods are also increasing alongside price hikes.

Kainat Shahid, a housewife in Lahore, sees on a daily basis that prices are increasing. In addition, changes have also occurred in quality and weight. According to her, inflation has badly affected household budgets, and now more money has to be spent to buy the same quantity of goods as before.

Some consumers have complaints about reductions in the quantity of packaged products, possible differences in the weight of loose goods, and the quality of food. They say that if the quantity is reduced despite an increase in price, or if a product of the required quality is not available, the consumer has to bear a double loss.

An increase in petroleum product prices can raise the costs of freight, the transportation of agricultural produce and the delivery of goods to markets, with the possibility that these costs will be passed on to retail prices. However, to understand the reasons for price increases in different goods, it is necessary to examine production costs, wholesale rates, transportation expenses and profit margins separately.

Pakistan's consumers have little reason to expect that a scrutiny similar to that in the developed countries will arrive here automatically. In a market where shoppers already contend with rising prices and household budgets under pressure, quietly reducing quantities adds another layer of uncertainty. The question is not whether manufacturers can ever justify changing a product's size when costs rise. It is whether consumers should be left to discover those changes for themselves.

A smaller biscuit may seem a trivial matter. But when the same calculation is repeated across the weekly shopping basket, the difference is no longer confined to the tea break. And if the price remains unchanged, the shopper may never know quite how much less is being bought for the same money.

According to Ayub Mehar, a former adviser to the Economic Cooperation Organisation, when inflation increases, the cost for producers also increases, as a result of which they reduce the quantity of their products. To prevent this, the better solution is to formulate economic policies through which the cost of products does not increase in the first place. For this, the federal government can offer exemptions in various taxes, reduce the interest rate, and provide subsidies to producers under various heads.

Speaking to The Express Tribune, Mehar said that because there are various regulatory bodies in the country, companies cannot increase the prices of goods according to their own wishes. Therefore, when the cost of goods increases, they reduce the quality of their products. For example, in such a situation, some pharmaceutical companies do not reduce the quantity of their products but reduce their quality. Meanwhile, when pressure from government health regulatory bodies increases, those companies stop manufacturing certain medicines altogether.

According to Mehar, the most dangerous aspect of shrinkflation is that some companies reduce their services. For example, in the education sector, some schools close their cafeterias, while others reduce their use of air conditioning. Similarly, services are also reduced in the travel and hotel industries.

Meanwhile, the Consumer Rights Commission of Pakistan, is an independent, non-profit, and non-governmental organisation established in 1998 under the Trust Act, 1882. As the country's first national consumer organisation, it is dedicated to promoting consumer protection, market governance, and citizens' rights.

The Sindh Consumer Protection Act was passed in Sindh in 2014, but it makes no direct mention of “shrinkflation”. Section 21-A of the said law deals only with preventing “false or misleading” information. Under this provision, it is illegal to provide incorrect information regarding the quality, weight or quantity of any product.

In 2023, the Sindh government amended the said law and established consumer courts in the province, but ordinary people do not approach them. According to local lawyer Advocate Muhammad Ismail Memon Rajput, most people are not well informed about consumer rights. Even those who have some awareness are reluctant to approach consumer courts because of lengthy court proceedings. He said that he had not yet seen anyone come to a consumer court with a complaint related to “shrinkflation.”

According to Abdullah Malik, head of civil society, reducing the size of packaging is not, in itself, illegal in every case. However, the weight stated on the packet, the actual quantity and the price must be correct. Similarly, providing accurate weight when selling loose goods and checking food quality are basic requirements for consumer protection.

In Punjab, a legal system exists for monitoring the prices of essential commodities and preventing unjustified profiteering, while district administrations, relevant departments and food safety authorities are responsible for taking action within their respective jurisdictions. Despite this, the real question is how effective the results have been in enforcing official price lists, inspecting shops, verifying weights and taking action against substandard food. Merely issuing official price lists is not enough. It is also necessary to monitor their implementation and action against those who violate them.

Citizens have demanded that official price lists be displayed at prominent places in markets, that loose goods be weighed in front of consumers, and that the quantities of packaged products be checked regularly. Samples should be collected to assess the quality of milk, meat, ghee, cooking oil and other food products, and action should be taken on the basis of laboratory analysis. Alongside this, an easy system should also be provided for registering complaints about price violations, underweight goods and poor quality, and for resolving those complaints.

According to economist and Dean of Punjab University’s Hailey College, Dr Hafiz Zafar Ahmed, monitoring weight and quality alongside prices also becomes important so that consumers can obtain goods of the required quantity and appropriate quality for the amount they pay.

He said that a situation of uncertainty has increased because industries are facing daily increases in the cost of raw materials. As a result, industries are now caught in a dilemma, as the prices of the raw materials they purchase keep increasing.

There is a need for federal and provincial governments to regularly publish comparative data on the prices of essential commodities and for district administrations to transparently make public the results of price-control operations, fines, weight violations and food-quality checks. Only through effective monitoring and the uniform enforcement of the law can efforts to prevent unjustified profiteering and provide relief to ordinary consumers be made effective.
Dr Ahmed believes that the government should establish an organised system to control consumer prices, particularly grocery prices, so that the common man can be protected from inflation.

When asked about complaints concerning quantity, quality and measurements, officials from the K-P Food Safety and Halal Food Authority and the district administration shared that they conduct regular raids and take action against shopkeepers and other traders found violating standards or compromising on measurements, quality and quantity.

Yet enforcement against such violations does not necessarily address the less obvious problem of products that shrink while their prices remain unchanged. When the packet gets smaller but the bill does not, consumers are left paying more for less — one shopping trip at a time.

headline: The vanishing wings
description: Migratory birds disappear along the Kabul and Indus rivers as wetlands shrink, climate pressures mount
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
There was a time when the winter skies over Nowshera came alive with thousands of migratory birds, their flocks stretching across the horizon as they descended on wetlands, ponds and green fields after travelling thousands of kilometres from Siberia and Central Asia. For villagers living along the Kabul River, the arrival of these seasonal visitors was more than a spectacle. It was a cherished sign of winter, a familiar rhythm of life passed down through generations.

Today, many of those wetlands have disappeared beneath concrete houses, agricultural expansion and human settlements. The skies that once echoed with the calls of migratory birds have grown increasingly silent.

Climate change, shrinking wetlands, polluted rivers, excessive hunting and the destruction of natural habitats are threatening migratory birds visiting Pakistan, particularly Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), where the Kabul and Indus rivers have historically provided important wintering and feeding grounds.

For Faqir Khan, a resident of Taro Jabba near the Kabul River in Nowshera, the disappearance of these birds is a painful reminder of how dramatically the landscape has changed. "I still remember the days when huge flocks of birds arrived from Siberia, Afghanistan and other regions. There were large ponds, green fields and natural wetlands that stretched across the area. Watching hundreds of birds take flight together was a beautiful sight," he told The Express Tribune. "Today, houses stand where those ponds once existed. The birds no longer find the natural environment they need, and gradually they have stopped coming."

Khan’s memories reflect a wider environmental transformation taking place across parts of K-P, where expanding settlements, deteriorating water quality and changing weather patterns are placing increasing pressure on wildlife.

Migration under threat

Pakistan lies along the Central Asian Flyway, one of the world's major migratory bird routes, connecting breeding grounds in northern Eurasia with wintering areas across South Asia and beyond.

The flyway supports more than 180 migratory waterbird species, according to international conservation assessments, highlighting the ecological importance of wetlands across the region. Every year, migratory ducks, geese, waders, herons and birds of prey travel long distances in search of warmer conditions, food and suitable resting grounds.

The Kabul River, its associated wetlands and the Indus River system have traditionally offered important feeding and wintering habitats for several migratory species. However, environmental experts say these natural stopover sites are increasingly coming under pressure, threatening the habitats on which birds depend to complete their seasonal journeys.

Professor Dr Muhammad Nafees, an environmental expert associated with the University of Peshawar, told The Express Tribune that a study conducted in 2004 examined migratory bird populations along the Kabul and Indus river corridors. According to him, the study had already identified a decline of approximately 40 to 45 per cent in migratory bird numbers at the time.

"Today, the decline in migratory bird populations in K-P has exceeded 90 per cent compared with earlier levels," Dr Nafees claimed. The figure represents the expert's assessment and requires confirmation through updated, province-wide scientific surveys.

Polluted river water, shrinking habitats, changing temperatures and indiscriminate hunting are major factors behind the decline. Dr Nafees raised concerns about the possible impact of electromagnetic fields associated with communication towers on bird navigation, suggesting that such disturbances could contribute to birds losing their routes and becoming vulnerable to hunting. However, the extent to which telecommunications infrastructure affects long-distance bird migration remains scientifically uncertain and requires species-specific research.

Dr Nafees added that pesticide use in agricultural fields also posed a threat to birds feeding on insects, seeds and other food sources. "Exposure to harmful chemicals through contaminated food and water could affect their health and survival," he informed.

He further pointed to pollution in the Kabul River, reduced water availability in parts of the Indus system and changing seasonal temperatures as additional pressures on migratory birds.

"These birds need a safe environment, clean water and adequate food. When these conditions disappear, their survival and seasonal return become increasingly difficult," he explained.

Climate pressures

Dr Asif Khan, a climate change expert associated with a private university, identified the disappearance of marshes and wetlands, declining fish populations, reduced river flows, deforestation and excessive hunting as major reasons behind the decreasing arrival of migratory birds.

He added that rising temperatures and climate-induced changes in river flows were further damaging the natural habitats on which migratory birds depend.

According to Dr Khan, scientific research by universities and environmental institutions is urgently needed to understand changing migration patterns and develop long-term conservation strategies.

He stressed that without systematic research and monitoring, the region will struggle to address the growing challenges facing migratory wildlife.

Manahil Wahab, Divisional Wildlife Officer, Peshawar, said climate change had emerged as a significant environmental challenge affecting migratory birds and their habitats worldwide.

"The Kabul River and its associated wetlands provide important feeding, resting and wintering habitats for migratory waterbirds and birds of prey," she said.

According to Wahab, changes in temperature, rainfall patterns and water availability can influence seasonal bird movements, feeding opportunities and the duration of their stay.

She emphasised the importance of protecting natural habitats, improving aquatic ecosystems, raising public awareness and strengthening coordination among relevant institutions.

Conservation specialists say wetlands are particularly important because they provide food, shelter and resting places for birds exhausted after long-distance journeys. When these areas disappear, birds may be forced to travel farther in search of suitable conditions, increasing the energy required to complete their migration.

Muhammad Ismail, an ecologist associated with the Ministry of Climate Change, said migratory birds traditionally travelled from Siberia and other colder regions towards Pakistan, Afghanistan and India as temperatures dropped in their breeding areas. He said many birds historically arrived in the region between September and November, seeking relatively warmer climates and suitable feeding grounds. However, climate change and habitat destruction have increasingly affected the conditions that once attracted these birds.

"Many of the areas where migratory birds once found natural habitats have now been occupied by housing societies and other developments. Pollution has further damaged the environment," he explains.

Ismail noted that these changes were contributing to declining bird arrivals and potentially altering traditional migration routes. He warned that the destruction of wetlands and natural ecosystems could make it increasingly difficult for migratory birds to find suitable wintering grounds.

Disappearing habitats

Beyond rising temperatures and habitat loss, agricultural chemicals are emerging as another concern.

Migratory birds often feed in agricultural fields, consuming insects, seeds and other organisms. Excessive or improper pesticide use can contaminate these food sources, exposing birds to potentially harmful substances. Environmental experts warn that such exposure can affect birds directly or through the food chain. Similarly, untreated domestic sewage, industrial discharge and other pollutants entering rivers can damage aquatic ecosystems, reducing the availability of fish, insects and aquatic plants on which many species depend.

The conversion of wetlands into residential settlements is also reducing the number of safe resting places available to birds during their long journeys.

The decline of migratory birds is not merely a loss of seasonal beauty. It also raises questions about the health of rivers, wetlands and the wider environment.

Migratory birds are important indicators of ecosystem conditions. Changes in their numbers and distribution can provide valuable clues about habitat degradation, water availability and environmental pressures.

Experts say regular bird counts, wetland restoration, pollution control, enforcement against illegal hunting and scientific monitoring are essential to understanding and reversing the decline. They also stress the need for coordinated conservation efforts involving wildlife authorities, universities, local communities and environmental organisations.

For residents like Khan, however, the environmental crisis is already visible without scientific instruments or statistical reports. The ponds of his childhood have vanished, and the flocks that once filled the winter sky are now largely memories. As another winter approaches, the question is no longer simply how many migratory birds will return to K-P, but whether enough of their natural habitats will remain to welcome them.

Unless the region's wetlands and river ecosystems are protected, future generations may know the great winter migration only through the stories of those who once watched the skies come alive.

"Today, the decline in migratory bird populations in K-P has exceeded 90 per cent compared with earlier levels," Dr Nafees claimed. The figure represents the expert's assessment and requires confirmation through updated, province-wide scientific surveys.

Polluted river water, shrinking habitats, changing temperatures and indiscriminate hunting are major factors behind the decline. However, the extent to which telecommunications infrastructure affects long-distance bird migration remains scientifically uncertain and requires species-specific research.

Climate pressures

He added that rising temperatures and climate-induced changes in river flows were further damaging the natural habitats on which migratory birds depend.

He stressed that without systematic research and monitoring, the region will struggle to address the growing challenges facing migratory wildlife.

She emphasised the importance of protecting natural habitats, improving aquatic ecosystems, raising public awareness and strengthening coordination among relevant institutions.

headline: Live and let go
description: In the age of screenshots, cancel culture, and ghosting, forgiveness may be the most underrated skill of our time
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
Right now, someone is lying awake at 2 am, rehearsing an argument with another person who stopped thinking about it years ago. Somewhere else, two sisters sit at opposite ends of a wedding hall, silently sulking and brewing over something neither can fully remember. And somewhere, maybe in your own head, a conversation from years back is still playing on a loop.

We call it standing our ground. We call it self-respect. We call it never forgetting.

But let’s call it what it really is: a bill. It arrives daily, in your sleep, your mood, your relationships, your peace. And the person who hurt you isn’t paying it. You are.

The people who changed history understood this. Nelson Mandela walked out of 27 years in prison and chose reconciliation over revenge. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) at the height of his power, forgave the people who had persecuted him. In 2006, Amish families, within hours of a school shooting in Pennsylvania, visited the gunman’s widow to comfort her.

None of them were weak. They had worked out something most of us haven’t. Forgiveness isn’t weakness. It’s strategy. It’s freedom. In the age of screenshots, cancel culture, and ghosting, it may be the most underrated skill of our time.

If the word “forgiveness” makes you bristle, you’re not alone. Most people resist it because they think it means something it doesn’t.

Forgiveness is not saying “it’s okay.” It wasn’t okay, and you don’t have to pretend it was. Forgiveness is not forgetting. You can forgive and still remember the lesson. Forgiveness is not trusting them again. Trust is earned. Forgiveness is given. Forgiveness is not letting them off the hook. You’re taking yourself off the hook, the one where you’re stuck replaying the injury.

So what is it? Forgiveness is deciding that what happened will no longer control your mood, your choices, or your future. That’s it. No hugging required.

Forgiveness in your daily life

This isn't only about huge betrayals. Look at the small stuff. The friend who forgot your birthday. You say nothing and get quietly colder. Six months later the friendship is dead, and neither of you can say exactly why.

The sibling who said something cruel during an argument, years pass. You still won't sit next to each other at weddings. The parent who wasn't emotionally there, you're 35, and you still react to their tone like you're 12. The colleague who took credit for your idea, you stew in your seat for months, rehearsing the speech you'll never give. The ex. Enough said.

Notice the pattern. In every case the original wound is small compared with the damage done by holding on. A forgotten birthday takes a day. A grudge takes years. Unforgiveness is a subscription you never meant to sign up for. It bills you monthly in energy, sleep, and peace, and the person you're angry at isn't even paying.

Researchers have studied forgiveness for decades, and the findings point in a consistent direction. People who practice forgiveness tend to report lower stress, less anxiety, fewer symptoms of depression, and better relationships. Studies have also linked holding grudges to higher blood pressure and a heightened stress response, as if your body treats an old insult as a fresh emergency.

Programmes like the Stanford Forgiveness Project, led by psychologist Fred Luskin, found that people trained in forgiveness reported feeling less hurt and angry, and more hopeful and in control of their lives.

The most interesting finding is about control. When you hold a grudge, the person who wronged you still holds power over you. Every time you think of them, your heart rate jumps. They live in your head for free. Forgiveness takes the keys back.

Every culture on earth has wrestled with this question. They answered it in surprisingly similar ways.

After apartheid, the country could have descended into revenge. Instead, Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu helped create the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Perpetrators could confess publicly, and victims could be heard. It wasn't perfect, and many survivors still struggle with unanswered questions. But it helped a nation avoid civil war. Tutu said there is "no future without forgiveness."

After the 1994 genocide, neighbours had to live beside neighbors who had killed their families. Community courts called gacaca brought people face to face, with truth-telling, accountability, and, in many cases, painful, slow reconciliation. Many survivors describe it as the only way to keep living in the same villages.

When the gunman killed five Amish schoolgirls at a West Nickel Mines School in Pennsylvania. Within hours, Amish families visited the gunman's widow to comfort her and attended his funeral. The world was stunned. For the Amish, forgiveness isn't a feeling. It's a discipline practiced daily, long before a tragedy tests it.

The philosophy "I am because we are" teaches that harming another person damages the community, and so does refusing to restore them. Forgiveness is how the whole circle heals. This traditional practice of reconciliation uses four simple sentences: I'm sorry. Please forgive me. Thank you. I love you. It's still used in families today.

Buddhism says, “Anger is described as holding a hot coal to throw at someone else. You're the one who gets burned.” Christianity centres on the call to forgive. Judaism has Yom Kippur, a whole day set aside each year for seeking and offering forgiveness.

In Japan and China, concepts of "face" and harmony mean forgiveness often happens quietly, through gestures and restored respect rather than long apologies. Different languages, different rituals, one conclusion: communities that can't forgive can't survive.

Islam gives forgiveness a high place. Among the names of God are Al-Ghaffar and Al-Afuww, "The Constant Forgiver" and "The Pardoner."

The Qur'an encourages believers to pardon and overlook, and it asks a question that cuts deep: Don't you wish that God would forgive you? In other words, the mercy you want from God is tied to the mercy you give to people.

The clearest example is the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). When he returned to Mecca in victory, the city that had persecuted him, tortured his followers, and driven him out of his home, he faced the very people who had harmed him. He told them: "Go, you are free."

It was power used for mercy rather than revenge. The message is that the strongest person isn't the one who gets even. It's the one who could, and chooses not to.

Moreover, younger generations are navigating forgiveness differently than any before them.

Millennials grew up in an era of change: the 2008 financial crisis, rising rent, burnout. Many of them are the generation that made therapy mainstream. They've done real work on childhood wounds and family patterns, and many are breaking cycles their parents never could. But they've also popularised therapy language, and "toxic," "gaslighting," and "narcissist" sometimes get applied to ordinary human mistakes. Not every disagreement is abuse. Sometimes a person was just tired, careless, or flawed.

Gen Z has grown up online, where the rules around forgiveness are unclear. A bad joke from eight years ago can resurface in an instant. A screenshot lasts forever. Public "cancelling" often skips the step where a person can apologise, grow, and be given another chance. Gen Z is also the most openly boundary-minded generation, which is healthy. They're right to walk away from harmful people. Both generations face the same hazard: mistaking boundaries for grudges.

A boundary says, "I won't let you hurt me again." A grudge says, "I won't let you stop having hurt me."

Younger people also have new ways to hurt each other, like ghosting, being left on read, and being unfollowed, and these wounds are real. But they're also easier to nurse in silence. A quiet block can replace a hard conversation, and the hurt never gets resolved. It just goes dormant, waiting.

The good news is that these generations are unusually open about mental health, and that openness is exactly what forgiveness needs. They talk about feelings. They set limits. Add forgiveness to that toolkit, and they could be the healthiest generation yet.

When forgiveness has limits

Let's be honest. Forgiveness has limits, and pretending otherwise hurts people.

If someone is abusing you, forgiveness doesn't mean staying. You can release your anger from a safe distance. Forgiveness is an internal act. Reconciliation is a relationship decision, and they're separate.

Forgiveness also shouldn't be forced. If someone says "just forgive and move on" to a person in fresh pain, that isn't wisdom. It's pressure. Healing takes time, and some wounds require professional support.

And forgiving doesn't cancel accountability. A person can be forgiven in your heart and still face consequences in the world. The healthiest version looks like this: justice for the situation, peace for yourself.

Forgiveness sounds noble, but how do you do it? Here's a simple, realistic approach. Name the hurt honestly. Don't skip this bit. Say it out loud or write it down: "This happened. It hurt me." You can't release what you won't admit.

Anger is allowed. You can feel it, but don't feed it. Replaying the story a hundred times is not the same as processing it. You don’t have to excuse them, but try seeing them as a whole person. It’s just to remember that people act from fear, ignorance, stress, and their own wounds. Hurt people often hurt people.

Decide what you actually need. Is it a conversation, or distance, or an apology? Sometimes you'll never get closure from them, but you may have to give it to yourself. Let go in layers. You may forgive on Monday and feel angry again by Thursday. That's normal. Forgiveness isn't a single moment. It's a practice you repeat. You can forgive yourself too. This is the hardest one. Many people can pardon everyone except the person in the mirror. Your past mistakes were lessons, not a life sentence.

Think about the people you know who never let anything go. The uncle who hasn't spoken to his brother in 20 years. The friend who tells the same betrayal story at every gathering. The coworker whose face tightens at one name. Are they happy? Are they free?

Bitterness shrinks life. It makes the world smaller, relationships fewer, and trust harder. People who carry old pain into every new situation end up punishing innocent people for what someone else did. Forgiveness, by contrast, expands a life. It frees up attention, energy, and room for new connections. It turns "what happened to me" into "what I'm building now."

In a world that rewards outrage, clapbacks, and getting the last word, forgiveness is a quietly radical act. It's not a weakness. It takes more courage to release a grudge than to keep one.

The wisest people in history, from prophets to presidents to ordinary grandmothers, practiced it because they understood its power. And it's not for them. It's for you.

So here's your challenge. Think of one person you've been holding something against. You don't have to call them. You don't have to say it's okay. Just ask yourself:

"If I put this down today, what could I pick up instead?" Peace. Energy. Better sleep. A lighter heart. Maybe even a restored friendship. The grudge has had enough of your time. Let it go.

Rabia Khan is a freelance writer and researcher focusing on social issues, gender rights, and current affairs.

By Rabia Khan |
Photo: AI Generated

PUBLISHED November 01, 2026

Right now, someone is lying awake at 2 am, rehearsing an argument with another person who stopped thinking about it years ago. Somewhere else, two sisters sit at opposite ends of a wedding hall, silently sulking and brewing over something neither can fully remember. And somewhere, maybe in your own head, a conversation from years back is still playing on a loop.

We call it standing our ground. We call it self-respect. We call it never forgetting.

But let’s call it what it really is: a bill. It arrives daily, in your sleep, your mood, your relationships, your peace. And the person who hurt you isn’t paying it. You are.

The people who changed history understood this. Nelson Mandela walked out of 27 years in prison and chose reconciliation over revenge. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) at the height of his power, forgave the people who had persecuted him. In 2006, Amish families, within hours of a school shooting in Pennsylvania, visited the gunman’s widow to comfort her.

None of them were weak. They had worked out something most of us haven’t. Forgiveness isn’t weakness. It’s strategy. It’s freedom. In the age of screenshots, cancel culture, and ghosting, it may be the most underrated skill of our time.

If the word “forgiveness” makes you bristle, you’re not alone. Most people resist it because they think it means something it doesn’t.

Forgiveness is not saying “it’s okay.” It wasn’t okay, and you don’t have to pretend it was. Forgiveness is not forgetting. You can forgive and still remember the lesson. Forgiveness is not trusting them again. Trust is earned. Forgiveness is given. Forgiveness is not letting them off the hook. You’re taking yourself off the hook, the one where you’re stuck replaying the injury.

So what is it? Forgiveness is deciding that what happened will no longer control your mood, your choices, or your future. That’s it. No hugging required.

Forgiveness in your daily life

This isn't only about huge betrayals. Look at the small stuff. The friend who forgot your birthday. You say nothing and get quietly colder. Six months later the friendship is dead, and neither of you can say exactly why.

The sibling who said something cruel during an argument, years pass. You still won't sit next to each other at weddings. The parent who wasn't emotionally there, you're 35, and you still react to their tone like you're 12. The colleague who took credit for your idea, you stew in your seat for months, rehearsing the speech you'll never give. The ex. Enough said.

Notice the pattern. In every case the original wound is small compared with the damage done by holding on. A forgotten birthday takes a day. A grudge takes years. Unforgiveness is a subscription you never meant to sign up for. It bills you monthly in energy, sleep, and peace, and the person you're angry at isn't even paying.

Researchers have studied forgiveness for decades, and the findings point in a consistent direction. People who practice forgiveness tend to report lower stress, less anxiety, fewer symptoms of depression, and better relationships. Studies have also linked holding grudges to higher blood pressure and a heightened stress response, as if your body treats an old insult as a fresh emergency.

Programmes like the Stanford Forgiveness Project, led by psychologist Fred Luskin, found that people trained in forgiveness reported feeling less hurt and angry, and more hopeful and in control of their lives.

The most interesting finding is about control. When you hold a grudge, the person who wronged you still holds power over you. Every time you think of them, your heart rate jumps. They live in your head for free. Forgiveness takes the keys back.

Every culture on earth has wrestled with this question. They answered it in surprisingly similar ways.

After apartheid, the country could have descended into revenge. Instead, Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu helped create the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Perpetrators could confess publicly, and victims could be heard. It wasn't perfect, and many survivors still struggle with unanswered questions. But it helped a nation avoid civil war. Tutu said there is "no future without forgiveness."

After the 1994 genocide, neighbours had to live beside neighbors who had killed their families. Community courts called gacaca brought people face to face, with truth-telling, accountability, and, in many cases, painful, slow reconciliation. Many survivors describe it as the only way to keep living in the same villages.

When the gunman killed five Amish schoolgirls at a West Nickel Mines School in Pennsylvania. Within hours, Amish families visited the gunman's widow to comfort her and attended his funeral. The world was stunned. For the Amish, forgiveness isn't a feeling. It's a discipline practiced daily, long before a tragedy tests it.

The philosophy "I am because we are" teaches that harming another person damages the community, and so does refusing to restore them. Forgiveness is how the whole circle heals. This traditional practice of reconciliation uses four simple sentences: I'm sorry. Please forgive me. Thank you. I love you. It's still used in families today.

Buddhism says, “Anger is described as holding a hot coal to throw at someone else. You're the one who gets burned.” Christianity centres on the call to forgive. Judaism has Yom Kippur, a whole day set aside each year for seeking and offering forgiveness.

In Japan and China, concepts of "face" and harmony mean forgiveness often happens quietly, through gestures and restored respect rather than long apologies. Different languages, different rituals, one conclusion: communities that can't forgive can't survive.

Islam gives forgiveness a high place. Among the names of God are Al-Ghaffar and Al-Afuww, "The Constant Forgiver" and "The Pardoner."

The Qur'an encourages believers to pardon and overlook, and it asks a question that cuts deep: Don't you wish that God would forgive you? In other words, the mercy you want from God is tied to the mercy you give to people.

The clearest example is the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). When he returned to Mecca in victory, the city that had persecuted him, tortured his followers, and driven him out of his home, he faced the very people who had harmed him. He told them: "Go, you are free."

It was power used for mercy rather than revenge. The message is that the strongest person isn't the one who gets even. It's the one who could, and chooses not to.

Moreover, younger generations are navigating forgiveness differently than any before them.

Millennials grew up in an era of change: the 2008 financial crisis, rising rent, burnout. Many of them are the generation that made therapy mainstream. They've done real work on childhood wounds and family patterns, and many are breaking cycles their parents never could. But they've also popularised therapy language, and "toxic," "gaslighting," and "narcissist" sometimes get applied to ordinary human mistakes. Not every disagreement is abuse. Sometimes a person was just tired, careless, or flawed.

Gen Z has grown up online, where the rules around forgiveness are unclear. A bad joke from eight years ago can resurface in an instant. A screenshot lasts forever. Public "cancelling" often skips the step where a person can apologise, grow, and be given another chance. Gen Z is also the most openly boundary-minded generation, which is healthy. They're right to walk away from harmful people. Both generations face the same hazard: mistaking boundaries for grudges.

A boundary says, "I won't let you hurt me again." A grudge says, "I won't let you stop having hurt me."

Younger people also have new ways to hurt each other, like ghosting, being left on read, and being unfollowed, and these wounds are real. But they're also easier to nurse in silence. A quiet block can replace a hard conversation, and the hurt never gets resolved. It just goes dormant, waiting.

The good news is that these generations are unusually open about mental health, and that openness is exactly what forgiveness needs. They talk about feelings. They set limits. Add forgiveness to that toolkit, and they could be the healthiest generation yet.

When forgiveness has limits

Let's be honest. Forgiveness has limits, and pretending otherwise hurts people.

If someone is abusing you, forgiveness doesn't mean staying. You can release your anger from a safe distance. Forgiveness is an internal act. Reconciliation is a relationship decision, and they're separate.

Forgiveness also shouldn't be forced. If someone says "just forgive and move on" to a person in fresh pain, that isn't wisdom. It's pressure. Healing takes time, and some wounds require professional support.

And forgiving doesn't cancel accountability. A person can be forgiven in your heart and still face consequences in the world. The healthiest version looks like this: justice for the situation, peace for yourself.

Forgiveness sounds noble, but how do you do it? Here's a simple, realistic approach. Name the hurt honestly. Don't skip this bit. Say it out loud or write it down: "This happened. It hurt me." You can't release what you won't admit.

Anger is allowed. You can feel it, but don't feed it. Replaying the story a hundred times is not the same as processing it. You don’t have to excuse them, but try seeing them as a whole person. It’s just to remember that people act from fear, ignorance, stress, and their own wounds. Hurt people often hurt people.

Decide what you actually need. Is it a conversation, or distance, or an apology? Sometimes you'll never get closure from them, but you may have to give it to yourself. Let go in layers. You may forgive on Monday and feel angry again by Thursday. That's normal. Forgiveness isn't a single moment. It's a practice you repeat. You can forgive yourself too. This is the hardest one. Many people can pardon everyone except the person in the mirror. Your past mistakes were lessons, not a life sentence.

Think about the people you know who never let anything go. The uncle who hasn't spoken to his brother in 20 years. The friend who tells the same betrayal story at every gathering. The coworker whose face tightens at one name. Are they happy? Are they free?

Bitterness shrinks life. It makes the world smaller, relationships fewer, and trust harder. People who carry old pain into every new situation end up punishing innocent people for what someone else did. Forgiveness, by contrast, expands a life. It frees up attention, energy, and room for new connections. It turns "what happened to me" into "what I'm building now."

In a world that rewards outrage, clapbacks, and getting the last word, forgiveness is a quietly radical act. It's not a weakness. It takes more courage to release a grudge than to keep one.

The wisest people in history, from prophets to presidents to ordinary grandmothers, practiced it because they understood its power. And it's not for them. It's for you.

So here's your challenge. Think of one person you've been holding something against. You don't have to call them. You don't have to say it's okay. Just ask yourself:

"If I put this down today, what could I pick up instead?" Peace. Energy. Better sleep. A lighter heart. Maybe even a restored friendship. The grudge has had enough of your time. Let it go.

 

Rabia Khan is a freelance writer and researcher focusing on social issues, gender rights, and current affairs.
