Right now, someone is lying awake at 2 am, rehearsing an argument with another person who stopped thinking about it years ago. Somewhere else, two sisters sit at opposite ends of a wedding hall, silently sulking and brewing over something neither can fully remember. And somewhere, maybe in your own head, a conversation from years back is still playing on a loop.

We call it standing our ground. We call it self-respect. We call it never forgetting.

But let’s call it what it really is: a bill. It arrives daily, in your sleep, your mood, your relationships, your peace. And the person who hurt you isn’t paying it. You are.

The people who changed history understood this. Nelson Mandela walked out of 27 years in prison and chose reconciliation over revenge. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) at the height of his power, forgave the people who had persecuted him. In 2006, Amish families, within hours of a school shooting in Pennsylvania, visited the gunman’s widow to comfort her.

None of them were weak. They had worked out something most of us haven’t. Forgiveness isn’t weakness. It’s strategy. It’s freedom. In the age of screenshots, cancel culture, and ghosting, it may be the most underrated skill of our time.

If the word “forgiveness” makes you bristle, you’re not alone. Most people resist it because they think it means something it doesn’t.

Forgiveness is not saying “it’s okay.” It wasn’t okay, and you don’t have to pretend it was. Forgiveness is not forgetting. You can forgive and still remember the lesson. Forgiveness is not trusting them again. Trust is earned. Forgiveness is given. Forgiveness is not letting them off the hook. You’re taking yourself off the hook, the one where you’re stuck replaying the injury.

So what is it? Forgiveness is deciding that what happened will no longer control your mood, your choices, or your future. That’s it. No hugging required.

Forgiveness in your daily life

This isn't only about huge betrayals. Look at the small stuff. The friend who forgot your birthday. You say nothing and get quietly colder. Six months later the friendship is dead, and neither of you can say exactly why.

The sibling who said something cruel during an argument, years pass. You still won't sit next to each other at weddings. The parent who wasn't emotionally there, you're 35, and you still react to their tone like you're 12. The colleague who took credit for your idea, you stew in your seat for months, rehearsing the speech you'll never give. The ex. Enough said.

Notice the pattern. In every case the original wound is small compared with the damage done by holding on. A forgotten birthday takes a day. A grudge takes years. Unforgiveness is a subscription you never meant to sign up for. It bills you monthly in energy, sleep, and peace, and the person you're angry at isn't even paying.

Researchers have studied forgiveness for decades, and the findings point in a consistent direction. People who practice forgiveness tend to report lower stress, less anxiety, fewer symptoms of depression, and better relationships. Studies have also linked holding grudges to higher blood pressure and a heightened stress response, as if your body treats an old insult as a fresh emergency.

Programmes like the Stanford Forgiveness Project, led by psychologist Fred Luskin, found that people trained in forgiveness reported feeling less hurt and angry, and more hopeful and in control of their lives.

The most interesting finding is about control. When you hold a grudge, the person who wronged you still holds power over you. Every time you think of them, your heart rate jumps. They live in your head for free. Forgiveness takes the keys back.

Every culture on earth has wrestled with this question. They answered it in surprisingly similar ways.

After apartheid, the country could have descended into revenge. Instead, Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu helped create the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Perpetrators could confess publicly, and victims could be heard. It wasn't perfect, and many survivors still struggle with unanswered questions. But it helped a nation avoid civil war. Tutu said there is "no future without forgiveness."

After the 1994 genocide, neighbours had to live beside neighbors who had killed their families. Community courts called gacaca brought people face to face, with truth-telling, accountability, and, in many cases, painful, slow reconciliation. Many survivors describe it as the only way to keep living in the same villages.

When the gunman killed five Amish schoolgirls at a West Nickel Mines School in Pennsylvania. Within hours, Amish families visited the gunman's widow to comfort her and attended his funeral. The world was stunned. For the Amish, forgiveness isn't a feeling. It's a discipline practiced daily, long before a tragedy tests it.

The philosophy "I am because we are" teaches that harming another person damages the community, and so does refusing to restore them. Forgiveness is how the whole circle heals. This traditional practice of reconciliation uses four simple sentences: I'm sorry. Please forgive me. Thank you. I love you. It's still used in families today.

Buddhism says, “Anger is described as holding a hot coal to throw at someone else. You're the one who gets burned.” Christianity centres on the call to forgive. Judaism has Yom Kippur, a whole day set aside each year for seeking and offering forgiveness.

In Japan and China, concepts of "face" and harmony mean forgiveness often happens quietly, through gestures and restored respect rather than long apologies. Different languages, different rituals, one conclusion: communities that can't forgive can't survive.

Islam gives forgiveness a high place. Among the names of God are Al-Ghaffar and Al-Afuww, "The Constant Forgiver" and "The Pardoner."

The Qur'an encourages believers to pardon and overlook, and it asks a question that cuts deep: Don't you wish that God would forgive you? In other words, the mercy you want from God is tied to the mercy you give to people.

The clearest example is the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). When he returned to Mecca in victory, the city that had persecuted him, tortured his followers, and driven him out of his home, he faced the very people who had harmed him. He told them: "Go, you are free."

It was power used for mercy rather than revenge. The message is that the strongest person isn't the one who gets even. It's the one who could, and chooses not to.

Moreover, younger generations are navigating forgiveness differently than any before them.

Millennials grew up in an era of change: the 2008 financial crisis, rising rent, burnout. Many of them are the generation that made therapy mainstream. They've done real work on childhood wounds and family patterns, and many are breaking cycles their parents never could. But they've also popularised therapy language, and "toxic," "gaslighting," and "narcissist" sometimes get applied to ordinary human mistakes. Not every disagreement is abuse. Sometimes a person was just tired, careless, or flawed.

Gen Z has grown up online, where the rules around forgiveness are unclear. A bad joke from eight years ago can resurface in an instant. A screenshot lasts forever. Public "cancelling" often skips the step where a person can apologise, grow, and be given another chance. Gen Z is also the most openly boundary-minded generation, which is healthy. They're right to walk away from harmful people. Both generations face the same hazard: mistaking boundaries for grudges.

A boundary says, "I won't let you hurt me again." A grudge says, "I won't let you stop having hurt me."

Younger people also have new ways to hurt each other, like ghosting, being left on read, and being unfollowed, and these wounds are real. But they're also easier to nurse in silence. A quiet block can replace a hard conversation, and the hurt never gets resolved. It just goes dormant, waiting.

The good news is that these generations are unusually open about mental health, and that openness is exactly what forgiveness needs. They talk about feelings. They set limits. Add forgiveness to that toolkit, and they could be the healthiest generation yet.

When forgiveness has limits

Let's be honest. Forgiveness has limits, and pretending otherwise hurts people.

If someone is abusing you, forgiveness doesn't mean staying. You can release your anger from a safe distance. Forgiveness is an internal act. Reconciliation is a relationship decision, and they're separate.

Forgiveness also shouldn't be forced. If someone says "just forgive and move on" to a person in fresh pain, that isn't wisdom. It's pressure. Healing takes time, and some wounds require professional support.

And forgiving doesn't cancel accountability. A person can be forgiven in your heart and still face consequences in the world. The healthiest version looks like this: justice for the situation, peace for yourself.

Forgiveness sounds noble, but how do you do it? Here's a simple, realistic approach. Name the hurt honestly. Don't skip this bit. Say it out loud or write it down: "This happened. It hurt me." You can't release what you won't admit.

Anger is allowed. You can feel it, but don't feed it. Replaying the story a hundred times is not the same as processing it. You don’t have to excuse them, but try seeing them as a whole person. It’s just to remember that people act from fear, ignorance, stress, and their own wounds. Hurt people often hurt people.

Decide what you actually need. Is it a conversation, or distance, or an apology? Sometimes you'll never get closure from them, but you may have to give it to yourself. Let go in layers. You may forgive on Monday and feel angry again by Thursday. That's normal. Forgiveness isn't a single moment. It's a practice you repeat. You can forgive yourself too. This is the hardest one. Many people can pardon everyone except the person in the mirror. Your past mistakes were lessons, not a life sentence.

Think about the people you know who never let anything go. The uncle who hasn't spoken to his brother in 20 years. The friend who tells the same betrayal story at every gathering. The coworker whose face tightens at one name. Are they happy? Are they free?

Bitterness shrinks life. It makes the world smaller, relationships fewer, and trust harder. People who carry old pain into every new situation end up punishing innocent people for what someone else did. Forgiveness, by contrast, expands a life. It frees up attention, energy, and room for new connections. It turns "what happened to me" into "what I'm building now."

In a world that rewards outrage, clapbacks, and getting the last word, forgiveness is a quietly radical act. It's not a weakness. It takes more courage to release a grudge than to keep one.

The wisest people in history, from prophets to presidents to ordinary grandmothers, practiced it because they understood its power. And it's not for them. It's for you.

So here's your challenge. Think of one person you've been holding something against. You don't have to call them. You don't have to say it's okay. Just ask yourself:

"If I put this down today, what could I pick up instead?" Peace. Energy. Better sleep. A lighter heart. Maybe even a restored friendship. The grudge has had enough of your time. Let it go.

Rabia Khan is a freelance writer and researcher focusing on social issues, gender rights, and current affairs.

headline: Too precious to replace
description: From old beds to family recordings, people hold on to treasured possessions that preserve memories of their loved ones
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
There is usually something in every home that has outlived its usefulness. It could be an old watch that no longer tells the correct time, a chair that has seen better days, or a piece of furniture that has followed the family from one house to another. Replacing it might be easier, and sometimes cheaper, but the thought of letting it go is difficult. Not because of what it is worth, but because of who it reminds us of, or the memories associated with it.

At 72, Shakil Ahmed still sleeps on a bed he bought nearly 30 years ago. It is a single bed made of sheesham wood, with a short headboard and traditional carvings. Over the years, it has been polished and repainted, but Ahmed has never considered replacing it. The bed once belonged to his mother, and for him, that is reason enough to keep it.

Ahmed remembers how pleased his mother was when he bought it for her. She loved the bed and would proudly tell her friends about it. In the final years of her life, when her declining health left her mostly bedridden, it became the place where much of the family's time together was spent.

Her grandchildren would sit beside her or climb onto the bed to sleep. She would tell them stories, share meals with the family and laugh with them, even as her movements became increasingly restricted. For Ahmed, those everyday moments have stayed with him long after his mother's death.

“Even today, whenever I look at it, I can picture my mother sitting there with a smile on her face,” he says.

The bed has accompanied Ahmed through the years, even as he has moved between homes and travelled frequently. Although it has needed occasional maintenance, he says he has never paid much attention to how much was spent on keeping it in good condition. The quality of the wood has helped it survive, but it is the memories associated with it that make him unwilling to part with it.

There have been suggestions that he should replace the bed with something newer. Ahmed has always refused. He continues to sleep on it and says knowing that it belonged to his mother brings him comfort.

For someone else, it might simply be an ageing piece of furniture, old-fashioned and easily replaceable. For Ahmed, however, keeping the bed is a way of holding on to the years when his mother was still around, surrounded by the family.

And he is not the only one willing to keep an old possession long after replacing it might seem the more practical choice.

The cost of holding on

At the Liaquatabad Furniture Market in Karachi, 63-year-old Faryad Iqbal regularly comes across customers who would rather repair an old piece of furniture than buy a new one. Some bring beds, others chairs, stools or wooden storage boxes that have been in their families for generations. According to Iqbal, around 30 per cent of his customers come to him with old or inherited furniture.

While older furniture is often made from stronger wood, years of use can weaken its joints, damage its base or loosen the fittings. Polishing is among the most common requests, but some customers are particular about retaining the original material and design, even when repairs become expensive.

“Even if the wood is broken, they ask us to use the same wood, despite it being expensive. They want the same look and feel,” says Iqbal.

Matching the original wood and craftsmanship can sometimes cost more than buying new furniture. Yet, for many of his customers, changing the appearance is not an option.

Iqbal recalls a customer who repeatedly brought in his grandfather's chair for repairs. Eventually, the chair became too weak to withstand regular use. Rather than discard it, the man placed it in his room, where it remains unused.

“Most of them want to preserve the original look, which is a really difficult job to do,” Iqbal explains.

For some customers, restoring furniture means making it usable again. For others, like the man with his grandfather's chair, simply being able to keep it is enough.

Family heirlooms

Not every possession is kept because of memories of someone who has passed away. Some are preserved because they have become part of a family's traditions, passed from one generation to another with the expectation that the next will care for them just as carefully.

For 68-year-old Naila Latif, that responsibility came in the form of a gold necklace that, according to her family's history, dates back to 1928. For generations, it has been passed from a mother-in-law to the eldest daughter-in-law. Naila was the fourth generation to receive it, and she has since handed it over to her eldest son’s wife.

The necklace has three gold coins on either side, with stones and beads arranged between them and a traditional gold design at the centre. Rather than hanging from a gold chain, it is held together by a thread, a detail the family has deliberately preserved.

Over the years, the necklace has been polished occasionally, and the thread has been replaced once. But changing its original appearance has never been considered necessary.

When Naila received it as a new bride, her mother-in-law explained its history and the tradition associated with it. Years later, Naila found herself having the same conversation with her daughter-in-law, explaining where the necklace had come from and why it needed to be kept safe. “You don't realise it when it's passed on, but in a way, it keeps the family ties strong and preserves the family history,” she says.

While Naila’s family necklace has changed hands for nearly a century, 39-year-old Areeba Iqbal's attachment to her grandmother's brass paandaan began with childhood visits.

Whenever Areeba visited her grandmother, she was fascinated by the hexagonal brass container, decorated with traditional designs reminiscent of the pre-Partition era. She remembers being asked to bring it to her grandmother and then watching as she prepared paan, taking ingredients from its separate compartments.

Iqbal had wanted the paandaan since childhood. Two years ago, when her grandmother, now in her 90s, received a new steel one from her son, she decided to give the old brass container to the granddaughter who had always admired it.

“Although I don't use it, having it with me is a dream come true,” says Areeba.

She keeps it in her room and occasionally opens it to revisit those childhood memories. Karachi's weather means the brass requires regular attention, so every four to six months she takes it to a jeweller for polishing, with specific instructions not to rub too hard and damage its decorative patterns.

Areeba hopes to pass the paandaan to her daughter one day, along with the stories of how her grandmother used it. For Naila, passing on the necklace means continuing an established family tradition. For Areeba, it is a chance to begin one of her own.

The voices that remain

When Shahid Ismail's father returned to Pakistan from the United Kingdom in the 1960s, he brought home a reel-to-reel tape recorder with two large circular reels and a set of speakers. Such machines were rare in Pakistan at the time, and for Ismail, who was around eight years old, it soon became a source of fascination. His father would use it to record conversations at home, sometimes asking his children to speak into it, tell stories or simply talk to one another.

Nearly six decades later, the 70-year-old still has the machine, along with many of the recordings his father made. What began as ordinary family conversations have become some of his most treasured possessions, particularly since his father's death.

The tapes contain the voices of Ismail and his siblings as children, their conversations and stories, and moments when their father would offer advice about life. At the time, the children did not always understand what he was trying to teach them. It was only years later, as they grew older and began dealing with the responsibilities of adult life, that some of those conversations started to make sense.

“Some of the things our father told us didn't seem useful back then. But now, as adults, we can relate to what he was saying,” says Ismail.

Listening to the recordings also brings back memories of the family being together. The voices may be older recordings, but for Ismail, they still carry the familiarity of those childhood days. “It feels like I go back to those days, sitting in the same room with all my siblings,” he says.

Keeping the recorder working, however, has become increasingly difficult. The machine occasionally jams because of wear and tear in its internal components, while the tapes themselves have become fragile with age. Some portions of the recordings have already been lost because of damage, despite Ismail's efforts to repair and preserve them.

For years, the family has relied on the same technician to keep the machine running. Fareed Hassan, now 65, repaired the recorder when it belonged to the senior Ismail and continues to look after it. After repeated visits for a particular fault, Hassan even taught him how to fix the problem himself.

Hassan has been repairing tape recorders for more than 30 years. He first became familiar with the equipment while living in Saudi Arabia. After returning to Pakistan, he began experimenting with repairs at a time when such machines were expensive and owners preferred fixing them rather than purchasing replacements. He eventually opened his own repair shop.

Today, repairing these machines requires considerably more effort. Many of the components used in older tape recorders are no longer manufactured, leaving Hassan dependent on whatever spare parts he can find. He has kept several old machines in his workshop, removing components from them whenever another recorder needs repairing.

“There are some parts which I make myself to keep the tape recorder working,” he explains.

Even that is not always enough. Hassan says there are occasions when he tells customers their machines cannot be repaired because the necessary parts are unavailable. Some become upset and insist that he try again, prompting him to look for alternatives or make replacement components. Such work can take considerable time, particularly because he must avoid damaging other ageing parts.

His children also work with him, but their attention is largely on newer electronics, including LCD televisions, mobile phones and sound systems. Hassan understands why. Repairing older equipment is time-consuming and generally less profitable. Still, he continues because he has seen how much these possessions mean to their owners.

“I feel the emotions attached to people who want their old things repaired, and that is why I do it,” he says, although he is uncertain how much longer he will be able to continue.

Ismail, meanwhile, has already transferred his family recordings into digital form to protect what remains of them. But he has no intention of giving up the original recorder. He wants his children and grandchildren to experience the recordings through the same machine that once filled his childhood home with familiar voices.

“Now we send thousands of voice notes, and they get lost somewhere among all the others,” he says. “Things like these tapes are gold.”

What we leave behind

What happens to these possessions when the people who have cared for them are no longer around is something their owners have also begun to consider. After spending years protecting old furniture, jewellery and household objects, many hope that the next generation will find a reason to keep them.

For Naila, that responsibility has already passed to her daughter-in-law, along with the gold necklace and the story behind it. Areeba, meanwhile, hopes her daughter will one day take care of the brass paandaan that she spent much of her childhood admiring. Whether her daughter will feel the same attachment to it remains to be seen, but Areeba wants her to know how it was used and why her grandmother treasured it.

Ismail has similar hopes for his father's tape recorder. Although he has preserved the recordings digitally, he wants his children and grandchildren to hear them on the original machine, just as he did growing up. Keeping it working may become more difficult with time, but for now, he continues to have it repaired.

For Ahmed, the question is what will become of his mother's bed. He believes his brothers and sons, who were equally close to her, will understand why he has kept it for so long. He hopes one of them will continue looking after it when he no longer can.

“My brothers share my sentiments and understand the emotional value of the bed,” he says. “My sons also loved and cared for their grandmother deeply.”

For now, he is content knowing that whenever he wants to remember her, he still has something his mother once loved and was so proud to call her own.

There is usually something in every home that has outlived its usefulness. It could be an old watch that no longer tells the correct time, a chair that has seen better days, or a piece of furniture that has followed the family from one house to another. Replacing it might be easier, and sometimes cheaper, but the thought of letting it go is difficult. Not because of what it is worth, but because of who it reminds us of, or the memories associated with it.

At 72, Shakil Ahmed still sleeps on a bed he bought nearly 30 years ago. It is a single bed made of sheesham wood, with a short headboard and traditional carvings. Over the years, it has been polished and repainted, but Ahmed has never considered replacing it. The bed once belonged to his mother, and for him, that is reason enough to keep it.

Ahmed remembers how pleased his mother was when he bought it for her. She loved the bed and would proudly tell her friends about it. In the final years of her life, when her declining health left her mostly bedridden, it became the place where much of the family's time together was spent.

Her grandchildren would sit beside her or climb onto the bed to sleep. She would tell them stories, share meals with the family and laugh with them, even as her movements became increasingly restricted. For Ahmed, those everyday moments have stayed with him long after his mother's death.

“Even today, whenever I look at it, I can picture my mother sitting there with a smile on her face,” he says.

The bed has accompanied Ahmed through the years, even as he has moved between homes and travelled frequently. Although it has needed occasional maintenance, he says he has never paid much attention to how much was spent on keeping it in good condition. The quality of the wood has helped it survive, but it is the memories associated with it that make him unwilling to part with it.

There have been suggestions that he should replace the bed with something newer. Ahmed has always refused. He continues to sleep on it and says knowing that it belonged to his mother brings him comfort.

For someone else, it might simply be an ageing piece of furniture, old-fashioned and easily replaceable. For Ahmed, however, keeping the bed is a way of holding on to the years when his mother was still around, surrounded by the family.

And he is not the only one willing to keep an old possession long after replacing it might seem the more practical choice.

The cost of holding on

At the Liaquatabad Furniture Market in Karachi, 63-year-old Faryad Iqbal regularly comes across customers who would rather repair an old piece of furniture than buy a new one. Some bring beds, others chairs, stools or wooden storage boxes that have been in their families for generations. According to Iqbal, around 30 per cent of his customers come to him with old or inherited furniture.

While older furniture is often made from stronger wood, years of use can weaken its joints, damage its base or loosen the fittings. Polishing is among the most common requests, but some customers are particular about retaining the original material and design, even when repairs become expensive.

“Even if the wood is broken, they ask us to use the same wood, despite it being expensive. They want the same look and feel,” says Iqbal.

Matching the original wood and craftsmanship can sometimes cost more than buying new furniture. Yet, for many of his customers, changing the appearance is not an option.

Iqbal recalls a customer who repeatedly brought in his grandfather's chair for repairs. Eventually, the chair became too weak to withstand regular use. Rather than discard it, the man placed it in his room, where it remains unused.

“Most of them want to preserve the original look, which is a really difficult job to do,” Iqbal explains.

For some customers, restoring furniture means making it usable again. For others, like the man with his grandfather's chair, simply being able to keep it is enough.

Family heirlooms

Not every possession is kept because of memories of someone who has passed away. Some are preserved because they have become part of a family's traditions, passed from one generation to another with the expectation that the next will care for them just as carefully.

For 68-year-old Naila Latif, that responsibility came in the form of a gold necklace that, according to her family's history, dates back to 1928. For generations, it has been passed from a mother-in-law to the eldest daughter-in-law. Naila was the fourth generation to receive it, and she has since handed it over to her eldest son’s wife.

The necklace has three gold coins on either side, with stones and beads arranged between them and a traditional gold design at the centre. Rather than hanging from a gold chain, it is held together by a thread, a detail the family has deliberately preserved.

Over the years, the necklace has been polished occasionally, and the thread has been replaced once. But changing its original appearance has never been considered necessary.

When Naila received it as a new bride, her mother-in-law explained its history and the tradition associated with it. Years later, Naila found herself having the same conversation with her daughter-in-law, explaining where the necklace had come from and why it needed to be kept safe. “You don't realise it when it's passed on, but in a way, it keeps the family ties strong and preserves the family history,” she says.

While Naila’s family necklace has changed hands for nearly a century, 39-year-old Areeba Iqbal's attachment to her grandmother's brass paandaan began with childhood visits.

Whenever Areeba visited her grandmother, she was fascinated by the hexagonal brass container, decorated with traditional designs reminiscent of the pre-Partition era. She remembers being asked to bring it to her grandmother and then watching as she prepared paan, taking ingredients from its separate compartments.

Iqbal had wanted the paandaan since childhood. Two years ago, when her grandmother, now in her 90s, received a new steel one from her son, she decided to give the old brass container to the granddaughter who had always admired it.

“Although I don't use it, having it with me is a dream come true,” says Areeba.

She keeps it in her room and occasionally opens it to revisit those childhood memories. Karachi's weather means the brass requires regular attention, so every four to six months she takes it to a jeweller for polishing, with specific instructions not to rub too hard and damage its decorative patterns.

Areeba hopes to pass the paandaan to her daughter one day, along with the stories of how her grandmother used it. For Naila, passing on the necklace means continuing an established family tradition. For Areeba, it is a chance to begin one of her own.

The voices that remain

When Shahid Ismail's father returned to Pakistan from the United Kingdom in the 1960s, he brought home a reel-to-reel tape recorder with two large circular reels and a set of speakers. Such machines were rare in Pakistan at the time, and for Ismail, who was around eight years old, it soon became a source of fascination. His father would use it to record conversations at home, sometimes asking his children to speak into it, tell stories or simply talk to one another.

Nearly six decades later, the 70-year-old still has the machine, along with many of the recordings his father made. What began as ordinary family conversations have become some of his most treasured possessions, particularly since his father's death.

The tapes contain the voices of Ismail and his siblings as children, their conversations and stories, and moments when their father would offer advice about life. At the time, the children did not always understand what he was trying to teach them. It was only years later, as they grew older and began dealing with the responsibilities of adult life, that some of those conversations started to make sense.

“Some of the things our father told us didn't seem useful back then. But now, as adults, we can relate to what he was saying,” says Ismail.

Listening to the recordings also brings back memories of the family being together. The voices may be older recordings, but for Ismail, they still carry the familiarity of those childhood days. “It feels like I go back to those days, sitting in the same room with all my siblings,” he says.

Keeping the recorder working, however, has become increasingly difficult. The machine occasionally jams because of wear and tear in its internal components, while the tapes themselves have become fragile with age. Some portions of the recordings have already been lost because of damage, despite Ismail's efforts to repair and preserve them.

For years, the family has relied on the same technician to keep the machine running. Fareed Hassan, now 65, repaired the recorder when it belonged to the senior Ismail and continues to look after it. After repeated visits for a particular fault, Hassan even taught him how to fix the problem himself.

Hassan has been repairing tape recorders for more than 30 years. He first became familiar with the equipment while living in Saudi Arabia. After returning to Pakistan, he began experimenting with repairs at a time when such machines were expensive and owners preferred fixing them rather than purchasing replacements. He eventually opened his own repair shop.

Today, repairing these machines requires considerably more effort. Many of the components used in older tape recorders are no longer manufactured, leaving Hassan dependent on whatever spare parts he can find. He has kept several old machines in his workshop, removing components from them whenever another recorder needs repairing.

“There are some parts which I make myself to keep the tape recorder working,” he explains.

Even that is not always enough. Hassan says there are occasions when he tells customers their machines cannot be repaired because the necessary parts are unavailable. Some become upset and insist that he try again, prompting him to look for alternatives or make replacement components. Such work can take considerable time, particularly because he must avoid damaging other ageing parts.

His children also work with him, but their attention is largely on newer electronics, including LCD televisions, mobile phones and sound systems. Hassan understands why. Repairing older equipment is time-consuming and generally less profitable. Still, he continues because he has seen how much these possessions mean to their owners.

“I feel the emotions attached to people who want their old things repaired, and that is why I do it,” he says, although he is uncertain how much longer he will be able to continue.

Ismail, meanwhile, has already transferred his family recordings into digital form to protect what remains of them. But he has no intention of giving up the original recorder. He wants his children and grandchildren to experience the recordings through the same machine that once filled his childhood home with familiar voices.

“Now we send thousands of voice notes, and they get lost somewhere among all the others,” he says. “Things like these tapes are gold.”

What we leave behind

What happens to these possessions when the people who have cared for them are no longer around is something their owners have also begun to consider. After spending years protecting old furniture, jewellery and household objects, many hope that the next generation will find a reason to keep them.

For Naila, that responsibility has already passed to her daughter-in-law, along with the gold necklace and the story behind it. Areeba, meanwhile, hopes her daughter will one day take care of the brass paandaan that she spent much of her childhood admiring. Whether her daughter will feel the same attachment to it remains to be seen, but Areeba wants her to know how it was used and why her grandmother treasured it.

Ismail has similar hopes for his father's tape recorder. Although he has preserved the recordings digitally, he wants his children and grandchildren to hear them on the original machine, just as he did growing up. Keeping it working may become more difficult with time, but for now, he continues to have it repaired.

“Even today, whenever I look at it, I can picture my mother sitting there with a smile on her face,” he says.

The bed has accompanied Ahmed through the years, even as he has moved between homes and travelled frequently. Although it has needed occasional maintenance, he says he has never paid much attention to how much was spent on keeping it in good condition. The quality of the wood has helped it survive, but it is the memories associated with it that make him unwilling to part with it.

There have been suggestions that he should replace the bed with something newer. Ahmed has always refused. He continues to sleep on it and says knowing that it belonged to his mother brings him comfort.

For someone else, it might simply be an ageing piece of furniture, old-fashioned and easily replaceable. For Ahmed, however, keeping the bed is a way of holding on to the years when his mother was still around, surrounded by the family.

And he is not the only one willing to keep an old possession long after replacing it might seem the more practical choice.

According to Iqbal, around 30 per cent of his customers come to him with old or inherited furniture.

While older furniture is often made from stronger wood, years of use can weaken its joints, damage its base or loosen the fittings. Polishing is among the most common requests, but some customers are particular about retaining the original material and design, even when repairs become expensive.

“Even if the wood is broken, they ask us to use the same wood, despite it being expensive. They want the same look and feel,” says Iqbal.

Matching the original wood and craftsmanship can sometimes cost more than buying new furniture. Yet, for many of his customers, changing the appearance is not an option.

Iqbal recalls a customer who repeatedly brought in his grandfather's chair for repairs. Eventually, the chair became too weak to withstand regular use. Rather than discard it, the man placed it in his room, where it remains unused.

“Most of them want to preserve the original look, which is a really difficult job to do,” Iqbal explains.

For some customers, restoring furniture means making it usable again. For others, like the man with his grandfather's chair, simply being able to keep it is enough.

Not every possession is kept because of memories of someone who has passed away. Some are preserved because they have become part of a family's traditions, passed from one generation to another with the expectation that the next will care for them just as carefully.

For generations, it has been passed from a mother-in-law to the eldest daughter-in-law. Naila was the fourth generation to receive it, and she has since handed it over to her eldest son’s wife.

Areeba hopes to pass the paandaan to her daughter one day, along with the stories of how her grandmother used it. For Naila, passing on the necklace means continuing an established family tradition. For Areeba, it is a chance to begin one of her own.

headline: Charity, (in)justice and hunger
description: A society with justice rarely needs charity, and one without it will not establish justice through charity
author: Ali Hassan Bangwar
article_text:
Have you ever seen a politician, bureaucrat, or any other member of the elite waiting in line for free food, subsidised petrol, or a government relief package? Have you ever spotted them outside charitable organisations, NGO offices or public departments in Pakistan? You probably haven't. However, you might not have missed pictures of them standing in queues abroad. Why not in the country? The country's queues are reserved for the people. For people who stand in lines for survival or service, the queues might seem like lifelines - a grand favour or a blessing. They are, in fact, the queues of decay: of life, of hope, of dignity as humans, of rights and potential, of responsive and efficient governance. For most of these borrowed lifelines lead to a lifeless life.

Though we take pride in being one of the world's most philanthropic nations, boasting hundreds of charities and NGOs, we still harbour a deeply marginalised population. Reports indicate that half the country is trapped in abject poverty - to say nothing of the even more horrendous ground realities. Per the Global Hunger Index 2026, Pakistan faces severe, systemic hunger, alongside grappling with rampant begging, injustice and governance failures.

One might wonder how philanthropy on such a massive scale can coexist with endemic poverty, hunger and crisis. The truth is, it is not the sheer volume of charity that determines a society's well-being, but its underlying intent, how it is received by the masses, and - critically - the presence of justice. Unjustly depriving people of their systemic rights, only to meet their basic needs as a mere courtesy, does not fix the system; instead, it fosters a self-sustaining culture of dependency.

Granted, charity helps sustain lives and makes up for the governmental vacuum in service delivery; yet the ultimate acceptance of this as a culture costs the people in many ways.

First, charity absolves the ruling elite of its responsibility vis-à-vis delivering to the masses and allows it to evade potential accountability for its failures. Second, the culture of charitable settings and NGOs makes people live unquestioningly at the receiving end. Third, it reinforces begging tendencies and causes people to abandon the traditional means of survival they once relied on, thereby rendering them subservient to others. In short, charity prevents people from becoming self-reliant.

Fourth, an excessive emphasis on these cultivated servile tendencies makes the victims internalise dependence as their fait accompli. Fifth, by operating under the dictates of the rulers, charitable settings also carry out propaganda, and thereby strengthen the stakes of the system. Behind their magnanimity, they advance agendas that serve their stakeholders, donors included.

Last, they tend to present an improved picture of people's development and prosperity, casting people's plight in an overly optimistic light and sweeping under the carpet all that people truly struggle with.

A society with justice rarely needs charity, and one without it will not establish justice through charity. An ungenerous society with justice will not need charity. An unjust one, however much charity it may have, will remain unjust - or grow even more unjust over time. Charity is no substitute for justice and rights. It should follow the provision of people's rights, filling gaps in delivery or resource constraints.

When charity precedes justice and rights, it both blinds people to their rights and deepens the unjust divide between the rich and the marginalised. Behind the scenes, charity, presented as a grand favour, generates an ill-conceived goodwill in the hearts of the people toward those who usurp rights.

Today, we have multiplying charitable organisations, growing hunger and dysfunctional institutions - all existing within a strange mix of goodwill and complicity. It suggests that systemic injustice and the denial of rights are merely being atoned for with ever more charity.

The day you see the elite standing in queues in the country will either be the day of equitable justice or the day of equitable injustice.

article_html:
Have you ever seen a politician, bureaucrat, or any other member of the elite waiting in line for free food, subsidised petrol, or a government relief package? Have you ever spotted them outside charitable organisations, NGO offices or public departments in Pakistan? You probably haven't. However, you might not have missed pictures of them standing in queues abroad. Why not in the country? The country's queues are reserved for the people. For people who stand in lines for survival or service, the queues might seem like lifelines - a grand favour or a blessing. They are, in fact, the queues of decay: of life, of hope, of dignity as humans, of rights and potential, of responsive and efficient governance. For most of these borrowed lifelines lead to a lifeless life.

Though we take pride in being one of the world's most philanthropic nations, boasting hundreds of charities and NGOs, we still harbour a deeply marginalised population. Reports indicate that half the country is trapped in abject poverty - to say nothing of the even more horrendous ground realities. Per the Global Hunger Index 2026, Pakistan faces severe, systemic hunger, alongside grappling with rampant begging, injustice and governance failures.

One might wonder how philanthropy on such a massive scale can coexist with endemic poverty, hunger and crisis. The truth is, it is not the sheer volume of charity that determines a society's well-being, but its underlying intent, how it is received by the masses, and - critically - the presence of justice. Unjustly depriving people of their systemic rights, only to meet their basic needs as a mere courtesy, does not fix the system; instead, it fosters a self-sustaining culture of dependency.

Granted, charity helps sustain lives and makes up for the governmental vacuum in service delivery; yet the ultimate acceptance of this as a culture costs the people in many ways.

First, charity absolves the ruling elite of its responsibility vis-à-vis delivering to the masses and allows it to evade potential accountability for its failures. Second, the culture of charitable settings and NGOs makes people live unquestioningly at the receiving end. Third, it reinforces begging tendencies and causes people to abandon the traditional means of survival they once relied on, thereby rendering them subservient to others. In short, charity prevents people from becoming self-reliant.

Fourth, an excessive emphasis on these cultivated servile tendencies makes the victims internalise dependence as their fait accompli. Fifth, by operating under the dictates of the rulers, charitable settings also carry out propaganda, and thereby strengthen the stakes of the system. Behind their magnanimity, they advance agendas that serve their stakeholders, donors included.

Last, they tend to present an improved picture of people's development and prosperity, casting people's plight in an overly optimistic light and sweeping under the carpet all that people truly struggle with.

A society with justice rarely needs charity, and one without it will not establish justice through charity. An ungenerous society with justice will not need charity. An unjust one, however much charity it may have, will remain unjust - or grow even more unjust over time. Charity is no substitute for justice and rights. It should follow the provision of people's rights, filling gaps in delivery or resource constraints.

When charity precedes justice and rights, it both blinds people to their rights and deepens the unjust divide between the rich and the marginalised. Behind the scenes, charity, presented as a grand favour, generates an ill-conceived goodwill in the hearts of the people toward those who usurp rights.

Today, we have multiplying charitable organisations, growing hunger and dysfunctional institutions - all existing within a strange mix of goodwill and complicity. It suggests that systemic injustice and the denial of rights are merely being atoned for with ever more charity.

The day you see the elite standing in queues in the country will either be the day of equitable justice or the day of equitable injustice.

headline: Destination Singapore
description: Destination Singapore
author: editorial
article_text:
Looking toward the East has always been a key strategy for Pakistan to enrich its economic base. The tremendous success achieved by ASEAN member states in less than two decades of proactive engagement is a landmark achievement. Singapore, in particular, stands out as a prime example of self-reliance. The city-state has scaled the heights of success through political stability, economic diversification and an unwavering reliance on entrepreneurship. Pakistan is right to resolve once again to benefit from Singapore's success story by broadening economic partnerships and tapping new avenues in higher education, technology and banking.

The recent visit of Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan to Islamabad coincided with the 60th anniversary of bilateral diplomatic relations. The fact that this is the first high-profile visit since 2005 hints at a collective oversight. Yet, it is never too late; the visit offers a vital opportunity to synchronise priorities and share experiences in governance. Ranked 1st in the 2026 Index of Economic Freedom with a score of 84.4, Singapore operates one of the world's most competitive economies. It is time for Pakistan to move past rhetoric and learn from the city-state, which is set to assume the chairmanship of ASEAN in 2027.

While Pakistan has been a Sectoral Dialogue Partner in the league since 1993, Singapore's leadership could help elevate it to a full dialogue partner. Likewise, bilateral trade of approximately $1.2 billion falls well below potential and requires professional hands to undo past policy stagnation. Furthermore, the suspension of PIA and Singapore Airlines' operations since 2007 and 2010, respectively, continues to dent tourism, trade and regional interactivity.

While Balakrishnan expressed interest in learning from Pakistan's disaster management experiences, Islamabad can benefit heavily from Singapore's expertise in AI, IT and banking. Crucially, Singapore's strides in building the world's safest and cleanest city offer invaluable blueprints for a country navigating rapid urban population growth and security challenges.

headline: Our hepatitis crisis
description: Our hepatitis crisis
author: editorial
article_text:
Pakistan's growing hepatitis C burden has become a damning indictment of its public healthcare system. Figures recently presented by the Ministry of National Health Services to the National Assembly reveal that an estimated nine million people are living with hepatitis C, placing Pakistan at the top of the global list. fdre5. It is therefore clear that the country is confronting a public health crisis that can no longer be allowed to worsen.

Pakistan's predicament is especially alarming as the disease continues to spread through largely avoidable practices. Unsafe injections and the reuse of contaminated syringes remain major transmission risks. The proliferation of unregulated clinics and poorly supervised healthcare facilities compounds the danger. What makes this crisis particularly unacceptable is the availability of highly effective treatment. Modern antiviral medicines can cure more than 95% of hepatitis C infections, often within eight to twelve weeks. However, access to early diagnosis and treatment remains limited, particularly among low-income communities and rural populations. The infection can remain asymptomatic for years, allowing it to progress undetected until irreversible liver damage has occurred.

The government's commitment to eliminating hepatitis C by 2030 must therefore translate into a coordinated national response rather than another ambitious declaration. The PM's Hepatitis Control Programme provides an existing framework, but its effectiveness depends heavily on implementation at the provincial and district levels. Health authorities must enforce strict sterilisation protocols and eliminate syringe reuse and strengthen the regulation of blood banks and private healthcare establishments.

With the 2030 elimination deadline approaching, the country has little time to squander. The tragedy is that a curable disease continues to claim thousands of lives because the healthcare system has failed to prevent its spread.

Figures recently presented by the Ministry of National Health Services to the National Assembly reveal that an estimated nine million people are living with hepatitis C, placing Pakistan at the top of the global list. fdre5. It is therefore clear that the country is confronting a public health crisis that can no longer be allowed to worsen.

Pakistan's predicament is especially alarming as the disease continues to spread through largely avoidable practices. Unsafe injections and the reuse of contaminated syringes remain major transmission risks. The proliferation of unregulated clinics and poorly supervised healthcare facilities compounds the danger. What makes this crisis particularly unacceptable is the availability of highly effective treatment. Modern antiviral medicines can cure more than 95% of hepatitis C infections, often within eight to twelve weeks. However, access to early diagnosis and treatment remains limited, particularly among low-income communities and rural populations. The infection can remain asymptomatic for years, allowing it to progress undetected until irreversible liver damage has occurred.

The government's commitment to eliminating hepatitis C by 2030 must therefore translate into a coordinated national response rather than another ambitious declaration. The PM's Hepatitis Control Programme provides an existing framework, but its effectiveness depends heavily on implementation at the provincial and district levels. Health authorities must enforce strict sterilisation protocols and eliminate syringe reuse and strengthen the regulation of blood banks and private healthcare establishments.

With the 2030 elimination deadline approaching, the country has little time to squander. The tragedy is that a curable disease continues to claim thousands of lives because the healthcare system has failed to prevent its spread.

headline: NUST's triumph
description: 45 researchers from NUST ranked in world's top 2% of scientists
author: editorial
article_text:
The announcement that 45 researchers from the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST) have been ranked among the world's top 2% of scientists is a moment of genuine national pride. Data compiled by the prestigious Stanford University and academic publishing giant Elsevier places NUST and its faculty among the world's finest, crediting their work with advancing knowledge across disciplines. In a country where education-related headlines are usually limited to lacklustre education standards and dilapidated buildings, this is a reminder of what Pakistan can achieve when merit, investment and institutional vision align.

The achievement reflects decades of hard work. NUST's representation in the prestigious list has grown from 23 researchers in 2022 to 31 in 2023, 43 in 2024, and 47 in 2025. Although the number fell to 45 in 2026, it includes 16 scholars who have appeared consistently over successive years, which should be taken as proof of durable scholarly impact rather than fleeting recognition. It is also worth noting that the researchers' areas of expertise span AI, nanotechnology, biomedical engineering, cyber security, materials science and fluid mechanics, which is a breadth of expertise that any world-class university would envy.

In fact, they are a major reason why NUST itself is now a member of the world's elite - the university currently ranks 384th in the QS World University Rankings, was third in South Asia in last year's Asia ranking, and had more citations per paper than several universities ranked higher than it in both scales. If properly leveraged, these statistics could also be critical in making the university in particular, and Pakistan's academic sector in general, more attractive for foreign investment and collaboration.

At the same time, there is no doubt that there is room for improvement - being the best in Pakistan is akin to being the big fish in a small pond. If NUST's administration and faculty keep up the good work, the university could one day be one of the biggest fish in the ocean.

headline: Expanding AML powers: promise and pitfalls
description: Effectiveness will depend less on enlarging statutory powers than on institutional competence, accountability
author: Dr Ikramul Haq
article_text:
Pakistan's decision to expand its anti-money laundering framework represents a necessary response to evolving financial crimes. Its effectiveness, however, will depend less on enlarging statutory powers than on the institutional competence, accountability and constitutional safeguards governing their exercise.

On Oct 27, the National Executive Committee on Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism approved three significant measures: including maritime piracy among predicate offences under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (AMLA); recognising the Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (PVARA) as an AML/CFT regulator; and raising the currency transaction reporting threshold from Rs2 million to Rs3 million. These measures deserve careful examination.

First, the reference to piracy concerns maritime piracy under section 28 of the Pakistan Maritime Zones Act, 2023, not infringement of intellectual property. Section 29 already prescribes imprisonment extending to ten years for piracy, with more severe punishment where murder is committed. Separately, section 4 of AMLA provides imprisonment extending to ten years, a fine up to Rs25 million and forfeiture for money laundering.

Making piracy a predicate offence enables investigators to pursue criminal proceeds arising from maritime offences. It does not automatically establish money laundering whenever piracy occurs. The prosecution must establish the statutory ingredients of laundering and the criminal origin of the property. This distinction matters because Pakistan's enforcement history demonstrates how expansive powers can become instruments of harassment when legal safeguards are disregarded.

The inclusion is consistent with the FATF framework, which identifies piracy among designated categories of predicate offences. However, the Committee's approval must be followed by the legally required notification and implementation arrangements. An executive announcement cannot substitute for statutory compliance.

Second, PVARA's inclusion in Schedule IV of AMLA, has greater economic significance. Virtual assets present opportunities for investment, financial innovation and cross-border payments. They also create risks involving anonymous ownership structures, rapid movement of funds, sanctions evasion, fraud and concealment of criminal proceeds.

Licensing alone cannot establish effective supervision. PVARA must develop enforceable standards for beneficial ownership identification, customer due diligence, suspicious transaction reporting, blockchain analytics, asset segregation and compliance with FATF's Travel Rule.

Coordination with SBP, SECP, FMU and investigating agencies is indispensable. Regulatory overlap without clearly defined responsibilities will create confusion rather than accountability.

Third, increasing the cash transaction reporting threshold to Rs3 million requires particular caution. Reducing unnecessary reporting can improve the quality of financial intelligence. However, criminals can structure transactions below prescribed thresholds. Banks must therefore maintain effective suspicious transaction monitoring irrespective of transaction amounts. A higher reporting threshold must never become a safe harbour for illicit funds.

The proposed extension of AML investigative powers to provincial anti-corruption establishments raises another concern. Without transparent procedures, trained investigators, independent supervision and judicial safeguards, these powers may become instruments of selective prosecution.

Articles 4, 10A, 14 and 24 of the Constitution require legality, due process, respect for privacy and protection against arbitrary deprivation of property. Lack of laws has never been a challenge. There has been a longstanding proposal for coordinated financial-crime intelligence, specialised prosecution and meaningful institutional accountability. AI can improve transaction monitoring and asset tracing, but automated suspicion must never replace admissible evidence and judicial scrutiny.

The real measure of reform is not the number of offences added to statutory schedules or regulators granted additional powers. It is whether criminal proceeds are detected, successfully prosecuted and recovered without victimising innocent citizens or legitimate businesses.

Coordination with SBP, SECP, FMU and investigating agencies is indispensable. Regulatory overlap without clearly defined responsibilities will create confusion rather than accountability.

Third, increasing the cash transaction reporting threshold to Rs3 million requires particular caution. Reducing unnecessary reporting can improve the quality of financial intelligence. However, criminals can structure transactions below prescribed thresholds. Banks must therefore maintain effective suspicious transaction monitoring irrespective of transaction amounts. A higher reporting threshold must never become a safe harbour for illicit funds.

The proposed extension of AML investigative powers to provincial anti-corruption establishments raises another concern. Without transparent procedures, trained investigators, independent supervision and judicial safeguards, these powers may become instruments of selective prosecution.

Articles 4, 10A, 14 and 24 of the Constitution require legality, due process, respect for privacy and protection against arbitrary deprivation of property. Lack of laws has never been a challenge. There has been a longstanding proposal for coordinated financial-crime intelligence, specialised prosecution and meaningful institutional accountability. AI can improve transaction monitoring and asset tracing, but automated suspicion must never replace admissible evidence and judicial scrutiny.

The real measure of reform is not the number of offences added to statutory schedules or regulators granted additional powers. It is whether criminal proceeds are detected, successfully prosecuted and recovered without victimising innocent citizens or legitimate businesses.

headline: State of the state
description: Dictatorships may have concentrated more power through extra-constitutional means, but resistance was also stronger
author: Fahd Husain
article_text:
The state today is the master of all it surveys. That should concern it.

It has been a very long time since so much power was concentrated in so few hands. Such power is defined not just by the ability of the powerbrokers to bend others to their will, but also to the level of resistance to such power. In times of unalloyed dictatorships, the concentration of power through extra-constitutional levers may have been more, but so was the resistance from those at the wrong end of the stick.

Not so today.

With all other branches of the state weakened at the expense of the executive, and with the political opposition quasi-emasculated, there is nothing that the state seems to fear. Its control is total. Its will has hardened. It will bend those who must bend, and those who do not, it will break.

When the state reaches such a state, it runs risks. One such risk is not knowing when to lay down the stick and pick up the carrot. This is a classic by-product of the dilution of the system's checks and balances. In today's situation, nothing illustrates this more vividly than the state's approach towards the opposition.

The opposition is in a mess. Even the opposition acknowledges this. Ever since the PTI lost its government in Khyber-Pukhthunkhwa, it has been flailing around trying to figure out what to do and whom to blame. The PTI's leadership is, on a daily basis, mocked by the PTI's leadership. And by its massive support base. Even the staunchest supporters of the party take solace in the argument that the party leadership matters not. The party, they say with sound logic, is just one man. That man remains as popular as ever, despite the party leadership's embarrassing failures to hold itself together.

If the PTI is in a shambles, the TTAP is not helping it either. In fact, probably on the contrary. Holding the two most prestigious offices that the opposition holds, the TTAP leadership has a leading role in terms of the opposition's political strategy. Yet, the leader of the opposition in the National Assembly is himself being seen as part of the problem by many within the PTI ranks. He remains offensive in his approach towards negotiations with the government even though many within the PTI believe that their leader in Adiala appointed him for his experience in guiding the opposition through tricky political situations. Well, today is as tricky as tricky gets.

The opposition finds itself out of power, out of ideas, and frankly, out of options. Which is the exact spot where the state should engage it. But the fear is that – in its hubris – the state will miss the opportunity.

It will miss it because the political input coming from the government for the state is, at best, recommendatory in nature. There is little pushback if the state is resistant to this input. The power imbalance, and the dilution of checks and balances, has skewed the system's dynamics in such a way that juggernaut of the state feeds more on its sheer momentum than on the logic of a given situation. With the two political parties within the ruling setup concerned more with the protection and promotion of their provincial domains, the Centre just does not seem to carry the political heft needed to inject its input into the state's fuel tank. They all prefer to just go with the flow.

That flow is ensuring that once the state has the opposition's back to the wall – as it does now – it prefers to break the back and the wall instead of bringing it back into the fold. The PTI is vulnerable. It is looking for a way out of this corner. It needs political oxygen. This is the time for the state to engage it and find space for it under the huge tent. That's what good politics demands. That's what good statecraft demands.

But don't hold your breath.

Not for this, and not for other developments that need more carrots and less sticks. The hubris, the momentum, the uber-confidence, the lack of pushback, the geo-strategic grandstanding, all of these are propelling the state into a state where its ability to weigh the costs and benefits of its actions dispassionately is weakening. The hammer-and-nail approach to dealing with human rights activists, journalists, opposition members and any one else who may not be ready and willing to say "yes sir, yes sir, three bags full" can be a recipe for consequential problems further down.

There are major reforms on the way. The 28th Amendment may still be under wraps, but it is a work in progress. One hears of many other sweeping changes to the governance architecture being considered. The power wielders say such mega changes require the state to cross all hurdles that are usually placed in the way of reforms that undercut vested interests. The ability to remove these hurdles, and to prevail over any resistance is, these people say, the true measure of the state's resolve to do the right thing.

While there may be merit in many of these reforms – smaller administrative units, empowered local governments – the fact is that done wrong, these reforms can create more problems than solve them. Doing them right means taking everyone along as much as possible. It means not rushing through decisions without painstaking consultations and deliberations and discussions. It also means creating an environment that is conducive to such deliberations and discussions. In fact, it also means realising that carrots are often much more useful than sticks.

It is precisely when the state is at its strongest that it must reach out to those that do not agree with its policies. We may be divided into political, social and institutional groupings, but we all unite under one flag. That's the north star that should guide those who wield the most power in today's Pakistan.

Doing them right means taking everyone along as much as possible. It means not rushing through decisions without painstaking consultations and deliberations and discussions. It also means creating an environment that is conducive to such deliberations and discussions. In fact, it also means realising that carrots are often much more useful than sticks.

It is precisely when the state is at its strongest that it must reach out to those that do not agree with its policies. We may be divided into political, social and institutional groupings, but we all unite under one flag. That's the north star that should guide those who wield the most power in today's Pakistan.

headline: Two leaders and their political twilight
description: Resuming hostilities may help Netanyahu and Trump regain political ground, but the consequences could be far-reaching
author: Dr Muhammad Ali Ehsan
article_text:
Today, the world fears the final, dangerous act in the twilight of what has become the world's most consequential and controversial bilateral partnership. It is a partnership sustained by the overwhelming power of one benefactor, the United States, and the relentless disregard for international law and human values by its malefactor, the state of Israel. Today, both leaders confront mounting political uncertainty at home. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has failed to secure a majority in the recently concluded Israeli elections, while opinion polls increasingly point towards a defeat for President Donald Trump in the upcoming US midterm elections.

What makes this political predicament dangerous is the possibility that the war against Iran could become a strategic gamble and disaster from which neither leader can afford to retreat. At 77, Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is set to continue as interim prime minister until fresh elections next year seek to resolve the deadlock in the Knesset. This arrangement could persist if Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's party remain committed to their declared refusal to form a coalition with the Arab parties, which have secured 19 seats and consequently emerged as potential kingmakers. Netanyahu, popularly known as 'Mr Security', has already abandoned Israel's traditional security doctrine of fighting short, limited wars of defence. Instead, he has presided over the country's longest-running military campaigns, fighting on multiple fronts, including Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The elimination of the Iranian regime has long been Netanyahu's overriding political objective. The 53 seats secured by his party in the latest elections suggest that a substantial section of Israeli society continues to endorse his approach. Now entering its ninth month, the US-Israeli war against Iran carries the danger of becoming something far more dangerous than a military confrontation. For two leaders facing electoral setbacks and eroding political credibility, the temptation to finish what they started may weigh heavier than the political wisdom of ending it.

The erosion of American influence and global credibility can be attributed to several factors, but one that stands out is the transformation of US statecraft into a system that increasingly divides the world into favoured and disfavoured regimes. Israel tops the list of US-favoured states, and the distinction in how the US treats the two categories has become an open secret. While the US routinely calls out governments it disapproves of for repression, tyranny and human rights abuses, it overlooks similar conduct by its allies and strategic partners.

Since 1972, the US has cast at least 45 vetoes against UNSC resolutions critical of Israel. American patronage, therefore, extends well beyond the economic and military assistance it provides to Israel. Its diplomatic protection has been equally consequential, shielding Israel from international accountability and emboldening it to pursue policies that contribute to global instability, disorder and an erosion of the international rules-based system.

One of the principal military justifications for going to war with Iran was to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons. The nuclear ambitions of Iraq, Libya and Syria, similarly, were treated as matters of grave international insecurity. Yet Israel's undeclared nuclear arsenal remains largely beyond the reach of the same international scrutiny. The only American president to openly challenge Israel over its nuclear ambitions was John F Kennedy. In 1961, Kennedy warned that American support for Israel could be seriously jeopardised if Washington's concerns over Israel's nuclear programme remained unresolved. He did not live long enough to witness the eventual trajectory of that programme.

Today, whenever an attempt is made to bring Israel's undeclared nuclear capabilities under discussion at IAEA, American influence becomes a big obstacle. The contrast is difficult to ignore as nuclear ambitions in adversarial states are presented as threats to global security. Such selective application of international norms not only speaks of an American inconsistency but also a wider failure of the US-led Western order to uphold the principles of justice, equality and accountability on which its legitimacy rests.

They say when you refuse to visit disorder, disorder eventually comes knocking at your own door. This is precisely the predicament confronting Europe and the wider West today. Having failed to uphold an international order grounded in justice, freedom and equality, the US and its European partners are now confronting the domestic consequences of their own political and strategic choices. The promises of the Western-led global order have hardly translated into meaningful benefits for much of the developing world, where poverty, inequality and political instability continue to persist. Nor has the Western world itself remained immune to the resulting consequences. Across Europe, political dissatisfaction is increasingly finding expression through the rise of populist and far-right movements. Countries such as France, Spain, Italy and Poland are witnessing growing political polarisation, while far-right parties have gained significant ground in countries including the Czech Republic, Finland, Slovakia and Croatia.

Public confidence in democracy and its ability to deliver is also showing signs of erosion. A recent Pew Research Center survey found that 69% of respondents in France, 68% in Spain, 62% in Italy and 69% in the US expressed declining optimism about democracy. The West has invested far more political capital and military resources in fighting wars of questionable necessity than in strengthening democratic institutions and delivering the social and economic dividends that make democracy meaningful. No wonder a growing numbers of Western citizens are gravitating towards populist movements and far-right politics.

The greatest danger confronting the world today is not only the possibility of another war with Iran, but also the strategic miscalculation that could accompany its recommencement. For Netanyahu and Trump, resuming hostilities may offer them an opportunity to recover lost political ground, but the consequences could extend far beyond their domestic political fortunes. A war restarted to rescue two embattled political careers could plunge an already fragile international order into an even deeper crisis. The world cannot afford to become the collateral damage of two leaders unwilling to accept their political twilight.
