headline: Why does our climate response collapse?
description: Pakistan’s disaster crisis isn't a lack of advanced weather tech, but an institutional failure of policy
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
By late September 2025, when the monsoon rains finally abated across the Indus River Basin, Pakistan found itself standing in an eerily familiar ruin. Three years after the catastrophic floods of 2022 submerged a third of the country, prompting international commitments and global pledges at climate summits, a new wave of flooding left more than 6.9 million people directly affected and forced over three million from their homes. The damage spanned across Pakistan's agricultural heartland, its northern mountain corridors, and its southern coastal delta. Over two million hectares of cropland were inundated—resulting in a staggering $1.23 billion in agricultural losses across Punjab, Sindh, and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa—while hundreds of thousands of homes, hundreds of bridges, and thousands of kilometres of roads were damaged or destroyed, according to UN OCHA. The central tragedy of Pakistan’s ongoing climate crisis is no longer a lack of meteorological awareness or scientific data, but rather the profound, structural failure of institutional translation—a systemic paralysis that occurs in the vast space between top-down federal policy and ground-level provincial execution.

A major indicator of state readiness is the ability to protect vulnerable populations before floodwaters strike. On paper, Pakistan’s technical capability to anticipate hydrometeorological hazards has advanced significantly over the last decade. National forecasting centres utilise satellite data, telemetry systems, and computer modeling to project seasonal precipitation and river flows. However, a comprehensive review conducted by Unesco on Pakistan’s Flood Early Warning System highlights a persistent–and deadly– breakdown known as ‘the last-mile gap’. Despite the forecasts, rural communities routinely experience what disaster management experts term ‘zero effective lead time’—the window between receiving an official warning and actually being able to evacuate or protect assets.

This failure stems from a reliance on inadequate communication infrastructure and the transmission of abstract technical data rather than localised instructions. A Unesco study reveals that warning dissemination relies heavily on GSM-based mobile networks and internet connectivity—something that routinely collapses during severe storm fronts and heavy rain. When electricity grids go offline, cellular towers lose backup power, cutting off text alerts exactly when hazards accelerate. Furthermore, state institutions operate under an administrative framework where technical alerts regarding cusecs of river discharge or millimetre levels of rainfall are passed down administrative chains without being converted into actionable guidance. A rural farmer does not need to know the discharge rate at a distant barrage; they need to know which roads will submerge, and which evacuation shelters are operational. When should they begin to move their livestock?

Where life-saving interventions succeed during disasters, it is rarely due to official state channels or coordinated government action. Instead, we witness informal community networks that step in to fill the institutional vacuum. During a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood in Gilgit-Baltistan’s Ghizer District in August 2025, it was a local shepherd who spotted rising upstream hazards and alerted village elders. The warning spread rapidly via mosque loudspeakers and local volunteers, enabling an entire community to evacuate before floodwaters arrived. While property was lost, lives were saved and there were no deaths. This reliance on human initiative highlights how community has become a necessary substitute for functional state mechanics. It exposes how weak the official disaster management framework remains when stripped of on-ground local human intervention.

The impact of climate events across Pakistan's provinces reveals distinct governance vulnerabilities where local policy failures continuously amplify natural hazards. In Punjab, last year’s floods breached the banks of the Sutlej, Ravi, Jhelum, and Chenab rivers, creating the worst riverine flooding the province had seen in four decades. According to data by international relief agencies, over 1.1 million hectares of agricultural land were affected in Punjab alone, representing nearly 10 percent of the province’s total cultivated area, while Sindh suffered similar vast crop losses across its southern farming belts. The devastation was not caused solely by rain, but was exacerbated by decades of riverbed encroachment, unmonitored commercial development along natural drainage basins, and the systematic neglect of flood protection embankments. When water levels rose, natural drainage pathways were blocked by illegal constructions, turning agricultural heartlands into temporary lakes and triggering a steep spike in basic food prices within weeks.

In the northern mountain corridors, rapid-onset flash floods, landslides, and glofs present a different set of severe operational challenges. As per the World Economic Forum, Pakistan’s glaciers sustain over 220 million people downstream but are melting at accelerating rates, giving rise to over 3,000 glacial lakes, dozens of which are classified as highly dangerous and prone to sudden breach. While donor-funded initiatives have installed early-warning hardware and gabion walls across two dozen valleys, provincial institutions lack the sustained funding, technical personnel, and heavy machinery needed to maintain these assets over time. When flash floods strike, mountain highways and bridges are destroyed, isolating entire districts for weeks because provincial disaster management authorities lack decentralised equipment stocks in high-altitude zones. In 2026, despite advanced meteorological mapping and early evacuations of over 10,000 people, mountain road and bridge collapses exposed persistent last-mile gaps, forcing rescuers to travel hours on foot while rural communities relied on local volunteers for survival.

The deep structural inequities across Pakistan's federal framework are further quantified in the District Resilience Index by an Islamabad based think tank. Evaluating 130 districts across human capital, economic security, standard of living, and infrastructure, the index exposes a wide gap in state preparedness across regions. Highly developed urban centres like Lahore score at the top of the index due to their administrative density and centralised state resources, whereas peripheral districts, in Balochistan for example, score at the absolute bottom due to the complete absence of local municipal governance and minimal health infrastructure. This disparity explains why disaster recovery in far-flung areas often stalls completely once media coverage fades. These neglected districts lack the fiscal reserves and municipal capacity needed to process relief claims or reconstruct infrastructure, leaving displaced populations in long-term vulnerability.

Pakistan’s slow disaster response over the last two years is not an operational accident, but the predictable outcome of three entrenched structural traps within its political economy. The single greatest institutional obstacle to disaster resilience is the complete absence of empowered local governments. While constitutional amendments devolved significant powers from the federal to the provinces, provincial capitals have largely retained authority rather than passing resources and decision-making power down to elected district and municipal councils. When a flood hits, a District Disaster Management Authority often consists of a handful of civil servants operating with minimal budgets, no dedicated emergency machinery, and limited authority to act without explicit approval from provincial headquarters. Without local governance bodies, there are no formal channels for grievance redressal, no local risk assessments, and no municipal crews to clear drainage channels before monsoon seasons arrive.

At the same time, state policy remains bound to a reactive framework. Following every major disaster, government actions focus almost entirely on grants through social protection networks, emergency tents, and dry food rations. While essential for immediate survival, these short-term relief measures swallow emergency budgets, leaving almost no funds for proactive adaptation. Projects aimed at long-term adaptation—such as an internationally grant-funded $77.8 million project to restore natural wetlands and aquifers across high-risk sites in DI Khan, Chakar Lehri, and Manchhar Lake—are routinely sidelined. Consequently, the state spends billions repeatedly repairing infrastructure destroyed by predictable seasonal events.

This system is further compounded by how state response mechanisms routinely fail marginalised groups, including landless farmers, women, religious minorities, and displaced populations. Relief distribution routinely depends on national identity cards and official land titles. In rural provinces, where labourers operate under informal agricultural arrangements and women face lower rates of formal documentation, thousands of displaced families are systematically excluded from official relief registries. State aid structures assume a formal household framework that does not reflect rural social realities, leaving vulnerable groups reliant on charity and feudal patrons.

What state institutions continue to treat as unprecedented disasters are no longer unexpected anomalies; they have fully solidified into a fixed climate pattern. Just as the arrival of winter brings a predictable smog season that smothers urban centres across Punjab, the summer monsoons and accelerated glacial melt now bring an annual flood season with absolute regularity. Natural disasters in Pakistan have permanently transitioned from rare events into recurring seasonal cycles that arrive like clockwork year after year. Treating each monsoon or toxic air crisis as an unforeseen emergency reflects an obsolete governance mindset that actively undermines national stability.

The state must recognise that climate events are now as structural to Pakistan's calendar as fiscal budget cycles. Preparing for an annual flood season requires the same institutional permanence as collecting revenue or maintaining national defense. When a disaster occurs every 12 months, the governance model cannot remain anchored in temporary relief camps, ad-hoc committees, and emergency appeals to the international community.

If Pakistan is to break this cycle of recurrent disaster and slow recovery, its climate response strategy must shift fundamentally from emergency reaction to permanent structural adaptation. Transitioning away from this institutional dysfunction requires empowering local municipal councils with direct operational authority and fiscal resources so that district authorities can maintain drainage and civil defense infrastructure year-round. Forecasting bodies must focus on impact-based messaging that translates technical meteorological data into practical on-ground instructions delivered through robust offline channels, like mosques and sirens. Furthermore, provincial assemblies must strictly enforce floodplain zoning to prevent illegal encroachments while formalising relief access so that undocumented populations are not left behind when disaster strikes. Pakistan’s climate crisis is fundamentally a crisis of governance. Until the state builds a permanent administrative infrastructure designed to handle a predictable climate calendar, every passing season will remain an unpredictable, unavoidable human tragedy.

Over two million hectares of cropland were inundated—resulting in a staggering $1.23 billion in agricultural losses across Punjab, Sindh, and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa—while hundreds of thousands of homes, hundreds of bridges, and thousands of kilometres of roads were damaged or destroyed, according to UN OCHA. Despite the forecasts, rural communities routinely experience what disaster management experts term ‘zero effective lead time’—the window between receiving an official warning and actually being able to evacuate or protect assets.

This failure stems from a reliance on inadequate communication infrastructure and the transmission of abstract technical data rather than localised instructions. A Unesco study reveals that warning dissemination relies heavily on GSM-based mobile networks and internet connectivity—something that routinely collapses during severe storm fronts and heavy rain. When electricity grids go offline, cellular towers lose backup power, cutting off text alerts exactly when hazards accelerate. headline: The war behind the Ukraine war
description: An exploration of geopolitical rivalries, competing narratives, diplomatic failures and the devastating global consequences of the Russia–Ukraine conflict.
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
The Russia–Ukraine war has generated an extraordinary volume of political commentary, military analysis and international media coverage. Yet much of the prevailing discourse remains confined to competing accusations, battlefield developments and the geopolitical positions of major powers. In Ukraine War – Beyond the Headlines: An Alternative Narrative on the Crisis, Pakistani journalist and geopolitical analyst Munir Ahmed attempts to widen this conversation by examining the historical circumstances, strategic calculations and diplomatic failures that preceded the conflict, alongside its far-reaching consequences for the international order.

The book's central proposition is that the Ukraine war cannot be adequately understood through the events of February 2022 alone. Rather, the author situates the conflict within a longer history of post-Cold War geopolitical restructuring, NATO's eastward expansion, Russia's evolving security perceptions and the increasingly contentious relationship between Moscow and Western capitals.

This approach distinguishes the book from conventional battlefield narratives. Instead of concentrating primarily on military operations, Ahmed explores the political environment in which confrontation became increasingly likely. He raises questions about whether European security arrangements following the Soviet Union's dissolution sufficiently accommodated the concerns of all major stakeholders, and whether diplomatic opportunities were neglected before hostilities escalated.

A particularly significant dimension of the book is its examination of the events surrounding Ukraine's political upheaval in 2014, the subsequent confrontation in eastern Ukraine and the deterioration of relations between Russia and the West. These developments are presented as essential historical reference points for understanding the conflict's origins. Such an interpretation invites scrutiny, however, because explaining Russia's security concerns does not, in itself, justify its invasion of Ukraine or diminish Ukraine's sovereignty and right to determine its political future.

Ahmed's treatment of international power politics extends beyond Russia and Ukraine. The US, EU, NATO and China feature in his broader assessment of strategic competition and the emergence of an increasingly fragmented international system. The conflict is considered not merely as a regional war but as a manifestation of changing global power relationships, with implications for international institutions, economic alliances and the future balance of influence.

One of the book's more compelling themes is the economic and humanitarian cost of prolonged warfare. The destruction of infrastructure, displacement of millions of people, disruption of agricultural production and pressure on global energy markets demonstrate how a conflict concentrated geographically in Eastern Europe has affected societies far beyond the battlefield.

Particularly relevant for developing countries is the discussion of food insecurity, inflation and rising energy costs. Ukraine and Russia have historically occupied important positions in international grain and commodity markets. Disruptions associated with the conflict have therefore created serious challenges for import-dependent economies, illustrating the vulnerability of global supply chains to geopolitical confrontation.

The environmental consequences of warfare provide another noteworthy perspective. Damage to industrial facilities, agricultural land, water resources and energy infrastructure raises questions about the long-term ecological legacy of armed conflict. By incorporating environmental destruction into the geopolitical discussion, Ahmed draws attention to costs that often receive less consideration than territorial changes and military expenditures.

The book also examines the limitations of international diplomacy and the role of the military-industrial complex in sustaining global security competition. Its discussion of negotiations, competing strategic interests and the difficulties of achieving a durable settlement encourages readers to consider whether continued militarisation can deliver the security that political dialogue has failed to establish.

The preface by Lt Gen (Retd) Muhammad Asad Durrani, Pakistan's former intelligence chief and an established author on strategic affairs, adds a distinctive security-policy perspective to the publication. It also places the work within a wider tradition of critical examination of international power politics.

As an alternative geopolitical interpretation, the book's strength lies in challenging readers to examine assumptions and consider perspectives that may be underrepresented in dominant Western narratives. Its analytical approach nevertheless demands careful distinction between documented historical developments, contested political claims and interpretations of strategic intentions. An alternative narrative becomes most persuasive when it subjects all competing accounts, including those advanced by Moscow, to equally rigorous scrutiny.

Ultimately, Ukraine War – Beyond the Headlines, offers a thought-provoking contribution to discussions about one of the 21st century's most consequential conflicts. Its principal value lies not in providing a definitive explanation of the war, but in encouraging a broader examination of its origins, international dimensions and enduring consequences.

For students of international relations, journalists, policymakers and readers interested in geopolitics, the book offers an opportunity to reconsider the conflict beyond immediate headlines and to reflect on a fundamental question: can sustainable peace emerge from military confrontation, or must it ultimately rest upon diplomacy, mutual security arrangements and respect for international law?

By Saaref Haares |
facebook twitter whatsup linkded email
PUBLISHED November 01, 2026

The Russia–Ukraine war has generated an extraordinary volume of political commentary, military analysis and international media coverage. Yet much of the prevailing discourse remains confined to competing accusations, battlefield developments and the geopolitical positions of major powers. In Ukraine War – Beyond the Headlines: An Alternative Narrative on the Crisis, Pakistani journalist and geopolitical analyst Munir Ahmed attempts to widen this conversation by examining the historical circumstances, strategic calculations and diplomatic failures that preceded the conflict, alongside its far-reaching consequences for the international order.

The book's central proposition is that the Ukraine war cannot be adequately understood through the events of February 2022 alone. Rather, the author situates the conflict within a longer history of post-Cold War geopolitical restructuring, NATO's eastward expansion, Russia's evolving security perceptions and the increasingly contentious relationship between Moscow and Western capitals.

This approach distinguishes the book from conventional battlefield narratives. Instead of concentrating primarily on military operations, Ahmed explores the political environment in which confrontation became increasingly likely. He raises questions about whether European security arrangements following the Soviet Union's dissolution sufficiently accommodated the concerns of all major stakeholders, and whether diplomatic opportunities were neglected before hostilities escalated.

A particularly significant dimension of the book is its examination of the events surrounding Ukraine's political upheaval in 2014, the subsequent confrontation in eastern Ukraine and the deterioration of relations between Russia and the West. These developments are presented as essential historical reference points for understanding the conflict's origins. Such an interpretation invites scrutiny, however, because explaining Russia's security concerns does not, in itself, justify its invasion of Ukraine or diminish Ukraine's sovereignty and right to determine its political future.

Ahmed's treatment of international power politics extends beyond Russia and Ukraine. The US, EU, NATO and China feature in his broader assessment of strategic competition and the emergence of an increasingly fragmented international system. The conflict is considered not merely as a regional war but as a manifestation of changing global power relationships, with implications for international institutions, economic alliances and the future balance of influence.

One of the book's more compelling themes is the economic and humanitarian cost of prolonged warfare. The destruction of infrastructure, displacement of millions of people, disruption of agricultural production and pressure on global energy markets demonstrate how a conflict concentrated geographically in Eastern Europe has affected societies far beyond the battlefield.

Particularly relevant for developing countries is the discussion of food insecurity, inflation and rising energy costs. Ukraine and Russia have historically occupied important positions in international grain and commodity markets. Disruptions associated with the conflict have therefore created serious challenges for import-dependent economies, illustrating the vulnerability of global supply chains to geopolitical confrontation.

The environmental consequences of warfare provide another noteworthy perspective. Damage to industrial facilities, agricultural land, water resources and energy infrastructure raises questions about the long-term ecological legacy of armed conflict. By incorporating environmental destruction into the geopolitical discussion, Ahmed draws attention to costs that often receive less consideration than territorial changes and military expenditures.

The book also examines the limitations of international diplomacy and the role of the military-industrial complex in sustaining global security competition. Its discussion of negotiations, competing strategic interests and the difficulties of achieving a durable settlement encourages readers to consider whether continued militarisation can deliver the security that political dialogue has failed to establish.

The preface by Lt Gen (Retd) Muhammad Asad Durrani, Pakistan's former intelligence chief and an established author on strategic affairs, adds a distinctive security-policy perspective to the publication. It also places the work within a wider tradition of critical examination of international power politics.

As an alternative geopolitical interpretation, the book's strength lies in challenging readers to examine assumptions and consider perspectives that may be underrepresented in dominant Western narratives. Its analytical approach nevertheless demands careful distinction between documented historical developments, contested political claims and interpretations of strategic intentions. An alternative narrative becomes most persuasive when it subjects all competing accounts, including those advanced by Moscow, to equally rigorous scrutiny.

Ultimately, Ukraine War – Beyond the Headlines, offers a thought-provoking contribution to discussions about one of the 21st century's most consequential conflicts. Its principal value lies not in providing a definitive explanation of the war, but in encouraging a broader examination of its origins, international dimensions and enduring consequences.

For students of international relations, journalists, policymakers and readers interested in geopolitics, the book offers an opportunity to reconsider the conflict beyond immediate headlines and to reflect on a fundamental question: can sustainable peace emerge from military confrontation, or must it ultimately rest upon diplomacy, mutual security arrangements and respect for international law?

headline: The language of solitude
description: Bringing together original fiction and Urdu translations, Blue Glass explores the complexities of solitude and the human experience
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
In our increasingly fast-paced world, casual readers do not have time to go through weighty tomes and may instead prefer shorter pieces. For those readers who instinctively gravitate towards fiction, short stories are the ideal form, tailor-made for their modern-day lifestyles, characterised by limited attention spans and the constant tussle between different mediums to capture their interest.

Be that as it may, fiction writers don't choose their form based on sheer convenience. In an introductory note to a compendium of her short fiction, titled The Complete Stories, Booker-shortlisted author Anita Desai states that the length of a story depends heavily on the "element of chance". "Each form requires a different set of abilities," she asserts, "Brevity and concision will do for one while the other requires doubt, mystery, mistake and stamina."

Known as a publisher, printmaker and photographer, Shahbano Alvi has also emerged as a promising, prolific writer of short fiction. Her stories are not only concise, but also seem to have been produced at a rapid pace – a reminder that stamina is required for both long and short pieces. Blue Glass, her third collection, has been released almost four years after her debut compilation of stories and over a year after her second. It brings together Shahbano Alvi's different avatars as both a short-story writer in English and a translator of Urdu short fiction. The first section of the collection consists of Alvi's own stories. The second contains her translations of four stories by respected Urdu writer Zaheda Hina.

Fuelled by these dual impulses, the collection carries the echoes of Urdu and English, and attempts to build a bridge between both languages. This is a noble pursuit in the context of Pakistan, where Urdu and English have been locked in a persistent battle for hegemony.

Over the decades, cynical readers have argued that literature in Urdu truly captures the country's cultural zeitgeist while English is merely a tragic remnant of the subcontinent's encounter with colonialism. The latter is perceived as the language of the elite while the former enjoys mainstream appeal. Faced with linguistic dichotomies, writers in both Urdu and English have often kept a quiet distance from each other. Alvi attempts to erase these invisible barriers by making a voyage between both languages.

At first, it seems somewhat unusual for an author to place her own creative output alongside her translated works. However, this crisscrossing of boundaries among genres isn't an entirely new technique. This year's Nobel Prize for Literature has been awarded to an author who seamlessly blends genres. Writers, therefore, aren’t bound by any restrictions on what they can do with their canvas.

What may surprise some readers is Alvi's willingness to share the limelight with another author. In a fiercely competitive literary world where everyone wants to spotlight their own achievements, a collaborative endeavour of this nature would likely be viewed as an anomaly. Therefore, Alvi's keen interest in creative synergies is a lesson that artistic collaborations can be rewarding.

Blue Glass is a radical departure from Alvi's debut collection of stories A Woman and the Afternoon Sun (2021), which employed a lush, unsentimental voice in tales spanning multiple genres. Her latest offering is also fundamentally distinct from her sophomore collection A New Pigeon on the Block, which provided poignant reflections on migration, loneliness and grief. While the second collection contained pieces of varying lengths, the shorter pieces were often overshadowed by the longer ones.

Alvi's ten stories in Blue Glass predominantly fall under the category of flash fiction. Even so, these tales possess a distinct sense of completeness and readers seldom feel short-changed by their length. In fact, many of the flash pieces stand out for their polished, pristine prose and keen eye for detail. Through stories that unfold across a few pages, Alvi retains her quiet, detached narrative voice that has come to define her signature literary style.

Animals figure prominently in some of the stories and serve as a testament to the author's deep affinity with sentient non-humans. In 'A Boy, a Lame Wolf, and the River', an unnamed boy and a mountain wolf with a limp separately embark on an unusual spiritual quest to explore the mysteries of a mighty river. The motivations behind their curiosity with the meandering river vary, but they are united by their single-minded devotion to understand its place in the universe. The tale has the trappings of a conventional fable and is imbued with a valuable lesson about how living beings aren’t always in stiff competition with one another.

The desire for peaceful coexistence between sentient beings recurs in 'Bangalore Town'. The title instantly brings to mind one of Karachi's upscale neighbourhoods, and readers will naturally expect a story set in one of the locality's posh houses. However, the narrator deceives readers with the promise of a story they wish to hear, only to tell them a tale they need to appreciate. The reader is drawn into the narrative through captivating insights into how the neighbourhood has evolved over the decade before the story mysteriously shifts gears. 'Bangalore Town' is unconcerned with the lives of the neighbourhood's elite. Instead, it explores the struggle of a starving rag-picker who competes with a stray dog for a piece of bread in a garbage heap. Mercifully, neither of them is made to compromise on their needs. They learn how to share in a city where resources are limited. Yet, readers are left with a lingering sense of discomfort as they wonder whether such conflicts can be resolved amicably in real-life scenarios. 'The Mugger' is another intriguing tale about our fear of nature and the numerous creatures who rely on it. At its core, the story highlights humankind's alarming capacity to inflict harm.

Inanimate objects assume a life of their own in Alvi's stories and are frequently granted life-like qualities. Since they aren't driven by the same compulsions as humans, these objects emerge as neutral observers of people and their eccentricities, and often view their antics from a different lens than we are accustomed to. In 'The Ceiling Fan and the Blue Room', the eponymous objects keep vigil for a reclusive man who derives pleasure from his own solitude.

The pale ceiling fan and the blue walls of this room are confronted with a challenge: they don't fully comprehend the man's psyche or understand his dilemma. However, their curiosity knows no bounds and they are troubled by his desire for seclusion. The story reverses the stereotypical idea that only human beings are curious about their surroundings; in some exceptional cases, our surroundings are equally curious about our wellbeing.

'The Blue Glass Bottle and the Delft Pepper Shaker' doesn't view the ornaments placed on a polished oak sideboard as lifeless bric-a-brac with no connection to reality. Instead, these objects dance off the page as full-fledged characters plagued by a complex network of unspoken fears and frustrations. After a male-shaped Dutch salt shaker breaks into pieces, his counterpart – the pepper shaker who resembles a woman – finds herself somewhat bereft. A blue glass bottle, which remains a secondary character in the story, comes through as a saviour of sorts amid a climate of chaos. But it cannot spare the characters from their tragic fate. Curiously enough, the plight of the salt and pepper shakers mirror that of The house’s inhabitants, a couple who remain on the periphery of the tale. Ambitious in its scope, 'The Blue Glass Bottle and the Delft Pepper Shaker' offers an intriguing glimpse at the complex workings of grief from a cold, measured perspective.

Not all of Alvi’s stories approach the challenges faced by humans with the detached eye of a stranger. In fact, some of Alvi's tales centralise the lingering effects of the pain individuals endure as they cope with life's adversities. 'Anonymous' offers a sensitive, poignant portrait of the ways in which street crimes have plagued the lives of Karachi's citizens. The story offers a haunting image of a criminal’s blood blending with that of a victim. This disturbing visual lurks in the reader's mind long after the story comes to an end. Many readers might even wonder how the battle lines can be drawn when street crimes are linked to an overarching financial crisis and blood is being shed indiscriminately. In 'The Weeping Willow and the Jacaranda,' the quagmires faced by street children as well as women shackled by patriarchal demands assume centre-stage. The two-part tale offers a powerful evocation of human suffering. In addition, it stands out for its knowledgeable reflections on trees that are, by turns, a narrative foil and a symbol of hope amid distress.

A vast majority of the stories in the first section highlight the importance of solitude as an antidote to misery. Using the crippling realities of the pandemic as a springboard, 'Cold Walls' reveals how confinement becomes a source of relief. Separately, 'Emperor of the Night' features a garrulous family whose endless chatter inadvertently subdues the voice of a neighbourhood stray dog. As a result, the voiceless creature only finds the freedom to howl and "be himself...in the stillness of human-less nights." Alvi's tale is a breathtaking reminder of the ways in which an overpowering desire to fill silences with words can undermine solitude.

The centrepiece of Alvi's collection is undoubtedly 'Mosaic: Tesserae of Life', a tale consisting of five vignettes that reveal some familiar and shocking realities of the human condition. Each anecdote introduces a character and offers a detailed exploration of their emotional and spiritual challenges. The first two sketches capture the highs and lows of parent-child relationships and personal ambition. The third vignette fashions a warbler perched on an old oak tree into a tender witness to a series of curious happenings at a farm. The last two sketches have a darker, sombre quality and examine the stultifying effects of social and political oppression. Barring the final sketch, each of these episodic tales ends with the character's name. This serves a refreshing reminder of the ways in which names can individualise experiences that are universal.

Alvi's short fiction is not only defined by its cast of compelling characters, but also by its overpowering narrative voice. More often than not, the detached narrators of her tales confine characters within specific bounds and carry the weight of the entire story on their own shoulders. Sometimes, they are possessed by a desire to offer explanations, delay the climax or a moment of revelation, and elide certain details. Some readers might initially be thrown off by the exceedingly controlled narrative voice. Once they finish the first section, they might begin to understand why some of her characters need to keep within boundaries as they are capable of self-destruction. The narrator, therefore, shields the characters from revealing too much of their inner turmoil and darkness.

The section on Zaheda Hina's stories is equally intriguing. The Urdu writer's translated stories have characters with itinerant souls who fashion homes in foreign lands. Their lives are radically altered by multiple migrations and, in some cases, the weight of history.

As the blurb by Aamer Hussein on the back cover of Blue Glass suggests, the translations of Zaheda Hina's work "provide fascinating parallels and contrasts" to Alvi's storytelling techniques. Zaheda Hina's stories don't maintain a cold distance from their subjects – a quality that is evident in Alvi’s stories. Instead, the narrators of her four tales venture into the landscape of emotions with comparative ease.

Fuelled by a longing for a forgotten era, 'Hear Me Surayya' skilfully employs the second-person voice to show how the vicissitudes of time rob people of happiness and certainty. Using the first-person voice to great effect, 'Echoes of Twilight' chronicles the experiences of a woman who carries the memories of those she loved as she traverses geographical boundaries in search of new beginnings. Narrated in the detached third-person voice, 'The Babylonian Well of Solitude' juxtaposes ignorance of centuries-old philosophical traditions from the East with the anxieties of a post-9/11 Western milieu. With its stunning evocation of the unusual ways in which different worlds intersect, 'There Was Once a Somebody and a Nobody...' offers a poignant tale featuring multiple tragedies. The piece is interspersed with translations of Urdu and Persian poetry, including that of the 14th Century poet Hafiz.

A rich, inventive collection, Blue Glass offers a thought-provoking glimpse into solitude, despair and the intricacies of the human experience.

The writer is a critically acclaimed author

By Taha Kehar |

PUBLISHED November 01, 2026

In our increasingly fast-paced world, casual readers do not have time to go through weighty tomes and may instead prefer shorter pieces. For those readers who instinctively gravitate towards fiction, short stories are the ideal form, tailor-made for their modern-day lifestyles, characterised by limited attention spans and the constant tussle between different mediums to capture their interest.

Be that as it may, fiction writers don't choose their form based on sheer convenience. In an introductory note to a compendium of her short fiction, titled The Complete Stories, Booker-shortlisted author Anita Desai states that the length of a story depends heavily on the "element of chance". "Each form requires a different set of abilities," she asserts, "Brevity and concision will do for one while the other requires doubt, mystery, mistake and stamina."

Known as a publisher, printmaker and photographer, Shahbano Alvi has also emerged as a promising, prolific writer of short fiction. Her stories are not only concise, but also seem to have been produced at a rapid pace – a reminder that stamina is required for both long and short pieces. Blue Glass, her third collection, has been released almost four years after her debut compilation of stories and over a year after her second. It brings together Shahbano Alvi's different avatars as both a short-story writer in English and a translator of Urdu short fiction. The first section of the collection consists of Alvi's own stories. The second contains her translations of four stories by respected Urdu writer Zaheda Hina.

Fuelled by these dual impulses, the collection carries the echoes of Urdu and English, and attempts to build a bridge between both languages. This is a noble pursuit in the context of Pakistan, where Urdu and English have been locked in a persistent battle for hegemony.

Over the decades, cynical readers have argued that literature in Urdu truly captures the country's cultural zeitgeist while English is merely a tragic remnant of the subcontinent's encounter with colonialism. The latter is perceived as the language of the elite while the former enjoys mainstream appeal. Faced with linguistic dichotomies, writers in both Urdu and English have often kept a quiet distance from each other. Alvi attempts to erase these invisible barriers by making a voyage between both languages.

At first, it seems somewhat unusual for an author to place her own creative output alongside her translated works. However, this crisscrossing of boundaries among genres isn't an entirely new technique. This year's Nobel Prize for Literature has been awarded to an author who seamlessly blends genres. Writers, therefore, aren’t bound by any restrictions on what they can do with their canvas.

What may surprise some readers is Alvi's willingness to share the limelight with another author. In a fiercely competitive literary world where everyone wants to spotlight their own achievements, a collaborative endeavour of this nature would likely be viewed as an anomaly. Therefore, Alvi's keen interest in creative synergies is a lesson that artistic collaborations can be rewarding.

Blue Glass is a radical departure from Alvi's debut collection of stories A Woman and the Afternoon Sun (2021), which employed a lush, unsentimental voice in tales spanning multiple genres. Her latest offering is also fundamentally distinct from her sophomore collection A New Pigeon on the Block, which provided poignant reflections on migration, loneliness and grief. While the second collection contained pieces of varying lengths, the shorter pieces were often overshadowed by the longer ones.

Alvi's ten stories in Blue Glass predominantly fall under the category of flash fiction. Even so, these tales possess a distinct sense of completeness and readers seldom feel short-changed by their length. In fact, many of the flash pieces stand out for their polished, pristine prose and keen eye for detail. Through stories that unfold across a few pages, Alvi retains her quiet, detached narrative voice that has come to define her signature literary style.

Animals figure prominently in some of the stories and serve as a testament to the author's deep affinity with sentient non-humans. In 'A Boy, a Lame Wolf, and the River', an unnamed boy and a mountain wolf with a limp separately embark on an unusual spiritual quest to explore the mysteries of a mighty river. The motivations behind their curiosity with the meandering river vary, but they are united by their single-minded devotion to understand its place in the universe. The tale has the trappings of a conventional fable and is imbued with a valuable lesson about how living beings aren’t always in stiff competition with one another.

Instead, it explores the struggle of a starving rag-picker who competes with a stray dog for a piece of bread in a garbage heap. Mercifully, neither of them is made to compromise on their needs. They learn how to share in a city where resources are limited. Yet, readers are left with a lingering sense of discomfort as they wonder whether such conflicts can be resolved amicably in real-life scenarios. 'The Mugger' is another intriguing tale about our fear of nature and the numerous creatures who rely on it. At its core, the story highlights humankind's alarming capacity to inflict harm.

The pale ceiling fan and the blue walls of this room are confronted with a challenge: they don't fully comprehend the man's psyche or understand his dilemma. However, their curiosity knows no bounds and they are troubled by his desire for seclusion. The story reverses the stereotypical idea that only human beings are curious about their surroundings; in some exceptional cases, our surroundings are equally curious about our wellbeing.

'The Blue Glass Bottle and the Delft Pepper Shaker' doesn't view the ornaments placed on a polished oak sideboard as lifeless bric-a-brac with no connection to reality. Instead, these objects dance off the page as full-fledged characters plagued by a complex network of unspoken fears and frustrations. After a male-shaped Dutch salt shaker breaks into pieces, his counterpart – the pepper shaker who resembles a woman – finds herself somewhat bereft. A blue glass bottle, which remains a secondary character in the story, comes through as a saviour of sorts amid a climate of chaos. But it cannot spare the characters from their tragic fate. Curiously enough, the plight of the salt and pepper shakers mirror that of The house’s inhabitants, a couple who remain on the periphery of the tale. Ambitious in its scope, 'The Blue Glass Bottle and the Delft Pepper Shaker' offers an intriguing glimpse at the complex workings of grief from a cold, measured perspective.

Not all of Alvi’s stories approach the challenges faced by humans with the detached eye of a stranger. In fact, some of Alvi's tales centralise the lingering effects of the pain individuals endure as they cope with life's adversities. 'Anonymous' offers a sensitive, poignant portrait of the ways in which street crimes have plagued the lives of Karachi's citizens. The story offers a haunting image of a criminal’s blood blending with that of a victim. This disturbing visual lurks in the reader's mind long after the story comes to an end. Many readers might even wonder how the battle lines can be drawn when street crimes are linked to an overarching financial crisis and blood is being shed indiscriminately. In 'The Weeping Willow and the Jacaranda,' the quagmires faced by street children as well as women shackled by patriarchal demands assume centre-stage. The two-part tale offers a powerful evocation of human suffering. In addition, it stands out for its knowledgeable reflections on trees that are, by turns, a narrative foil and a symbol of hope amid distress.

A vast majority of the stories in the first section highlight the importance of solitude as an antidote to misery. Using the crippling realities of the pandemic as a springboard, 'Cold Walls' reveals how confinement becomes a source of relief. Separately, 'Emperor of the Night' features a garrulous family whose endless chatter inadvertently subdues the voice of a neighbourhood stray dog. As a result, the voiceless creature only finds the freedom to howl and "be himself...in the stillness of human-less nights." Alvi's tale is a breathtaking reminder of the ways in which an overpowering desire to fill silences with words can undermine solitude.

The centrepiece of Alvi's collection is undoubtedly 'Mosaic: Tesserae of Life', a tale consisting of five vignettes that reveal some familiar and shocking realities of the human condition. Each anecdote introduces a character and offers a detailed exploration of their emotional and spiritual challenges. The first two sketches capture the highs and lows of parent-child relationships and personal ambition. The third vignette fashions a warbler perched on an old oak tree into a tender witness to a series of curious happenings at a farm. The last two sketches have a darker, sombre quality and examine the stultifying effects of social and political oppression. Barring the final sketch, each of these episodic tales ends with the character's name. This serves a refreshing reminder of the ways in which names can individualise experiences that are universal.

Alvi's short fiction is not only defined by its cast of compelling characters, but also by its overpowering narrative voice. More often than not, the detached narrators of her tales confine characters within specific bounds and carry the weight of the entire story on their own shoulders. Sometimes, they are possessed by a desire to offer explanations, delay the climax or a moment of revelation, and elide certain details. Some readers might initially be thrown off by the exceedingly controlled narrative voice. Once they finish the first section, they might begin to understand why some of her characters need to keep within boundaries as they are capable of self-destruction. The narrator, therefore, shields the characters from revealing too much of their inner turmoil and darkness.

The section on Zaheda Hina's stories is equally intriguing. The Urdu writer's translated stories have characters with itinerant souls who fashion homes in foreign lands. Their lives are radically altered by multiple migrations and, in some cases, the weight of history.

As the blurb by Aamer Hussein on the back cover of Blue Glass suggests, the translations of Zaheda Hina's work "provide fascinating parallels and contrasts" to Alvi's storytelling techniques. Zaheda Hina's stories don't maintain a cold distance from their subjects – a quality that is evident in Alvi’s stories. Instead, the narrators of her four tales venture into the landscape of emotions with comparative ease.

Fuelled by a longing for a forgotten era, 'Hear Me Surayya' skilfully employs the second-person voice to show how the vicissitudes of time rob people of happiness and certainty. Using the first-person voice to great effect, 'Echoes of Twilight' chronicles the experiences of a woman who carries the memories of those she loved as she traverses geographical boundaries in search of new beginnings. Narrated in the detached third-person voice, 'The Babylonian Well of Solitude' juxtaposes ignorance of centuries-old philosophical traditions from the East with the anxieties of a post-9/11 Western milieu. With its stunning evocation of the unusual ways in which different worlds intersect, 'There Was Once a Somebody and a Nobody...' offers a poignant tale featuring multiple tragedies. The piece is interspersed with translations of Urdu and Persian poetry, including that of the 14th Century poet Hafiz.

A rich, inventive collection, Blue Glass offers a thought-provoking glimpse into solitude, despair and the intricacies of the human experience.

cleaned_blocks.text: In our increasingly fast-paced world, casual readers do not have time to go through weighty tomes and may instead prefer shorter pieces. For those readers who instinctively gravitate towards fiction, short stories are the ideal form, tailor-made for their modern-day lifestyles, characterised by limited attention spans and the constant tussle between different mediums to capture their interest.

Be that as it may, fiction writers don't choose their form based on sheer convenience. In an introductory note to a compendium of her short fiction, titled The Complete Stories, Booker-shortlisted author Anita Desai states that the length of a story depends heavily on the "element of chance". "Each form requires a different set of abilities," she asserts, "Brevity and concision will do for one while the other requires doubt, mystery, mistake and stamina."

Known as a publisher, printmaker and photographer, Shahbano Alvi has also emerged as a promising, prolific writer of short fiction. Her stories are not only concise, but also seem to have been produced at a rapid pace – a reminder that stamina is required for both long and short pieces. Blue Glass, her third collection, has been released almost four years after her debut compilation of stories and over a year after her second. It brings together Shahbano Alvi's different avatars as both a short-story writer in English and a translator of Urdu short fiction. The first section of the collection consists of Alvi's own stories. The second contains her translations of four stories by respected Urdu writer Zaheda Hina.

Fuelled by these dual impulses, the collection carries the echoes of Urdu and English, and attempts to build a bridge between both languages. This is a noble pursuit in the context of Pakistan, where Urdu and English have been locked in a persistent battle for hegemony.

Over the decades, cynical readers have argued that literature in Urdu truly captures the country's cultural zeitgeist while English is merely a tragic remnant of the subcontinent's encounter with colonialism. The latter is perceived as the language of the elite while the former enjoys mainstream appeal. Faced with linguistic dichotomies, writers in both Urdu and English have often kept a quiet distance from each other. Alvi attempts to erase these invisible barriers by making a voyage between both languages.

At first, it seems somewhat unusual for an author to place her own creative output alongside her translated works. However, this crisscrossing of boundaries among genres isn't an entirely new technique. This year's Nobel Prize for Literature has been awarded to an author who seamlessly blends genres. Writers, therefore, aren’t bound by any restrictions on what they can do with their canvas.

What may surprise some readers is Alvi's willingness to share the limelight with another author. In a fiercely competitive literary world where everyone wants to spotlight their own achievements, a collaborative endeavour of this nature would likely be viewed as an anomaly. Therefore, Alvi's keen interest in creative synergies is a lesson that artistic collaborations can be rewarding.

Blue Glass is a radical departure from Alvi's debut collection of stories A Woman and the Afternoon Sun (2021), which employed a lush, unsentimental voice in tales spanning multiple genres. Her latest offering is also fundamentally distinct from her sophomore collection A New Pigeon on the Block, which provided poignant reflections on migration, loneliness and grief. While the second collection contained pieces of varying lengths, the shorter pieces were often overshadowed by the longer ones.

Alvi's ten stories in Blue Glass predominantly fall under the category of flash fiction. Even so, these tales possess a distinct sense of completeness and readers seldom feel short-changed by their length. In fact, many of the flash pieces stand out for their polished, pristine prose and keen eye for detail. Through stories that unfold across a few pages, Alvi retains her quiet, detached narrative voice that has come to define her signature literary style.

Animals figure prominently in some of the stories and serve as a testament to the author's deep affinity with sentient non-humans. In 'A Boy, a Lame Wolf, and the River', an unnamed boy and a mountain wolf with a limp separately embark on an unusual spiritual quest to explore the mysteries of a mighty river. The motivations behind their curiosity with the meandering river vary, but they are united by their single-minded devotion to understand its place in the universe. The tale has the trappings of a conventional fable and is imbued with a valuable lesson about how living beings aren’t always in stiff competition with one another.

The desire for peaceful coexistence between sentient beings recurs in 'Bangalore Town'. The title instantly brings to mind one of Karachi's upscale neighbourhoods, and readers will naturally expect a story set in one of the locality's posh houses. However, the narrator deceives readers with the promise of a story they wish to hear, only to tell them a tale they need to appreciate. The reader is drawn into the narrative through captivating insights into how the neighbourhood has evolved over the decade before the story mysteriously shifts gears. 'Bangalore Town' is unconcerned with the lives of the neighbourhood's elite. Instead, it explores the struggle of a starving rag-picker who competes with a stray dog for a piece of bread in a garbage heap. Mercifully, neither of them is made to compromise on their needs. They learn how to share in a city where resources are limited. Yet, readers are left with a lingering sense of discomfort as they wonder whether such conflicts can be resolved amicably in real-life scenarios. 'The Mugger' is another intriguing tale about our fear of nature and the numerous creatures who rely on it. At its core, the story highlights humankind's alarming capacity to inflict harm.

headline: THE LAST EMBRACE
description: In that beautiful valley, a child still remembers a half-frosted window
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
Our boarding house is perched high on a beautiful hill, affording grand views of the forests and orchards in the valley, and our curving blue lake. The place is so beautiful you never get tired of it.

Here I live with innumerable other children.

Some are very small and cannot tie their shoes yet. Some are almost grown up. We have come from different places and speak different tongues, but on this hill these differences melt away quickly.

It is not a dull or gloomy abode, like the sinister boarding houses in stories. There are no dark and dusty corners. The floorboards do not creak at night to scare us, and there are no horrid caretakers to lock doors or shout.

This is the most fun place you can imagine, overseen by a saintly old warden.

We simply call him “the grandfather”, though I also know his name now. I have learned to spell simple words, and the nameplate outside his office reads: Ibrahim.

Eric—my five-year-old German friend with a red, freckled face and straight golden hair—calls him “Abraham von Ur”. Eric has been living here for ages, but he likes to tell tales, and I doubt his claims about the grandfather’s Teutonic origins.

It is true that the grandfather is very tall and well-built and has a very fair complexion—his long silver-grey hair falling over his wide shoulders in a majestic manner.

However, his large black eyes and thick, full beard point to his Middle Eastern roots.

Or maybe the grandfather belongs to both the East and the West, for when he flings his arms out, it seems like he can gather up the whole lot of children in his embrace.

The grandfather has a lot of children to look after—the number of his wards is ever-increasing—but he manages in a miraculous manner to lavish love, care and attention on each and every child.

Despite his busy schedule, he even finds time to play silly games with us. When he joins us on the football field, the goal almost disappears behind his huge body, and when even the three-year-olds score against him, he falls down in despair amid the children’s laughter.

The grandfather understands every language, but he speaks only the language of love. Nobody has ever seen him angry. He has never punished anyone. He has never shouted or yelled at any child.

Many children believe that he is even more affectionate and loving than our real parents, some of whom, including my dear mom, sometimes visit us with lots of presents.

On her last visit, my mom brought me a small prism on a string. When the sun comes through the dorm window, it throws a rainbow across the floor, and the little children try to catch it.

In fact, the grandfather was the one who received me when I arrived at this place after walking through a dark tunnel one night in December.

I can remember that before embarking on that journey, I was lying in a hospital bed with a number of wires and tubes attached to my body. My chest hurt when I breathed. My arms were thin, and there were blue marks where the needles had been. The room smelled of medicine and cold air.

My dad was always by my bedside. He wore the same grey sweater every day. At night he held my hand while I slept. His hand was big and rough and warm, but it broke my heart when I heard him cry in the dead of the night.

But on that particular night in December, I was woken up at a moment when my poor father had probably been sent out to “arrange” some blood or platelets for me.

Someone had whispered in my ear that I was to leave now, and this sudden announcement about an immediate departure had filled me with a deep sorrow. The machine next to my bed was beeping more slowly than usual. The chair where my dad sat was empty.

I was not afraid of the journey. I just wanted to hug my father for the last time in a tight embrace.

My eyes were fixed on the half-frosted window in front of my bed.

This window gave a view of the corridor outside the room, and I waited with bated breath to at least catch a glimpse of my father for the last time. I kept staring at the corner where the corridor turned. I thought if I stared hard enough, he would appear, rubbing his hands from the cold.

Unfortunately, the journey started even before he could return, and I had to step into the tunnel with tears rolling down my cold face. The tunnel was dark and quiet and cold, and every step took me further from him.

However, as soon as I arrived at this beautiful valley, my sorrow was gone. The grandfather was standing with a broad, welcoming smile at the end, along with a number of other children. He knelt in the grass and lifted me up. The air smelled like pine and warm bread.

And now I live happily at this place of unending bliss. Yet, I still sometimes feel like sneaking out of the boarding house, finding the grove of trees that hides that secret tunnel, running back to that hospital room and hugging my poor father for one last time.

This is a work of fiction. Any names or characters, businesses or places, events or incidents, are fictitious

The writer can be reached at farrukhkamrani@gmail.com

PUBLISHED November 01, 2026

Our boarding house is perched high on a beautiful hill, affording grand views of the forests and orchards in the valley, and our curving blue lake. The place is so beautiful you never get tired of it.

Here I live with innumerable other children.

Some are very small and cannot tie their shoes yet. Some are almost grown up. We have come from different places and speak different tongues, but on this hill these differences melt away quickly.

It is not a dull or gloomy abode, like the sinister boarding houses in stories. There are no dark and dusty corners. The floorboards do not creak at night to scare us, and there are no horrid caretakers to lock doors or shout.

This is the most fun place you can imagine, overseen by a saintly old warden.

We simply call him “the grandfather”, though I also know his name now. I have learned to spell simple words, and the nameplate outside his office reads: Ibrahim.

Eric—my five-year-old German friend with a red, freckled face and straight golden hair—calls him “Abraham von Ur”. Eric has been living here for ages, but he likes to tell tales, and I doubt his claims about the grandfather’s Teutonic origins.

It is true that the grandfather is very tall and well-built and has a very fair complexion—his long silver-grey hair falling over his wide shoulders in a majestic manner.

However, his large black eyes and thick, full beard point to his Middle Eastern roots.

Or maybe the grandfather belongs to both the East and the West, for when he flings his arms out, it seems like he can gather up the whole lot of children in his embrace.

The grandfather has a lot of children to look after—the number of his wards is ever-increasing—but he manages in a miraculous manner to lavish love, care and attention on each and every child.

Despite his busy schedule, he even finds time to play silly games with us. When he joins us on the football field, the goal almost disappears behind his huge body, and when even the three-year-olds score against him, he falls down in despair amid the children’s laughter.

The grandfather understands every language, but he speaks only the language of love. Nobody has ever seen him angry. He has never punished anyone. He has never shouted or yelled at any child.

Many children believe that he is even more affectionate and loving than our real parents, some of whom, including my dear mom, sometimes visit us with lots of presents.

On her last visit, my mom brought me a small prism on a string. When the sun comes through the dorm window, it throws a rainbow across the floor, and the little children try to catch it.

In fact, the grandfather was the one who received me when I arrived at this place after walking through a dark tunnel one night in December.

I can remember that before embarking on that journey, I was lying in a hospital bed with a number of wires and tubes attached to my body. My chest hurt when I breathed. My arms were thin, and there were blue marks where the needles had been. The room smelled of medicine and cold air.

My dad was always by my bedside. He wore the same grey sweater every day. At night he held my hand while I slept. His hand was big and rough and warm, but it broke my heart when I heard him cry in the dead of the night.

But on that particular night in December, I was woken up at a moment when my poor father had probably been sent out to “arrange” some blood or platelets for me.

Someone had whispered in my ear that I was to leave now, and this sudden announcement about an immediate departure had filled me with a deep sorrow. The machine next to my bed was beeping more slowly than usual. The chair where my dad sat was empty.

I was not afraid of the journey. I just wanted to hug my father for the last time in a tight embrace.

My eyes were fixed on the half-frosted window in front of my bed.

This window gave a view of the corridor outside the room, and I waited with bated breath to at least catch a glimpse of my father for the last time. I kept staring at the corner where the corridor turned. I thought if I stared hard enough, he would appear, rubbing his hands from the cold.

Unfortunately, the journey started even before he could return, and I had to step into the tunnel with tears rolling down my cold face. The tunnel was dark and quiet and cold, and every step took me further from him.

However, as soon as I arrived at this beautiful valley, my sorrow was gone. The grandfather was standing with a broad, welcoming smile at the end, along with a number of other children. He knelt in the grass and lifted me up. The air smelled like pine and warm bread.

And now I live happily at this place of unending bliss. Yet, I still sometimes feel like sneaking out of the boarding house, finding the grove of trees that hides that secret tunnel, running back to that hospital room and hugging my poor father for one last time.

headline: Basant–a Festival Only for the Rich?
description: Basant revives tradition and livelihoods, but commercial growth doesn't mean ordinary families can afford to join in.
author: Nabil Tahir
article_text:
In the hands of Ustad Rafiq, at the kite market in Mochi Gate, are colourful paper and thin strips of bamboo. Approximately 70 years old, Ustad Rafiq has been associated with the work of making and selling kites for years. For him, Basant is not merely a festival but an occupation and a pastime connected to a past in which both the rich and the poor participated. However, after a ban lasting more than 18 years, the return of Basant this year has created new hope for his business. However, the rising prices of kites and string have also confronted him with a new concern.

Ustad Rafiq says, “Earlier, Basant belonged to everyone. The child of a rich person flew kites, and so did the child of a poor person. Kites were inexpensive, and string was also easily available. Now it seems that this festival has been left only for those who have more money.”

When Basant was celebrated in Lahore in February 2026 under official permission, after approximately 18 years, activities resumed in the city’s markets, on rooftops and in businesses associated with kite-making. For young people, it was an opportunity for a new experience, while older enthusiasts saw the festival of their past return. But along with this return, the prices of kites and string, the high rents charged for rooftops for kite-flying and the costs of safety arrangements raised a fundamental question: Is Basant still a festival for ordinary citizens, or is it gradually becoming restricted to the financially privileged?

For next year, Lahore’s district administration has set March 12 to 14, 2027, as the dates for the Basant festival. According to the notification, separate permission and arrangements will be required to celebrate Basant in other districts of Punjab. Thus, alongside preparations, attention must also be paid to how the festival’s economic benefits, public participation and citizens’ safety can be streamlined.

One festival, two generations

Following Basant’s return, the kite markets of Lahore revealed the experiences of two different generations. For young people such as 18-year-old Hassnain Khalid, buying and flying a kite while standing on a rooftop was a new experience. Now, once again, they are eager to celebrate next year’s Basantl.

In contrast, for older enthusiasts such as Abdul Aziz, kite-flying is a nostalgic pastime connected to his youth. His friends describe him as an addict of kite-flying. Abdul Aziz says that when he was young, kites were very inexpensive. He would buy kite paper from the market and make kites himself. Kites could also be made from thin plastic sheets, while he and his friends would either prepare the string themselves or get inexpensive string from the market. Now the costs of kite-flying could make the experience of Basant different for the new generation.

In Basant’s traditional form, a family bought a few kites and the adults and children spent time together on the rooftop of their home. More kites were flown from the rooftops of large houses, and special arrangements were also made for guests. But families living in smaller homes also participated in the festival according to their means.

Farzana, who lives near Bhati Gate, wants to preserve this tradition. A mother of two now, Farzana says her family has celebrated Basant since her childhood, but prices have now made this activity difficult. “We want to celebrate Basant with our children on the rooftop of our own home, but even buying one kite is becoming difficult. Our neighbours have rented out their rooftops, but we will fly kites on our own roof, if we can get the supplies,” she says.

Farzana’s problem is not limited to the price of kites. Rising rooftop rents and safety restrictions on old buildings have also created difficulties for some residents of the Walled City of Lahore. Restrictions on kite-flying had been imposed on the rooftops of many old houses after they were declared unsafe. In such circumstances, the scope for celebrating the festival could become even more limited for families that do not have an alternative location or the resources to bear additional expenses.

Kite and string prices

When Basant came around in February 2026, a significant increase was observed in the prices of kites and string. At the time, a tawa gadda (a kite made using approximately one and a half standard units of kite paper, ) was reportedly being sold for around Rs250 to Rs300, while a dedh-tawa gadda was said to cost Rs450 to Rs500. Similarly, the price of one panna (a reel or unit of kite string) reportedly started at approximately Rs4,000 and reached Rs7,000 or more in some places, while the prices of larger pannas were even higher.

According to Muhammad Rafiq, a shopkeeper at Mochi Gate, two pannas of string sold for Rs7,000 to Rs8,000, while four pannas sold for Rs12,000 to Rs15,000. The prices of large kites in the Mochi Gate market were also reported to have reached Rs1,200 to Rs1,400.

But the question is whether the prices of string and kites will be higher for next March. According to Ustad Rafiq, kite-makers want to produce inexpensive supplies, but rising raw-material prices and business expenses have made this difficult. He says that a person with a limited income is happy to buy a few kites and one panna of string, but rising prices make even this purchase difficult for him.

Mian Abdul Rehman, a kite-flying enthusiast from Lahore’s Baghbanpura area, says that during Basant, a family has to consider not only the prices of kites and string but also the expenses of food, entertaining guests and other necessities. If a rooftop is not available at home, rent becomes an additional expense. In comparison, families with greater financial resources can afford to buy supplies in large quantities and make special arrangements for their guests.

Rooftops renting

The tradition of Basant in Lahore has remained connected to the rooftops of homes. In areas of the Walled City, such as Bhati Gate, the rooftops of houses situated close to one another used to serve as centres of communal activities. Neighbours would also join those flying kites from a particular house. With Basant’s return, renting out rooftops has become a business.

According to Mohsin Faraz, a resident of Bhati Gate, Basant can benefit culture, tourism and local businesses. He says that the rent for some rooftops for two to three days can start at Rs50,000 and reach millions of rupees, depending on the location, area and facilities.

He said that during Basant in February 2026, the three-day rent for some rooftops in the Walled City of Lahore was reported to have reached Rs2.5 million to Rs3 million. Reports also emerged that rents for ordinary rooftops had reached several hundred thousand rupees.

This business provides income to rooftop owners, but the arrangement could prove expensive for families that do not have a rooftop of their own. If the rent for a place to celebrate Basant itself falls outside an ordinary family’s budget, the traditional way of participating in the festival becomes restricted.

This is why, along with the expansion of commercial activities associated with Basant, the availability of public spaces is also important. If citizens are given opportunities to fly kites in safe places under legal permission, their need to rent expensive rooftops could be reduced.

Business has grown, but who benefitted?

The revival of Basant created opportunities for businesses associated with kite-making, string production, retail, raw-material supplies, transport and food. However, the difference between increased sales and the purchasing power of ordinary citizens also became apparent.

According to the Kite Flying Association Lahore, sales of kites and strings, etcetera, worth approximately Rs2 billion took place in Lahore during Basant celebrations in February. Meanwhile, Aqeel Malik, founder of the All Pakistan Kite Flying Association, claimed that economic activity worth more than Rs20 billion took place that week. According to him, large numbers of people came to Lahore from other cities. Expressing concern over the rising prices of kites and string, he said that a list had been prepared of those charging excessive prices.

The question of safety

The history of the ban on Basant is also connected to the festival’s return. A ban on kite-flying was imposed in 2007. Before that, incidents of injuries and deaths involving motorcyclists and pedestrians caused by string coated with chemical and metallic manjha (abrasive kite string) had repeatedly been reported. Incidents involving celebratory gunfire, accidents caused by electrical wires and falls from rooftops had also raised concerns about public safety.

Following the approval of the relevant law in December 2025, the Punjab government paved the way for Basant’s return under safety conditions. During the three-day Basant festival this year, arrangements were made for registered businesses, approved types of kites and string, and action against violations.

According to a report submitted by the Punjab Home Department to the Lahore High Court, at least 17 people died during the three days. The report attributed 12 deaths to falls from rooftops, while the other deaths were attributed to electrocution and falls from trees.

Demands of kite sellers

Representatives of the Kite Sellers Association have stressed the need to complete the licensing and registration process on time before next Basant, so that artisans can purchase raw materials and prepare the required quantities of kites. Some representatives have also demanded permission for smaller charkhis (kite-string reels), while maintaining that strict action should be taken against dangerous strings, but that those conducting legal businesses should not face unnecessary difficulties.

Will Basant reach other cities and villages?

So far, the Punjab government has announced permission to celebrate Basant only in Lahore. However, citizens and the Kite Flying Association are demanding that permission also be granted in other cities of Punjab. This would reduce the burden on Lahore, while also bringing down the prices of string and kites.

Rana Ahmed Hassan, a young man who comes from a rural area near Lahore, says open spaces are available in his village, and children make kites themselves. He says that if Basant is permitted there, local people will also want to participate in the festival, but currently the prices are beyond their means.

If permission to celebrate Basant is granted in rural areas, safe open spaces, the registration of local kite-makers and the provision of approved supplies will be important. This could provide work for local artisans and reduce the need for residents to buy supplies from markets in distant places. However, safety arrangements would also be necessary, taking into account electrical wires, roads, populated areas and other possible risks.

Basant for all

To keep Basant within the reach of ordinary citizens, the problems of prices and the availability of supplies will have to be resolved. Kite sellers said that, since the government has announced the dates for Basant already, they have adequate time to plan production and purchase raw materials.

Clearly displayed price lists at registered shops, the availability of approved kites and string, and action against unusually high prices could also make purchasing easier for buyers. At the same time, small-scale artisans should receive fair compensation for their labour, so that efforts to keep prices low do not affect their livelihoods.

Citizens say that expanding opportunities for safe kite-flying in public places could also help families that do not have a rooftop of their own or cannot afford to pay high rents. Safety awareness for children and citizens, along with sustained action against dangerous strings, is also necessary.

The government, kite-makers, shopkeepers and citizens have an opportunity to prepare for Basant in March 2027. During this period, it will be important to see how far the supply of materials, price monitoring and safety arrangements improve.

Preparations are underway to fly colourful kites once again in Lahore’s skies, but the success of Basant cannot be measured only by the number of kites sold, the value of business conducted or the celebrations held on expensive rooftops. It will also be necessary to see to what extent families with limited incomes can participate in the festival.

According to Ustad Rafiq, if inexpensive supplies become available and kite-flying is made possible for ordinary people, the festival can once again belong to everyone. Farzana, too, wants her children not to be deprived of the joy of Basant.
