article_html:
By Asif Mehmood |
facebook twitter whatsup linkded email
PUBLISHED November 01, 2026

In the hands of Ustad Rafiq, at the kite market in Mochi Gate, are colourful paper and thin strips of bamboo. Approximately 70 years old, Ustad Rafiq has been associated with the work of making and selling kites for years. For him, Basant is not merely a festival but an occupation and a pastime connected to a past in which both the rich and the poor participated. However, after a ban lasting more than 18 years, the return of Basant this year has created new hope for his business. However, the rising prices of kites and string have also confronted him with a new concern.

Ustad Rafiq says, “Earlier, Basant belonged to everyone. The child of a rich person flew kites, and so did the child of a poor person. Kites were inexpensive, and string was also easily available. Now it seems that this festival has been left only for those who have more money.”

When Basant was celebrated in Lahore in February 2026 under official permission, after approximately 18 years, activities resumed in the city’s markets, on rooftops and in businesses associated with kite-making. For young people, it was an opportunity for a new experience, while older enthusiasts saw the festival of their past return. But along with this return, the prices of kites and string, the high rents charged for rooftops for kite-flying and the costs of safety arrangements raised a fundamental question: Is Basant still a festival for ordinary citizens, or is it gradually becoming restricted to the financially privileged?

For next year, Lahore’s district administration has set March 12 to 14, 2027, as the dates for the Basant festival. According to the notification, separate permission and arrangements will be required to celebrate Basant in other districts of Punjab. Thus, alongside preparations, attention must also be paid to how the festival’s economic benefits, public participation and citizens’ safety can be streamlined.

One festival, two generations

Following Basant’s return, the kite markets of Lahore revealed the experiences of two different generations. For young people such as 18-year-old Hassnain Khalid, buying and flying a kite while standing on a rooftop was a new experience. Now, once again, they are eager to celebrate next year’s Basantl.

In contrast, for older enthusiasts such as Abdul Aziz, kite-flying is a nostalgic pastime connected to his youth. His friends describe him as an addict of kite-flying. Abdul Aziz says that when he was young, kites were very inexpensive. He would buy kite paper from the market and make kites himself. Kites could also be made from thin plastic sheets, while he and his friends would either prepare the string themselves or get inexpensive string from the market. Now the costs of kite-flying could make the experience of Basant different for the new generation.

In Basant’s traditional form, a family bought a few kites and the adults and children spent time together on the rooftop of their home. More kites were flown from the rooftops of large houses, and special arrangements were also made for guests. But families living in smaller homes also participated in the festival according to their means.

Farzana, who lives near Bhati Gate, wants to preserve this tradition. A mother of two now, Farzana says her family has celebrated Basant since her childhood, but prices have now made this activity difficult. “We want to celebrate Basant with our children on the rooftop of our own home, but even buying one kite is becoming difficult. Our neighbours have rented out their rooftops, but we will fly kites on our own roof, if we can get the supplies,” she says.

Farzana’s problem is not limited to the price of kites. Rising rooftop rents and safety restrictions on old buildings have also created difficulties for some residents of the Walled City of Lahore. Restrictions on kite-flying had been imposed on the rooftops of many old houses after they were declared unsafe. In such circumstances, the scope for celebrating the festival could become even more limited for families that do not have an alternative location or the resources to bear additional expenses.

Kite and string prices

When Basant came around in February 2026, a significant increase was observed in the prices of kites and string. At the time, a tawa gadda (a kite made using approximately one and a half standard units of kite paper, ) was reportedly being sold for around Rs250 to Rs300, while a dedh-tawa gadda was said to cost Rs450 to Rs500. Similarly, the price of one panna (a reel or unit of kite string) reportedly started at approximately Rs4,000 and reached Rs7,000 or more in some places, while the prices of larger pannas were even higher.

According to Muhammad Rafiq, a shopkeeper at Mochi Gate, two pannas of string sold for Rs7,000 to Rs8,000, while four pannas sold for Rs12,000 to Rs15,000. The prices of large kites in the Mochi Gate market were also reported to have reached Rs1,200 to Rs1,400.

But the question is whether the prices of string and kites will be higher for next March. According to Ustad Rafiq, kite-makers want to produce inexpensive supplies, but rising raw-material prices and business expenses have made this difficult. He says that a person with a limited income is happy to buy a few kites and one panna of string, but rising prices make even this purchase difficult for him.

Mian Abdul Rehman, a kite-flying enthusiast from Lahore’s Baghbanpura area, says that during Basant, a family has to consider not only the prices of kites and string but also the expenses of food, entertaining guests and other necessities. If a rooftop is not available at home, rent becomes an additional expense. In comparison, families with greater financial resources can afford to buy supplies in large quantities and make special arrangements for their guests.

Rooftops renting

The tradition of Basant in Lahore has remained connected to the rooftops of homes. In areas of the Walled City, such as Bhati Gate, the rooftops of houses situated close to one another used to serve as centres of communal activities. Neighbours would also join those flying kites from a particular house. With Basant’s return, renting out rooftops has become a business.

According to Mohsin Faraz, a resident of Bhati Gate, Basant can benefit culture, tourism and local businesses. He says that the rent for some rooftops for two to three days can start at Rs50,000 and reach millions of rupees, depending on the location, area and facilities.

He said that during Basant in February 2026, the three-day rent for some rooftops in the Walled City of Lahore was reported to have reached Rs2.5 million to Rs3 million. Reports also emerged that rents for ordinary rooftops had reached several hundred thousand rupees.

This business provides income to rooftop owners, but the arrangement could prove expensive for families that do not have a rooftop of their own. If the rent for a place to celebrate Basant itself falls outside an ordinary family’s budget, the traditional way of participating in the festival becomes restricted.

This is why, along with the expansion of commercial activities associated with Basant, the availability of public spaces is also important. If citizens are given opportunities to fly kites in safe places under legal permission, their need to rent expensive rooftops could be reduced.

Business has grown, but who benefitted?

The revival of Basant created opportunities for businesses associated with kite-making, string production, retail, raw-material supplies, transport and food. However, the difference between increased sales and the purchasing power of ordinary citizens also became apparent.

According to the Kite Flying Association Lahore, sales of kites and strings, etcetera, worth approximately Rs2 billion took place in Lahore during Basant celebrations in February. Meanwhile, Aqeel Malik, founder of the All Pakistan Kite Flying Association, claimed that economic activity worth more than Rs20 billion took place that week. According to him, large numbers of people came to Lahore from other cities. Expressing concern over the rising prices of kites and string, he said that a list had been prepared of those charging excessive prices.

The question of safety

The history of the ban on Basant is also connected to the festival’s return. A ban on kite-flying was imposed in 2007. Before that, incidents of injuries and deaths involving motorcyclists and pedestrians caused by string coated with chemical and metallic manjha (abrasive kite string) had repeatedly been reported. Incidents involving celebratory gunfire, accidents caused by electrical wires and falls from rooftops had also raised concerns about public safety.

Following the approval of the relevant law in December 2025, the Punjab government paved the way for Basant’s return under safety conditions. During the three-day Basant festival this year, arrangements were made for registered businesses, approved types of kites and string, and action against violations.

According to a report submitted by the Punjab Home Department to the Lahore High Court, at least 17 people died during the three days. The report attributed 12 deaths to falls from rooftops, while the other deaths were attributed to electrocution and falls from trees.

Demands of kite sellers

Representatives of the Kite Sellers Association have stressed the need to complete the licensing and registration process on time before next Basant, so that artisans can purchase raw materials and prepare the required quantities of kites. Some representatives have also demanded permission for smaller charkhis (kite-string reels), while maintaining that strict action should be taken against dangerous strings, but that those conducting legal businesses should not face unnecessary difficulties.

Will Basant reach other cities and villages?

So far, the Punjab government has announced permission to celebrate Basant only in Lahore. However, citizens and the Kite Flying Association are demanding that permission also be granted in other cities of Punjab. This would reduce the burden on Lahore, while also bringing down the prices of string and kites.

Rana Ahmed Hassan, a young man who comes from a rural area near Lahore, says open spaces are available in his village, and children make kites themselves. He says that if Basant is permitted there, local people will also want to participate in the festival, but currently the prices are beyond their means.

If permission to celebrate Basant is granted in rural areas, safe open spaces, the registration of local kite-makers and the provision of approved supplies will be important. This could provide work for local artisans and reduce the need for residents to buy supplies from markets in distant places. However, safety arrangements would also be necessary, taking into account electrical wires, roads, populated areas and other possible risks.

Basant for all

To keep Basant within the reach of ordinary citizens, the problems of prices and the availability of supplies will have to be resolved. Kite sellers said that, since the government has announced the dates for Basant already, they have adequate time to plan production and purchase raw materials.

Clearly displayed price lists at registered shops, the availability of approved kites and string, and action against unusually high prices could also make purchasing easier for buyers. At the same time, small-scale artisans should receive fair compensation for their labour, so that efforts to keep prices low do not affect their livelihoods.

Citizens say that expanding opportunities for safe kite-flying in public places could also help families that do not have a rooftop of their own or cannot afford to pay high rents. Safety awareness for children and citizens, along with sustained action against dangerous strings, is also necessary.

The government, kite-makers, shopkeepers and citizens have an opportunity to prepare for Basant in March 2027. During this period, it will be important to see how far the supply of materials, price monitoring and safety arrangements improve.

Preparations are underway to fly colourful kites once again in Lahore’s skies, but the success of Basant cannot be measured only by the number of kites sold, the value of business conducted or the celebrations held on expensive rooftops. It will also be necessary to see to what extent families with limited incomes can participate in the festival.

According to Ustad Rafiq, if inexpensive supplies become available and kite-flying is made possible for ordinary people, the festival can once again belong to everyone. Farzana, too, wants her children not to be deprived of the joy of Basant.

Kites could also be made from thin plastic sheets, while he and his friends would either prepare the string themselves or get inexpensive string from the market. Now the costs of kite-flying could make the experience of Basant different for the new generation.

In Basant’s traditional form, a family bought a few kites and the adults and children spent time together on the rooftop of their home. More kites were flown from the rooftops of large houses, and special arrangements were also made for guests. But families living in smaller homes also participated in the festival according to their means.

Farzana, who lives near Bhati Gate, wants to preserve this tradition. A mother of two now, Farzana says her family has celebrated Basant since her childhood, but prices have now made this activity difficult. “We want to celebrate Basant with our children on the rooftop of our own home, but even buying one kite is becoming difficult. Our neighbours have rented out their rooftops, but we will fly kites on our own roof, if we can get the supplies,” she says.

Farzana’s problem is not limited to the price of kites. Rising rooftop rents and safety restrictions on old buildings have also created difficulties for some residents of the Walled City of Lahore. Restrictions on kite-flying had been imposed on the rooftops of many old houses after they were declared unsafe. In such circumstances, the scope for celebrating the festival could become even more limited for families that do not have an alternative location or the resources to bear additional expenses.

Kite and string prices

When Basant came around in February 2026, a significant increase was observed in the prices of kites and string. At the time, a tawa gadda (a kite made using approximately one and a half standard units of kite paper, ) was reportedly being sold for around Rs250 to Rs300, while a dedh-tawa gadda was said to cost Rs450 to Rs500. Similarly, the price of one panna (a reel or unit of kite string) reportedly started at approximately Rs4,000 and reached Rs7,000 or more in some places, while the prices of larger pannas were even higher.

According to Muhammad Rafiq, a shopkeeper at Mochi Gate, two pannas of string sold for Rs7,000 to Rs8,000, while four pannas sold for Rs12,000 to Rs15,000. The prices of large kites in the Mochi Gate market were also reported to have reached Rs1,200 to Rs1,400.

But the question is whether the prices of string and kites will be higher for next March. According to Ustad Rafiq, kite-makers want to produce inexpensive supplies, but rising raw-material prices and business expenses have made this difficult. He says that a person with a limited income is happy to buy a few kites and one panna of string, but rising prices make even this purchase difficult for him.

Mian Abdul Rehman, a kite-flying enthusiast from Lahore’s Baghbanpura area, says that during Basant, a family has to consider not only the prices of kites and string but also the expenses of food, entertaining guests and other necessities. If a rooftop is not available at home, rent becomes an additional expense. In comparison, families with greater financial resources can afford to buy supplies in large quantities and make special arrangements for their guests.

Rooftops renting

The tradition of Basant in Lahore has remained connected to the rooftops of homes. In areas of the Walled City, such as Bhati Gate, the rooftops of houses situated close to one another used to serve as centres of communal activities. Neighbours would also join those flying kites from a particular house. With Basant’s return, renting out rooftops has become a business.

According to Mohsin Faraz, a resident of Bhati Gate, Basant can benefit culture, tourism and local businesses. He says that the rent for some rooftops for two to three days can start at Rs50,000 and reach millions of rupees, depending on the location, area and facilities.

He said that during Basant in February 2026, the three-day rent for some rooftops in the Walled City of Lahore was reported to have reached Rs2.5 million to Rs3 million. Reports also emerged that rents for ordinary rooftops had reached several hundred thousand rupees.

This business provides income to rooftop owners, but the arrangement could prove expensive for families that do not have a rooftop of their own. If the rent for a place to celebrate Basant itself falls outside an ordinary family’s budget, the traditional way of participating in the festival becomes restricted.

This is why, along with the expansion of commercial activities associated with Basant, the availability of public spaces is also important. If citizens are given opportunities to fly kites in safe places under legal permission, their need to rent expensive rooftops could be reduced.

Business has grown, but who benefitted?

The revival of Basant created opportunities for businesses associated with kite-making, string production, retail, raw-material supplies, transport and food. However, the difference between increased sales and the purchasing power of ordinary citizens also became apparent.

According to the Kite Flying Association Lahore, sales of kites and strings, etcetera, worth approximately Rs2 billion took place in Lahore during Basant celebrations in February. Meanwhile, Aqeel Malik, founder of the All Pakistan Kite Flying Association, claimed that economic activity worth more than Rs20 billion took place that week. According to him, large numbers of people came to Lahore from other cities. Expressing concern over the rising prices of kites and string, he said that a list had been prepared of those charging excessive prices.

The question of safety

The history of the ban on Basant is also connected to the festival’s return. A ban on kite-flying was imposed in 2007. Before that, incidents of injuries and deaths involving motorcyclists and pedestrians caused by string coated with chemical and metallic manjha (abrasive kite string) had repeatedly been reported. Incidents involving celebratory gunfire, accidents caused by electrical wires and falls from rooftops had also raised concerns about public safety.

Following the approval of the relevant law in December 2025, the Punjab government paved the way for Basant’s return under safety conditions. During the three-day Basant festival this year, arrangements were made for registered businesses, approved types of kites and string, and action against violations.

According to a report submitted by the Punjab Home Department to the Lahore High Court, at least 17 people died during the three days. The report attributed 12 deaths to falls from rooftops, while the other deaths were attributed to electrocution and falls from trees.

Demands of kite sellers

Representatives of the Kite Sellers Association have stressed the need to complete the licensing and registration process on time before next Basant, so that artisans can purchase raw materials and prepare the required quantities of kites. Some representatives have also demanded permission for smaller charkhis (kite-string reels), while maintaining that strict action should be taken against dangerous strings, but that those conducting legal businesses should not face unnecessary difficulties.

Will Basant reach other cities and villages?

So far, the Punjab government has announced permission to celebrate Basant only in Lahore. However, citizens and the Kite Flying Association are demanding that permission also be granted in other cities of Punjab. This would reduce the burden on Lahore, while also bringing down the prices of string and kites.

Rana Ahmed Hassan, a young man who comes from a rural area near Lahore, says open spaces are available in his village, and children make kites themselves. He says that if Basant is permitted there, local people will also want to participate in the festival, but currently the prices are beyond their means.

If permission to celebrate Basant is granted in rural areas, safe open spaces, the registration of local kite-makers and the provision of approved supplies will be important. This could provide work for local artisans and reduce the need for residents to buy supplies from markets in distant places. However, safety arrangements would also be necessary, taking into account electrical wires, roads, populated areas and other possible risks.

Basant for all

To keep Basant within the reach of ordinary citizens, the problems of prices and the availability of supplies will have to be resolved. Kite sellers said that, since the government has announced the dates for Basant already, they have adequate time to plan production and purchase raw materials.

Clearly displayed price lists at registered shops, the availability of approved kites and string, and action against unusually high prices could also make purchasing easier for buyers. At the same time, small-scale artisans should receive fair compensation for their labour, so that efforts to keep prices low do not affect their livelihoods.

Citizens say that expanding opportunities for safe kite-flying in public places could also help families that do not have a rooftop of their own or cannot afford to pay high rents. Safety awareness for children and citizens, along with sustained action against dangerous strings, is also necessary.

The government, kite-makers, shopkeepers and citizens have an opportunity to prepare for Basant in March 2027. During this period, it will be important to see how far the supply of materials, price monitoring and safety arrangements improve.

Preparations are underway to fly colourful kites once again in Lahore’s skies, but the success of Basant cannot be measured only by the number of kites sold, the value of business conducted or the celebrations held on expensive rooftops. It will also be necessary to see to what extent families with limited incomes can participate in the festival.

According to Ustad Rafiq, if inexpensive supplies become available and kite-flying is made possible for ordinary people, the festival can once again belong to everyone. Farzana, too, wants her children not to be deprived of the joy of Basant.

headline: Refineries to sell petrol 'below cost'
description: Refineries to sell petrol 'below cost'
author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
article_text:
The government's surprise move to change the petrol pricing mechanism has set off alarm bells with oil refineries, which call it a "serious setback" to the industry.

In its decision, the federal cabinet has directed Pakistan's refineries to deposit Rs49 per litre into the petroleum levy account to offset the reduction of Rs14.71 per litre in the levy. Responding to the sudden revision in the pricing system, the refineries say they are being forced to sell petrol below production cost following a policy change announced without prior consultation.

On Friday night, the cabinet decided that a reduction of Rs14.71 per litre in the petroleum levy would be compensated through a contribution of Rs49 per litre by refineries to the oil levy account. "The decision has effectively shifted the financial burden of providing relief to consumers on to domestic refineries," industry officials argued.

According to a Petroleum Division letter issued on October 30, the federal cabinet approved a revised pricing mechanism under which refineries would receive an ex-refinery petrol price calculated by fixing the premium, incidentals and customs duty at their March 7, 2026 levels for the next 30 days. The difference between the import price determined on the basis of Pakistan State Oil's actual import costs and the revised ex-refinery price must be surrendered by refineries under the petroleum levy account.

Industry officials said the mechanism would require refineries to surrender approximately Rs49 per litre, substantially exceeding the Rs14.71-per-litre reduction in the petroleum levy. They questioned the rationale for requiring refineries to contribute Rs49 per litre to facilitate a much smaller reduction in the levy, particularly when the mechanism could force them to sell petrol below the actual cost.

Refinery executives said the decision came as a complete surprise and was taken without consultation with the industry. The move raises questions about the government's earlier assurances about stakeholder consultation. Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik had previously said, while defending the diesel price reduction, talks with refineries had been held. However, company officials said no such consultation preceded the latest decision on petrol pricing.

Negative margins

The vice chairman of Cnergyico Pk expressed serious concern over the cabinet's decision, cautioning that the latest intervention could push the company's gross refining margins (GRMs) into negative territory. He mentioned that Cnergyico had been importing higher-priced crude oil from the United States, which gave a higher gasoline yield than the Middle Eastern crude grades traditionally processed by the refinery.

"We are bringing US crude, which is high-priced, and we are already not recovering the actual diesel crack because of the government's intervention in restricting diesel cracks," he said.

The vice chairman explained that the US crude produced a higher proportion of gasoline compared with the Middle Eastern grades that Cnergyico previously imported, making the latest petrol pricing intervention particularly damaging for the refinery's economics. "US crude has more gasoline than the Middle Eastern grades we used to import. With this change in the pricing formula, our gross refining margins can go into negative territory," he said.

The executive's remarks highlight the cumulative impact of government interventions in both diesel and petrol pricing on refinery profitability. Industry officials said refineries were already facing pressure from restrictions on diesel cracks and the latest petrol pricing formula could further erode their margins. They warned that such interventions could discourage crude oil diversification, including imports from the US, at a time when Pakistan was seeking to strengthen its trade and energy relationship with Washington.

Regulatory uncertainty

The chief executive of another leading refinery also voiced concern over the unpredictable regulatory policies. "Nowhere in the world do policies change this quickly. The regulatory regime has become a joke and then the government expects foreign direct investment to flow into the country," the executive remarked.

He questioned how international investors could be expected to commit billions of dollars to Pakistan's refining sector when pricing policies could be changed overnight without consultation. Industry officials cautioned that abrupt interventions could undermine the financial viability of existing refineries and damage investor confidence at a time when the government was seeking substantial investment in refinery upgrades and expansion.

They maintained that while providing relief to consumers was important, the government should not achieve this objective by imposing additional financial burdens on domestic refineries. The latest decision has once again brought into focus concerns about regulatory uncertainty, policy inconsistency and the long-term implications for investment in Pakistan's petroleum sector.

Attock Refinery CEO Adil Khattak said that the latest change in the petrol pricing mechanism caused serious setback to refineries. "The refineries, which had already agreed on two occasions to cap their spread on high-speed diesel, first at $41.89 and subsequently at $38, are now confronted with yet another serious loss," he said.

The government's decision to incorporate pre-war premiums and incidentals into motor spirit pricing will reportedly cost refineries approximately Rs35 per litre. An additional diversion of Rs14 per litre from their customs duty recovery towards reducing the petroleum levy will bring the total adverse impact to Rs49 per litre.

"This decision strikes at the very foundation of the Brownfield Refineries Up-gradation Policy, which specifically requires that proceeds of 10% customs duty will be deposited into dedicated refinery accounts to partially finance their upgrade projects. Diverting these funds for other purposes defeats the objective of this provision," he said. "This decision undermines the policy's explicit assurance of protection against adverse changes during the project execution period. Such assurances are fundamental to establishing the financial viability and bankability of these multibillion-dollar investments."

ISLAMABAD:

The government's surprise move to change the petrol pricing mechanism has set off alarm bells with oil refineries, which call it a "serious setback" to the industry.

In its decision, the federal cabinet has directed Pakistan's refineries to deposit Rs49 per litre into the petroleum levy account to offset the reduction of Rs14.71 per litre in the levy. Responding to the sudden revision in the pricing system, the refineries say they are being forced to sell petrol below production cost following a policy change announced without prior consultation.

On Friday night, the cabinet decided that a reduction of Rs14.71 per litre in the petroleum levy would be compensated through a contribution of Rs49 per litre by refineries to the oil levy account. "The decision has effectively shifted the financial burden of providing relief to consumers on to domestic refineries," industry officials argued.

According to a Petroleum Division letter issued on October 30, the federal cabinet approved a revised pricing mechanism under which refineries would receive an ex-refinery petrol price calculated by fixing the premium, incidentals and customs duty at their March 7, 2026 levels for the next 30 days. The difference between the import price determined on the basis of Pakistan State Oil's actual import costs and the revised ex-refinery price must be surrendered by refineries under the petroleum levy account.

Industry officials said the mechanism would require refineries to surrender approximately Rs49 per litre, substantially exceeding the Rs14.71-per-litre reduction in the petroleum levy. They questioned the rationale for requiring refineries to contribute Rs49 per litre to facilitate a much smaller reduction in the levy, particularly when the mechanism could force them to sell petrol below the actual cost.

Refinery executives said the decision came as a complete surprise and was taken without consultation with the industry. The move raises questions about the government's earlier assurances about stakeholder consultation. Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik had previously said, while defending the diesel price reduction, talks with refineries had been held. However, company officials said no such consultation preceded the latest decision on petrol pricing.

Negative margins

The vice chairman of Cnergyico Pk expressed serious concern over the cabinet's decision, cautioning that the latest intervention could push the company's gross refining margins (GRMs) into negative territory. He mentioned that Cnergyico had been importing higher-priced crude oil from the United States, which gave a higher gasoline yield than the Middle Eastern crude grades traditionally processed by the refinery.

"We are bringing US crude, which is high-priced, and we are already not recovering the actual diesel crack because of the government's intervention in restricting diesel cracks," he said.

The vice chairman explained that the US crude produced a higher proportion of gasoline compared with the Middle Eastern grades that Cnergyico previously imported, making the latest petrol pricing intervention particularly damaging for the refinery's economics. "US crude has more gasoline than the Middle Eastern grades we used to import. With this change in the pricing formula, our gross refining margins can go into negative territory," he said.

The executive's remarks highlight the cumulative impact of government interventions in both diesel and petrol pricing on refinery profitability. Industry officials said refineries were already facing pressure from restrictions on diesel cracks and the latest petrol pricing formula could further erode their margins. They warned that such interventions could discourage crude oil diversification, including imports from the US, at a time when Pakistan was seeking to strengthen its trade and energy relationship with Washington.

Regulatory uncertainty

The chief executive of another leading refinery also voiced concern over the unpredictable regulatory policies. "Nowhere in the world do policies change this quickly. The regulatory regime has become a joke and then the government expects foreign direct investment to flow into the country," the executive remarked.

He questioned how international investors could be expected to commit billions of dollars to Pakistan's refining sector when pricing policies could be changed overnight without consultation. Industry officials cautioned that abrupt interventions could undermine the financial viability of existing refineries and damage investor confidence at a time when the government was seeking substantial investment in refinery upgrades and expansion.

They maintained that while providing relief to consumers was important, the government should not achieve this objective by imposing additional financial burdens on domestic refineries. The latest decision has once again brought into focus concerns about regulatory uncertainty, policy inconsistency and the long-term implications for investment in Pakistan's petroleum sector.

Attock Refinery CEO Adil Khattak said that the latest change in the petrol pricing mechanism caused serious setback to refineries. "The refineries, which had already agreed on two occasions to cap their spread on high-speed diesel, first at $41.89 and subsequently at $38, are now confronted with yet another serious loss," he said.

The government's decision to incorporate pre-war premiums and incidentals into motor spirit pricing will reportedly cost refineries approximately Rs35 per litre. An additional diversion of Rs14 per litre from their customs duty recovery towards reducing the petroleum levy will bring the total adverse impact to Rs49 per litre.

"This decision strikes at the very foundation of the Brownfield Refineries Up-gradation Policy, which specifically requires that proceeds of 10% customs duty will be deposited into dedicated refinery accounts to partially finance their upgrade projects. Diverting these funds for other purposes defeats the objective of this provision," he said. "This decision undermines the policy's explicit assurance of protection against adverse changes during the project execution period. Such assurances are fundamental to establishing the financial viability and bankability of these multibillion-dollar investments."

headline: WB okays $150m for raising revenue
description: WB okays $150m for raising revenue
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The World Bank Group's board of executive directors has approved $150 million in financing for the Sindh Property Revenues Enhancement Programme (Sindh PREP). The programme will improve urban property tax collection and strengthen municipal service delivery in Sindh.

"Cities that can raise their own revenues can plan and invest for the long term," said Bolormaa Amgaabazar, World Bank Country Director for Pakistan. "Today, Sindh's local councils depend on provincial transfers for more than 95% of their revenues. By helping Karachi collect property taxes from its residents and businesses and by reinvesting most of that revenue in local services, this programme will give Sindh's cities the means to finance the infrastructure they need."

Sindh PREP will support the provincial government in improving urban immovable property tax (UIPT) collection and strengthening municipal service delivery capacity in selected local councils. Despite being one of the world's largest cities, Karachi currently collects only around $8.5 million annually in property tax while cities of similar size collect 82 to 350 times more.

The programme aims to increase this to $85 million annually, raising compliance from 20% to 50%. It will do so by strengthening UIPT collection, compliance and administration, including through deployment of a UIPT management information system for billing, payment processing and grievance redress, and by rolling out integrated financial management information systems across local councils. About 70% of the collected UIPT revenues will be reinvested directly into municipal infrastructure and services in the participating local councils.

The programme will benefit Karachi's 25 local councils. Its primary beneficiaries are the 3.58 million people living in these councils, where service delivery investments will be financed. Funding will be linked to results: annual performance assessments, conducted by an independent verification agent, will determine the awards each council receives and these awards will finance the rehabilitation of climate-resilient municipal infrastructure and services, including drainage, sewerage, schools, fire stations, roads and street lighting.

The programme also includes an Investment Project Financing component of $40 million that will expand property surveys and UIPT administration to 20 local councils in Sindh's other urban centres, with an indirect benefit to about 4.5 million people.

"Karachi has significant untapped potential to generate revenues from its property base and use those resources to fund the infrastructure its residents and businesses need. This programme will help Sindh strengthen fiscal sustainability enabling cities to plan, invest and deliver services from their own resources effectively," said Davison Muchadenyika, Senior Urban Development Specialist at World Bank.

This programme will help Sindh strengthen fiscal sustainability enabling cities to plan, invest and deliver services from their own resources effectively," said Davison Muchadenyika, Senior Urban Development Specialist at World Bank.

headline: Exhibitions, trade delegations proposed with Sri Lanka
description: Exhibitions, trade delegations proposed with Sri Lanka
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) has proposed an exchange of trade delegations, single-country exhibitions in both countries and business outlets in each other's markets to expand Pakistan-Sri Lanka trade, putting the package to Sri Lanka's high commissioner at a meeting where he said longstanding political ties must begin yielding commercial benefit.

Rear Admiral (retd) Fred Senevirathne, Sri Lanka's high commissioner to Pakistan, told the chamber that relations between the two countries should be translated into increased commercial engagement, investment and business partnerships, and invited Pakistani businessmen to explore opportunities in Sri Lanka. He stressed that economic engagement should be strengthened so that friendly relations produced greater benefits for both business communities. LCCI President Ali Hussam Asghar said cordial and longstanding relations provided a strong foundation for expanding bilateral trade, but that both countries needed to make greater efforts to convert those ties into practical business opportunities.

He proposed the delegation exchange to help businessmen understand each other's markets, identify partners and explore new avenues of cooperation, alongside single-country exhibitions in Pakistan and Sri Lanka to showcase products, services and investment opportunities and enable companies to establish direct contacts.

Asghar highlighted Lahore's importance as a business and commercial centre and a significant contributor to Pakistan's exports, saying stronger engagement with Sri Lankan businesses could open new avenues for Pakistani exporters and investors while giving Sri Lankan companies opportunities in the Pakistani market.

He stressed the need to promote business-to-business contacts and strengthen chamber-to-chamber relations, saying direct interaction could help identify areas of mutual interest and develop lasting commercial partnerships. He also encouraged businessmen to explore establishing outlets in each other's markets, which he said would improve market access and strengthen commercial presence.

Sustained interaction, regular exchanges, exhibitions and intra-chamber cooperation could play a meaningful role in expanding bilateral trade, he said, and closer coordination between the chambers would help businesses identify practical opportunities and build stronger economic connections.

headline: Chinese park courts Pakistani pine nuts, rice
description: Chinese park courts Pakistani pine nuts, rice
author: News Desk
article_text:
The Hulunbuir E-commerce Industrial Park in China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region is exploring two-way trade with Pakistan, seeking to import pine nuts, rice and sesame seeds while helping Chinese enterprises expand overseas sales of meat, textiles and agricultural products into the Pakistani market.

The park is open to exploring imports of Pakistani products, its head, Wang Bin, told China Economic Net. "We can explore importing Pakistani pine nuts, rice and sesame seeds to the Chinese market," he said, pointing to the potential to connect businesses and consumers in both countries through e-commerce and international trade channels. Wang said the park is also interested in sharing food-processing expertise with Pakistani businesses, particularly modern techniques for slaughtering, processing and preserving beef to maintain its freshness and quality.

Pakistan already exports boiled beef to China, and such techniques would help enhance those exports. According to Chinese customs data, Pakistan shipped 2.38 million kilogrammes of boiled beef under HS code 16025090, with exports valued at $14.52 million.

Such cooperation could create opportunities for Pakistani agricultural exporters and food businesses to access China's market while enabling Chinese enterprises to explore new customers in Pakistan. Pakistan's agricultural sector offers products with potential for international trade, while its large consumer market provides opportunities for Chinese companies selling a broad range of goods. Developing two-way trade, however, requires appropriate import approvals, product standards, logistics arrangements and market research.

Established in late 2023 with an investment of 47 million yuan, the park aims to help local enterprises overcome barriers in branding, marketing, logistics and international trade. It has connected with 135 companies and brought together more than 1,200 varieties of products, including beef and mutton, corn, blueberries, sea buckthorn juice and other regional specialities.

The park provides warehousing and fulfilment services for 49 businesses, including established enterprises, state-owned companies, small and medium-sized enterprises and young entrepreneurs. Rather than requiring individual producers to manage every stage of sales, it helps coordinate product aggregation, online promotion, order processing, delivery and after-sales services. This enables businesses to concentrate on production and product quality while benefiting from shared sales and logistics networks.

It also operates livestreaming facilities and works with trading partners in Shanghai to connect local products with domestic and international buyers. Wang cited a corn producer from Molidawa Daur Autonomous Banner as an example of how e-commerce can help smaller businesses grow. With support from the park, the company connected with Chinese livestreaming platform Oriental Selection, where a single livestream generated around 500,000 yuan in sales, according to Wang. The company subsequently built a factory, created local employment opportunities and obtained import and export qualifications.

The park has established an airport-linked city cargo station to improve distribution of regional products. Wang said it could support same-day or next-day delivery to 25 Chinese cities, helping businesses transport products to distant markets more efficiently. The park is also exploring overseas opportunities for cold beverages and other consumer goods, including markets in Russia, the United States, Iraq and Southeast Asia.

For cooperation with Pakistan, Wang said the combination of digital sales channels, consolidated logistics and technical knowledge-sharing could help businesses explore opportunities in both directions.

He said the park's broader objective was to help local companies build their own brands and reach more customers rather than relying solely on supplying products for established businesses.

"For Pakistan, cooperation could extend beyond agricultural trade to food processing, product distribution and online retail. For Chinese businesses, importing Pakistani specialities could diversify product offerings and create new commercial links between the two markets," he said.

As China and Pakistan continue to explore opportunities for economic cooperation, cross-border e-commerce could provide an additional channel for small and medium-sized enterprises to identify partners, test market demand and develop trade in both directions.

headline: S&P revises Meta outlook to 'negative'
description: Cites significant uncertainty around social media giant's capital spending, free operating cash flow
author: Reuters
article_text:
Cites significant uncertainty around social media giant's capital spending, free operating cash flow

S&P Global Ratings on Friday revised its outlook on Meta Platforms to "negative" from "stable", citing significant uncertainty around the social media giant's capital spending and free operating cash flow.

headline: NBP revamp keeps finance veto
description: NBP revamp keeps finance veto
author: Shahbaz Rana
article_text:
The government has proposed major amendments to the National Bank of Pakistan (NBP) law to meet an International Monetary Fund (IMF) condition for improving its governance and operations, but has retained veto power over the appointment of the bank's president.

The Cabinet Committee on Legislative Cases, the body responsible for clearing rules and laws for final approval by the cabinet, has approved the draft of the NBP Amendment Act, 2026. Approval of the law by Parliament is a condition of the IMF programme.

The government has made many changes to the 1949 NBP Ordinance to meet the IMF condition. But the proposed changes may further complicate governance, as NBP is now planned to be managed under the NBP Act, the State-Owned Enterprises (SOE) Act and the Pakistan Sovereign Wealth Fund Act, under the regulatory control of the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP), and with one director appointed under the Securities and Exchange Companies Act.

NBP has been classified and declared a strategic state-owned enterprise by the federal government, under the jurisdiction of the Finance Division.

According to the proposal, the NBP president will be appointed, in accordance with Section 18 of the SOE Act, by the federal government, in consultation with the SBP, from among three candidates recommended by the central board of NBP by a three-fourths majority, which shall include the vote of the ex-officio director of the Finance Division.

By adding the condition of a compulsory yes vote by the Finance Division director, the government has undermined the independence of the board in sending three names of its choice to the federal government.

The proposed bill further states that the terms and conditions of the president's appointment will be determined by the board with the approval of the federal government. The president will be appointed for a term of three years on a performance-based contract, extendable by the federal government on demonstration of substantially satisfactory performance.

Wherever conflict arises between the SOE Act and the NBP Act, the SOE Act will take precedence, according to the proposed bill.

The SOE law's sections related to board composition, appointment of the chairman of the board and directors, fit-and-proper criteria, shareholders' responsibility and board meetings will also apply to NBP.

A majority of the board directors will be independent and from the private sector.

A person of eminence and known integrity from the private sector, being a professional banker or a person with relevant financial sector experience, will be appointed by the federal government as chairman. Four independent directors of known integrity and eminence from the private sector will be appointed by the federal government, in consultation with the SBP.

The chairman of the central board shall be appointed by the federal government from among the independent directors, being a person whose name is included in a panel of professional bankers or persons qualified to be chairman, which panel shall be determined, maintained and varied from time to time by the SBP.

The independent directors will be appointed by the federal government on the recommendation of the Board Nominations Committee, according to the proposal.

But the federal government will have the authority to increase or decrease the number of directors of the central board at any time, subject to the independent directors remaining in a majority and the total membership of the central board being not less than six and not more than nine.

No person shall be appointed or elected as, or shall continue to hold the office of, the chairman, a director or the president, if he is not a citizen of Pakistan and is disqualified under Section 11 of the SOE Act, according to the proposal.

A member of the Senate, the National Assembly or a provincial assembly, or an elected member of a local council constituted under any law relating to local councils, cannot be appointed as a director.

The government has proposed that where, and for so long as, the Pakistan Sovereign Wealth Fund established under the Pakistan Sovereign Wealth Fund Act owns or controls the bank, the provisions of the fund act relating to the exercise of ownership rights will also apply to NBP.

However, the SBP's authority would be of paramount importance, and would not be impacted by any laws applicable to NBP.

The proposed bill states that the central board will establish an audit committee whose members shall be financially literate and a majority of whom shall be independent directors. But the chairman of the central board and the president would not be members of the audit committee.

On commencement of the new law, all local boards of the bank, and all local bodies, area boards, regional committees, managing committees and similar bodies for the management of the bank, existing immediately before such commencement, will stand dissolved, and the members of the bodies so dissolved shall cease to hold office as such, without entitlement to any compensation on account of such dissolution or cessation.

headline: SECP acts against non-compliant, dormant firms
description: SECP acts against non-compliant, dormant firms
author: APP
article_text:
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has marked 39,704 companies "Inactive by Registrar" after they failed to file annual returns and/or financial statements for four years.

Marking non-filing companies as inactive would make the corporate register more reliable and help prevent dormant companies from being misused, said a press release issued by the SECP on Saturday.

The inactive status will appear in the SECP's system and be visible to banks and other stakeholders. These companies will not be able to open new bank accounts until they file their overdue documents with the SECP and regain active status. They will also be unable to access financial services or register changes in their directors.

The inactive companies include 13,927 in Lahore, 13,859 in Islamabad, 4,868 in Karachi, 2,031 in Peshawar, 1,861 in Multan, 1,384 in Faisalabad, 1,102 in Gilgit, 436 in Quetta and 236 in Sukkur.

Filing annual returns and financial statements, where required, are a legal requirement under the Companies Act, 2017.

These filings keep public information about companies, their ownership and their management up to date. The SECP said prolonged non-filing could weaken the corporate register and hinder efforts to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing.

The corporate register continues to grow. Pakistan had 317,002 registered companies at the end of September 2026.

The SECP registered 43,559 new companies in the previous financial year, 24% more than the year before. Company name reservation and incorporation are now fully digital, and 99.9% of new companies are registered online.

"A clean and credible registry is the bedrock of trust in the corporate sector. SECP is protecting the integrity of the financial system while giving companies a clear opportunity to return to compliance," SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu said.

ISLAMABAD:

The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has marked 39,704 companies "Inactive by Registrar" after they failed to file annual returns and/or financial statements for four years.

Marking non-filing companies as inactive would make the corporate register more reliable and help prevent dormant companies from being misused, said a press release issued by the SECP on Saturday.

The inactive status will appear in the SECP's system and be visible to banks and other stakeholders. These companies will not be able to open new bank accounts until they file their overdue documents with the SECP and regain active status. They will also be unable to access financial services or register changes in their directors.

The inactive companies include 13,927 in Lahore, 13,859 in Islamabad, 4,868 in Karachi, 2,031 in Peshawar, 1,861 in Multan, 1,384 in Faisalabad, 1,102 in Gilgit, 436 in Quetta and 236 in Sukkur.

Filing annual returns and financial statements, where required, are a legal requirement under the Companies Act, 2017.

These filings keep public information about companies, their ownership and their management up to date. The SECP said prolonged non-filing could weaken the corporate register and hinder efforts to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing.

The corporate register continues to grow. Pakistan had 317,002 registered companies at the end of September 2026.

The SECP registered 43,559 new companies in the previous financial year, 24% more than the year before. Company name reservation and incorporation are now fully digital, and 99.9% of new companies are registered online.

"A clean and credible registry is the bedrock of trust in the corporate sector. SECP is protecting the integrity of the financial system while giving companies a clear opportunity to return to compliance," SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu said.

headline: Pakistan, Saudi discuss early GCC FTA signing
description: Pakistan, Saudi discuss early GCC FTA signing
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have discussed early signing and implementation of the Pakistan-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Free Trade Agreement, with Federal Minister for Commerce Jam Kamal Khan saying it would enhance market access, expand bilateral trade and strengthen economic engagement.

He raised the agreement at a meeting with the newly appointed Saudi Ambassador to Pakistan, Dr Rajeh Albugamy, in Islamabad, according to a statement issued on Saturday.

The minister said Saudi Arabia's economic diversification under its Vision 2030 and Pakistan's production and industrial capabilities offered considerable opportunities for greater economic integration, highlighting the potential for cooperation in scaling up production, improving product quality, adopting modern technologies and strengthening industrial competitiveness.

He noted that collaboration in these areas could enable Pakistani businesses to better meet the requirements of the Saudi market while creating mutually beneficial economic opportunities.

The minister also underscored the importance of expanding Pakistan's export base and strengthening private-sector partnerships to translate the growing economic engagement into tangible trade outcomes.

He said the government had made sustained efforts over the past three years to strengthen bilateral relations through enhanced government-to-government, business-to-business and people-to-people engagement.

The Saudi ambassador reaffirmed the enduring bonds of brotherhood between the two countries and assured continued support for strengthening bilateral economic relations, highlighting opportunities for enhanced regional connectivity and cooperation, particularly in the agriculture sector.

The Saudi ambassador expressed his commitment to maintaining close engagement with the Ministry of Commerce to facilitate greater bilateral economic cooperation and identify new avenues for mutually beneficial partnerships.

Both sides agreed to maintain regular coordination and follow-up engagement to advance bilateral trade, investment and agricultural cooperation, with the stated objective of translating longstanding friendship into stronger economic ties.

The statement said the two sides discussed strengthening bilateral trade, economic cooperation and investment opportunities between the two countries.

headline: PSX sheds 3,560 points in October
description: PSX sheds 3,560 points in October
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The Pakistan Stock Exchange's (PSX) benchmark KSE-100 index declined 2.1%, or 3,560 points, in October to close at 166,409, as geopolitical uncertainty, foreign portfolio outflows and profit-taking in heavyweight stocks weighed on investor sentiment. The market staged a four-day recovery towards the end of the week, gaining more than 4,800 points to reclaim the 167,000 level on Thursday, before profit-taking pulled the index back below the threshold on Friday.

On a day-on-day basis, the market commenced the last trading week of October with a volatile session, but despite that the KSE-100 index gained 664 points (+0.41%) to close at 163,039, reclaiming the 163,000 level. On Tuesday, monetary policy caution and diplomatic optimism caused a balance, helping the bourse surge 1,429 points (+0.88%) to cross the 164,000 mark at 164,467.

On Wednesday, the index extended its recovery, rising 1,269 points (+0.77%) to close at 165,736. PSX continued the positive trend the next day, Thursday, where the benchmark index added 1,457 points (+0.88%) at 167,193, surpassing the 167k level. However, profit-taking dragged it below 167k on Friday after a four-day rally as the index fell 784 points (-0.47%) to settle at 166,409.

Arif Habib Limited (AHL) noted that the KSE-100 index dropped 3,560 points (-2.1%) in Oct'26 to close at 166,409. Persistent geopolitical tensions kept investor sentiment subdued, while oil price movements added to cautious trading. Also, the State Bank increased the policy rate by 50 basis points to 12% at its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting on October 26, citing higher energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty that impacted the domestic inflation outlook.

Earlier, AHL mentioned, Pakistan and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement on the fourth Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and third Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) reviews, paving the way for $1 billion and $210 million in disbursements, respectively, subject to the executive board approval, which would bring total disbursements under both programmes to $5.7 billion.

During the month, the committee reviewing Pakistan's Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-31 proposed reforms to boost exports, accelerate New Energy Vehicle (NEV) adoption and enhance competition. Key measures included lower sales tax on NEVs, reduced import tariffs, mandatory export targets for manufacturers, localisation requirements and incentives for incremental exports.

Treasury bill cut-off yields rose in Oct'26, largely following the SBP's 50-basis-point rate hike. The one-month yield went up from 11.68% to 12.11%, three-month from 11.99% to 12.43%, six-month from 12.45% to 12.65% and 12-month from 12.49% to 12.89%. Additionally, the central bank doubled the minimum capital requirement for banks to Rs20 billion, to be met by Dec'30, with statutory reserves now eligible.

Power generation rose 5% year-on-year to 13,217 gigawatt hours (GWh) in Sept'26, driven by higher hydel, local coal, imported coal and wind generation. The cost of generation soared 32% YoY to Rs9.35 per kilowatt-hour due to a higher share of re-gasified liquefied natural gas, high-speed diesel and furnace oil along with elevated crude prices, prompting distribution companies to seek a positive fuel cost adjustment of Rs2.56/kWh.

Gross Roshan Digital Account (RDA) inflows reached $14.2 billion as of Sept'26. Of these, $2.1 billion was repatriated and $8.9 billion utilised locally, leaving a net liability of $3.1 billion. Meanwhile, the KSE-100 index profitability (based on 96% of the index weight) increased 26% YoY in 9MCY26, reaching Rs1,638 billion. Average trading volumes at the PSX fell 21.8% month-on-month to 471.9 million shares in Oct'26, while average traded value dipped 20.2% to $70.1 million, AHL said. Topline Securities stated that the KSE-100 index declined 2.09% on a MoM basis during October 2026, primarily due to geopolitical uncertainty, foreign portfolio outflows, profit-taking in heavyweight stocks and cautious investor sentiment amid global financial market volatility and domestic macroeconomic concerns.

Major developments during the month included a moderation in Pakistan's CPI inflation to 10.26% in September 2026, compared to 11.15% in August 2026, while remaining above 5.76% recorded in September 2025. Automobile sales declined 12% YoY and 3% MoM to 15,104 units, as reported by the auto manufacturers association. Average daily traded volumes and value during the month stood at 600 million shares (up 27% MoM) and Rs23 billion (up 19% MoM), respectively, Topline added.

The market staged a four-day recovery towards the end of the week, gaining more than 4,800 points to reclaim the 167,000 level on Thursday, before profit-taking pulled the index back below the threshold on Friday.

The market staged a four-day recovery towards the end of the week, gaining more than 4,800 points to reclaim the 167,000 level on Thursday, before profit-taking pulled the index back below the threshold on Friday.

On a day-on-day basis, the market commenced the last trading week of October with a volatile session, but despite that the KSE-100 index gained 664 points (+0.41%) to close at 163,039, reclaiming the 163,000 level. On Tuesday, monetary policy caution and diplomatic optimism caused a balance, helping the bourse surge 1,429 points (+0.88%) to cross the 164,000 mark at 164,467.

On Wednesday, the index extended its recovery, rising 1,269 points (+0.77%) to close at 165,736. PSX continued the positive trend the next day, Thursday, where the benchmark index added 1,457 points (+0.88%) at 167,193, surpassing the 167k level. However, profit-taking dragged it below 167k on Friday after a four-day rally as the index fell 784 points (-0.47%) to settle at 166,409.

Arif Habib Limited (AHL) noted that the KSE-100 index dropped 3,560 points (-2.1%) in Oct'26 to close at 166,409. Persistent geopolitical tensions kept investor sentiment subdued, while oil price movements added to cautious trading. Also, the State Bank increased the policy rate by 50 basis points to 12% at its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting on October 26, citing higher energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty that impacted the domestic inflation outlook.

Earlier, AHL mentioned, Pakistan and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement on the fourth Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and third Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) reviews, paving the way for $1 billion and $210 million in disbursements, respectively, subject to the executive board approval, which would bring total disbursements under both programmes to $5.7 billion.

During the month, the committee reviewing Pakistan's Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-31 proposed reforms to boost exports, accelerate New Energy Vehicle (NEV) adoption and enhance competition. Key measures included lower sales tax on NEVs, reduced import tariffs, mandatory export targets for manufacturers, localisation requirements and incentives for incremental exports.

Treasury bill cut-off yields rose in Oct'26, largely following the SBP's 50-basis-point rate hike. The one-month yield went up from 11.68% to 12.11%, three-month from 11.99% to 12.43%, six-month from 12.45% to 12.65% and 12-month from 12.49% to 12.89%. Additionally, the central bank doubled the minimum capital requirement for banks to Rs20 billion, to be met by Dec'30, with statutory reserves now eligible.

Power generation rose 5% year-on-year to 13,217 gigawatt hours (GWh) in Sept'26, driven by higher hydel, local coal, imported coal and wind generation. The cost of generation soared 32% YoY to Rs9.35 per kilowatt-hour due to a higher share of re-gasified liquefied natural gas, high-speed diesel and furnace oil along with elevated crude prices, prompting distribution companies to seek a positive fuel cost adjustment of Rs2.56/kWh.

Gross Roshan Digital Account (RDA) inflows reached $14.2 billion as of Sept'26. Of these, $2.1 billion was repatriated and $8.9 billion utilised locally, leaving a net liability of $3.1 billion. Meanwhile, the KSE-100 index profitability (based on 96% of the index weight) increased 26% YoY in 9MCY26, reaching Rs1,638 billion. Average trading volumes at the PSX fell 21.8% month-on-month to 471.9 million shares in Oct'26, while average traded value dipped 20.2% to $70.1 million, AHL said. Topline Securities stated that the KSE-100 index declined 2.09% on a MoM basis during October 2026, primarily due to geopolitical uncertainty, foreign portfolio outflows, profit-taking in heavyweight stocks and cautious investor sentiment amid global financial market volatility and domestic macroeconomic concerns.

Major developments during the month included a moderation in Pakistan's CPI inflation to 10.26% in September 2026, compared to 11.15% in August 2026, while remaining above 5.76% recorded in September 2025. Automobile sales declined 12% YoY and 3% MoM to 15,104 units, as reported by the auto manufacturers association. Average daily traded volumes and value during the month stood at 600 million shares (up 27% MoM) and Rs23 billion (up 19% MoM), respectively, Topline added.

headline: WEXNET Quetta aids women enterprises
description: WEXNET Quetta aids women enterprises
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP) launched on Saturday the first edition of Wexnet Quetta, which marked an important milestone in efforts to promote women-led enterprises and strengthen their participation in economic and commercial activities.

The two-day event, Wexnet Quetta 2026 – Women Entrepreneurs Exhibition, was being held in collaboration with the Balochistan Board of Investment & Trade, Women Development Department, Quetta Chamber of Commerce & Industry, Exim Bank, Pakistan Horticulture Development & Export Company, Buitems and other development partners.

The ceremony was formally inaugurated by Dr Rubaba Buledi, Adviser on Women Development, Government of Balochistan, in the presence of senior members of the provincial assembly, government officials, representatives of public and private sector institutions, development partners and women entrepreneurs.

The exhibition, being held on October 31 and November 1, brings together women entrepreneurs from Balochistan and other regions of Pakistan, providing them with a dedicated platform to showcase their products, interact with potential buyers, explore new markets and develop business linkages.

Featuring 100 stalls across diverse product categories, the Wexnet Quetta 2026 highlights the entrepreneurial potential, creativity and commercial capabilities of women-led businesses. The exhibition also provides an opportunity to promote locally manufactured products, encourage business networking and facilitate greater access to domestic and international markets. Through such initiatives, TDAP says it continues to advance its mandate of trade promotion, enterprise development and market access, with a particular focus on creating opportunities for women entrepreneurs, strengthening SMEs and encouraging inclusive economic growth.

headline: CM Maryam rebukes spouse over women jibe
description: CM Maryam rebukes spouse over women jibe
author: ​ Our Correspondents
article_text:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has publicly voiced her dismay over derogatory remarks made by her husband, Captain (retd) Muhammad Safdar, about women advocating for bodily autonomy.

Speaking at a Khatm-e-Nabuwwat rally in Chiniot earlier this week, Safdar took aim at the slogan "mera jism, meri marzi" (my body, my choice).

Maryam responded to a post on X regarding the speech, which stated: "Maryam Nawaz's husband, Captain Safdar, also lost his mother-in-law to cancer, yet here he is mocking women who are battling cancer."

"The silent battles a woman, a wife, fights behind closed doors The strength she must find even when she feels like breaking. Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible," she said.

Meanwhile, lawyers' bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Punjab Chief Minister Maryram Nawaz husband Capt (retd) Muhammad Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018.

During a rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer "cursed".

Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements.

Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action.

"The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation," the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly "deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect".

The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance.

"The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition," he emphasised.

Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar.

"These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community," the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination.

"Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination."

headline: No need to mention FIR in character certificate: IHC
description: No need to mention FIR in character certificate: IHC
author: Fiaz Mahmood
article_text:
The federal capital's high court has ruled that police cannot mention the First Information Report (FIR) filed against a citizen in their character certificate if a court has acquitted that person in that case.

"An FIR in which the applicant has been acquitted by a competent court, and the acquittal has attained finality, shall not be reflected in the police character certificate.

"Citizens so situated ought not to be driven to this court individually in order to secure what the law already confers upon them," said an eight-page order issued by Islamabad High Court (IHC) Justice Ayyaz Shaukat.

The judge was hearing a petition filed by Aniba Arfan, who had moved the IHC after police in her character certificate issued for the purpose of travelling to the United Kingdom mentioned the FIR of a case in which a court had acquitted her nine years ago.

The IHC while allowing the petition noted that a police character certificate listing an FIR terminating in acquittal does precisely what this principle forbids. "It keeps the suspicion alive after the law has laid it to rest. The proposition admits of a fortiori reasoning," it said.

According to the verdict, the Supreme Court has held that the mere pendency of a criminal case cannot, without more, justify restraining a citizen's movement, referring in that context to the view that the mere registration of an FIR is no ground for depriving a citizen of constitutional rights.

"If neither the registration nor the pendency of a criminal case can ordinarily be allowed to prejudice a citizen, then an FIR which has ended in a final acquittal can furnish no ground whatever for an adverse disclosure," it added.

headline: CDA anti-encroachment drive to continue: Talal
description: CDA anti-encroachment drive to continue: Talal
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry on Saturday said the capital's anti-encroachment campaign would continue regardless of political influence.

He also questioned the legality of placing a security cabin and generator outside the Islamabad residence of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, and termed the defence of encroachments "inappropriate".

The remarks came a day after the Capital Development Authority (CDA) issued an encroachment notice for Fazl's residence, identifying illegal constructions and encroachments and directing their removal within 15 days.

The notice came amid an escalating war of words between the government and Fazl, who earlier this week criticised the government's alleged violation of the Constitution. Federal ministers hit back, accusing the JUI-F chief of overlooking his own role in forming and toppling governments.

"There will be no encroachments of any kind, and there will be zero tolerance for this," Chaudhry said during a televised address, adding that the campaign had been running for more than a year and a half. He added that notices had gone out in "every other street" of Islamabad. "Whoever committed any illegal encroachment received one," he said.

Chaudhry noted that a notice was issued "in routine" to Amanullah, the owner of the residence. It was, the minister said, a "completely simple notice" pasted on the house, giving 15 days to remove a four-by-four security cabin.

Chaudhry described the cabin as a "cage-like structure" in which a guard sits in summer and winter, outside a house large enough to park some 10 cars worth millions.

The minister said for the guard inside, "there is no shaded place," calling this a "human matter" but also a legal one. The same applied to the generator, he said, adding that the house was not on a one-or-two-marla plot but stood in one of the capital's large upscale areas where neighbours had received and complied with similar notices.

headline: AJK PM accuses JAAC of Bagh deaths
description: AJK PM accuses JAAC of Bagh deaths
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
.

AJK PM Iftikhar Gillani has expressed his sorrow over the loss of innocent lives in the Pindi area of Bagh district, while also holding the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (Jaac) responsible for the deaths.

In a series of posts on X, Gillani claimed on Saturday that five months of violence by Jaac had inflicted immense suffering on the people of that area, who, he stated, were made hostage to organisation's "terror".

"It was time the proscribed Jaac and associates responsible for targeting civilians and undermining peace must be held accountable. The people deserve peace, security and normalcy," he added.

headline: Locomotive derails near Garhi Shahu railway bridge
description: Locomotive derails near Garhi Shahu railway bridge
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
.

Railway traffic was disrupted after the locomotive of a GKN RMC train derailed near the Garhi Shahu railway bridge, forcing authorities to divert all up and down train services to an alternative loop line.

The train, carrying a load of 18 to 19 wagons, had departed from Garhi Shahu at 5:17am. As it entered Line No 1, the front portion of locomotive DE-4832 went off the track.

A railway crane was called to the site immediately after the derailment and recovery operations were launched to clear the main line. In view of repeated derailments and accidents, Pakistan Railways on Saturday declared an emergency until Dec 31.

headline: Govt collects Rs219.93b in passport fees
description: Govt collects Rs219.93b in passport fees
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The government has collected more than Rs219.93 billion under the head of passport fees over the past five years, as it ruled out any reduction in the fee.

The cost of obtaining a new passport has nearly doubled as the authorities have discontinued machine-readable passports and shifted exclusively to e-passports for new applications nationwide.

The normal fee for a five-year, 36-page passport has risen from Rs4,500 to Rs9,000, while the urgent fee has increased from Rs7,500 to Rs15,000.

The change applies to Lahore and the rest of the country, although machine-readable passports already issued to citizens will remain valid until their expiry dates.

Under the new fee structure, a five-year, 36-page e-passport costs Rs9,000 under normal processing and Rs15,000 under urgent processing.

The supplied report puts the former fast-track fee for a machine-readable passport at Rs12,500 and gives the corresponding e-passport fee as Rs22,000. It says fees for 72-page passports will also increase in the same proportion.

In a written response to a question by Senator Talha Mahmood, the Ministry of Interior said no proposal to lower passport fees was currently under consideration.

It also provided a year-wise breakdown of the revenue collected from passport fees between the 2021-22 and 2025-26 financial years.

According to the ministry, Rs21.618 billion was collected in 2021-22, followed by Rs34.495 billion in 2022-23 and Rs50.906 billion in 2023-24.

The revenue increased to Rs64.392 billion in 2024-25, before standing at Rs48.52 billion in 2025-26. The total amount collected over the five years was Rs219.931 billion, the written response stated.
